arXiv:2003.10320v2 [math.PR] 29 Jul 2022

Random walks on mated-CRT planar maps
and Liouville Brownian motion

Nathanaël Berestycki University of Vienna Ewain Gwynne University of Chicago
Abstract

We prove a scaling limit result for random walk on certain random planar maps with its natural time parametrization. In particular, we show that for γ∈(0,2)\gamma\in(0,2), the random walk on the mated-CRT map with parameter γ\gamma converges to γ\gamma-Liouville Brownian motion, the natural quantum time parametrization of Brownian motion on a γ\gamma-Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) surface. Our result applies if the mated-CRT map is embedded into the plane via the embedding which comes from SLE / LQG theory or via the Tutte embedding (a.k.a. the harmonic or barycentric embedding). In both cases, the convergence is with respect to the local uniform topology on curves and it holds in the quenched sense, i.e., the conditional law of the walk given the map converges.

Previous work by Gwynne, Miller, and Sheffield (2017) showed that the random walk on the mated-CRT map converges to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization. This is the first work to show the convergence of the parametrized walk. As an intermediate result of independent interest, we derive an axiomatic characterisation of Liouville Brownian motion, for which the notion of Revuz measure of a Markov process plays a crucial role.

1 Introduction

1.1 Background

The mathematical study of random walks on random planar maps goes back to the seminal paper of Benjamini and Schramm [BS01]. This paper was motivated by contemporary works by Ambjørn et al. [AAJ+99, ANR+98] which introduced and studied (in a nonrigorous way) a notion of diffusion in the geometry of Liouville quantum gravity. As we will discuss in more detail below (and partly make rigourous in this paper), this diffusion can heuristically be thought of as a continuum limit of random walk on random planar maps. Benjamini and Schramm proved recurrence of any local limit of a sequence of randomly rooted planar graphs, subject to a bounded degree assumption, and initiated a remarkably fruitful program of research aiming to describe properties of random walks on random planar maps, especially random walks on the so-called Uniform Infinite Planar Triangulation (UIPT) as well as other models of random planar maps in the same universality class.

In the years since then, this program of research has blossomed into a very rich and quickly expanding area of probability theory. We will not attempt to give a complete review of this literature here. Instead, we mention a few highlights and refer to [Cur16, GHS19b] as well as the excellent lecture notes by Nachmias [Nac20] for relevant expository articles. The UIPT was constructed by Angel and Schramm in [AS03]. Gurel-Gurevich and Nachmias [GGN13] removed the bounded degree assumption of [BS01] and replaced it by an exponential tail on the degree of the root vertex of the map (in particular applying to the UIPT). The random walk on the UIPT was proved to be subdiffusive by Benjamini and Curien in [BC13] through the consideration of the so-called pioneer points which were analyzed in great detail. More recently, the exact value of the diffusivity exponent on the UIPT (equal to 1/41/4) was obtained through the combination of two works: a paper by Gwynne and Miller [GM21] which proves the lower bound for the diffusivity exponent and also computes the spectral dimension, and a paper by Gwynne and Hutchcroft [GH20] which proves the upper bound for the diffusivity exponent.

Naturally, these developments cannot be dissociated from the remarkable progress in the understanding of the purely geometric features of these random maps, culminating for instance in the convergence of random planar maps (viewed as random metric spaces) to the Brownian map which was proven by Le Gall [Le 13] and Miermont [Mie13], see for instance the survey [LG14].

On the continuum side, the paper by Duplantier and Sheffield [DS11] provided a framework (corresponding to the DDK ansatz [Dav88, DK89]) for building a continuum theory of Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) based on a rigorous construction of the volume form associated with the formal metric tensor

eγ​h​(d​x2+d​y2)e^{\gamma h}\,(dx^{2}+dy^{2}) (1.1)

where hh is a variant of the Gaussian free field on a planar domain, d​x2+d​y2dx^{2}+dy^{2} is the Euclidean metric tensor on that domain, and γ∈(0,2)\gamma\in(0,2) is a constant (which is related to the type of random planar map being considered). In [DS11], the volume for associated with (1.1) is understood as a random measure (in fact, this random measure is a special case of the theory of Gaussian multiplicative chaos, which was initiated in [Kah85]; see [RV11] and [BP] for additional context and a modern approach). A rigorous construction of a continuum diffusion in the geometry associated with (1.1) was proposed in [GRV16, Ber15], for every parameter γ∈(0,2)\gamma\in(0,2). This diffusion, called Liouville Brownian motion (LBM) and described in more details below, is widely conjectured to be the scaling limit of simple random walks on many models of random planar maps. Much is now known about the behaviour of LBM, including a rigorous verification in [RV14b] of the predictions made in [ANR+98] about the spectral dimension; as well as several works considerably refining our understanding of its heat kernel: see, e.g., [GRV14, DZZ19, AK16, Jac18, MRVZ16, BGRV16]. There are also known scaling limit results for discrete approximations of (analogues of) Liouville Brownian motion on tree-like spaces and low-dimensional fractals: see, e.g. [CHK17], which is in the spirit of earlier works on the Bouchaud trap model and its scaling limit to the so-called FIN diffusion in dimension one [FIN02] and to fractional kinetics in higher dimensions [BAČ07].

However, prior to the present paper there were no rigorous results relating the behaviour of simple random walk on natural models of random planar maps to Liouville Brownian motion. The main purpose of this paper is to establish the first such result, in the case of random walk on the so-called mated-CRT random planar maps. These random planar maps are in some sense more directly connected to Liouville quantum gravity than other random planar map models (thanks to the results of [DMS21]) and will be described in more detail below. Interestingly, mated-CRT maps also provide a coarse-grained approximation to many other models of random planar maps (see Remark 1.1). The main result of this paper is that for any parameter γ∈(0,2)\gamma\in(0,2), the scaling limit of simple random walk on the mated-CRT planar map with parameter γ\gamma is Liouville Brownian motion with the same parameter. See Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 for precise statements, including the topology of convergence. Our results build on the earlier work [GMS21], which shows that the random walk on the mated-CRT map converges to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization.

1.2 Setup

Infinite-volume mated-CRT maps.

Mated-CRT maps are a one-parameter family of random planar maps, indexed by γ∈(0,2)\gamma\in(0,2), which were first used implicitly in [DMS21] and studied more explicitly in [GHS19a, GMS21].

We start with a brief description of infinite-volume mated-CRT maps, with the topology of the plane. In this case, the basic data is provided by a pair of correlated real-valued two-sided Brownian motions (Lt,Rt)t∈ℝ(L_{t},R_{t})_{t\in\mathbbm{R}} such that L0=R0=0L_{0}=R_{0}=0 and with correlation coefficient given by −cos⁡(π​γ2/4)-\cos(\pi\gamma^{2}/4), i.e.,

OPENcov⁡(Lt,Rt)=−cos⁡(π​γ24CLOSE)​|t|.\operatorname{cov}(L_{t},R_{t})=-\cos\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\pi\gamma^{2}}{4}}}\right)|t|.

The mated-CRT map is the map obtained by gluing discretized versions of the the (non compact) Continuum Random Trees defined by LL and RR. More precisely, for a given ε>0\varepsilon>0, the mated-CRT map with scale ε\varepsilon is the random graph 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} whose vertex set is 𝒱​𝒢ε=ε​ℤ\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} and where there is an edge between two vertices x,y∈ε​ℤx,y\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} (with x<yx<y) if and only if:

OPENOPEN(inft∈[x−ε,x]XtCLOSE)∨(inft∈[y−ε,y]XtCLOSE)≤inft∈[x,y−ε]Xt\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,x]}X_{t}}}\right)\vee\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\inf_{t\in[y-\varepsilon,y]}X_{t}}}\right)\leq\inf_{t\in[x,y-\varepsilon]}X_{t} (1.2)

where XX can be either LL or RR. Note that in this definition xx is always connected to x+εx+\varepsilon via both LL and RR, but we only include one such edge in this case (let us call such an edge trivial). If y>x+εy>x+\varepsilon it is possible that (1.2) is satisfied for neither, one, or both of LL and RR: in the case when (1.2) is satisfied for both LL and RR there are two edges joining xx and yy. When y>x+εy>x+\varepsilon and (1.2) is satisfied we call the corresponding edge nontrivial. A nontrivial edge can be of two types: type LL or type RR depending on whether (1.2) is satisfied with X=LX=L or X=RX=R. By Brownian scaling, it is clear that the law of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} viewed as a graph does not depend on ε\varepsilon, but for reasons we will explain just below it is convenient to consider the whole family of graphs {𝒢ε}ε>0\{\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0} constructed from the same pair (L,R)(L,R).

Note that the condition (1.2) says that there are times s∈[x−ε,x]s\in[x-\varepsilon,x] and t∈[y−ε,y]t\in[y-\varepsilon,y] such that ss and tt are identified in the equivalence relation used to construct the CRT associated with LL or RR. The definition of the mated-CRT map can therefore indeed be thought of as a gluing of discretized versions of the CRT’s associated to LL and RR.

In order to turn the graph 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} into a (rooted) planar map we first specify the root vertex to be the trivial edge from 00 to ε\varepsilon. In a planar map there is also a notion of counterclockwise cyclical order on the edges surrounding a given vertex. For the mated-CRT map, this ordering is obtained as follows. We order the LL-edges emanating from a given vertex x∈ε​ℤx\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} by giving them the order they inherit from their endpoints on ε​ℤ\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}. We order the RR-edges in the reverse way, and declare that the LL-edges come before the RR-edges. The LL-edges and the RR-edges are separated by the two trivial edges emanating from xx. With this order, it is easy to see why a proper planar embedding of this graph exists (i.e., an embedding in which the edges do not overlap). Simply draw the RR-edges on one side of ε​ℤ\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} in the plane and the LL-edges on the other, and observe that the RR-edges (and equivalently the LL-edges) can be drawn without overlapping: if s1<s2s_{1}<s_{2} and t1<t2t_{1}<t_{2} are identified in RR, then either s1<s2<t1<t2s_{1}<s_{2}<t_{1}<t_{2} or s1<t1<t2<t2s_{1}<t_{1}<t_{2}<t_{2}. See Figure 1 for an illustration. We note that with this planar map structure, the mated-CRT map is in fact a triangulation; see the caption of [GMS19, Figure 1] for an explanation.

Remark 1.1 (Connection to other random planar map models).

The above construction of the mated-CRT map is motivated by a class of combinatorial bijections called mating of trees bijections. Basically, such bijections tell us that certain natural random planar maps decorated by statistical mechanics models can be constructed via discrete analogs of the above construction of the mated-CRT map, with the two coordinates of a random walk on ℤ2\mathbbm{Z}^{2} (with an increment distribution depending on the map) used in place of (L,R)(L,R). Examples of planar maps which can be encoded in this way include uniform triangulations decorated by site percolation configurations [Ber07a, BHS18] as well as planar maps decorated by spanning trees [Mul67, Ber07b], the critical Fortuin-Kasteleyn cluster model [DS11, Ber07b], or bipolar orientations [KMSW19]. Due to the convergence of random walk to Brownian motion, the mated-CRT map can be viewed as a coarse-grained approximation of these other random planar maps. This coarse-graining can sometimes be used to transfer results from the mated-CRT map to other random planar maps, as is done, e.g., in [GHS20, GM21, GH20]. Currently, however, the estimates comparing mated-CRT maps to other maps are not sufficiently precise to transfer scaling limit results like the one proven in this paper.

Finite volume mated-CRT maps.

Mated-CRT planar maps can also be defined in finite volume with other topologies such as the disk. In this version, LL and RR are two correlated Brownian motions over the time-interval [0,1][0,1] (instead of the entire real line ℝ\mathbbm{R}), start from L0=R0=0L_{0}=R_{0}=0 and are conditioned so that (Lt,Rt)0≤t≤1(L_{t},R_{t})_{0\leq t\leq 1} remains in the positive quadrant [0,∞)2[0,\infty)^{2} until time 1 and ends up in the position (1,0)(1,0) at time one. (This is a degenerate conditioning; see [MS19] for a construction, building on the cone excursions studied by Shimura in [Shi85].) We call such a pair a Brownian excursion in the quadrant. The vertex set of the mated-CRT map with the disk topology is then taken to be 𝒱​𝒢ε=ε​ℤ∩[0,1]\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\cap[0,1] instead of ε​ℤ\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}, but apart from that the definitions above stay the same.

Note that the tree encoded by RR is a standard (compact) Continuum Random Tree, whereas the one encoded by LL also comes with a natural boundary. More precisely, we define boundary vertices ∂𝒢ε\partial\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} as the set of vertices x∈ε​ℤ∩[0,1]x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\cap[0,1] such that

inft∈[x−ε,x]Lt≤inft∈[x,1]Lt.\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,x]}L_{t}\leq\inf_{t\in[x,1]}L_{t}. (1.3)

See Figure 2 for an illustration.

Tutte embedding.

The advantage of working in the finite volume setup discussed above (as opposed to say the earlier whole plane setup) is that the Tutte embedding can be defined in a straightforward way. The Tutte embedding of a graph is a planar embedding which has the property that each interior vertex (i.e., a vertex not on the boundary) is equal to the average of its neighbours. Equivalently, the simple random walk on the graph is a martingale. A concrete construction in the case of a finite volume mated-CRT map is as follows. We first choose a marked root vertex of the mated-CRT map by sampling 𝕥\mathbbm{t} uniformly from [0,1][0,1] and letting 𝕩ε∈(ε​ℤ)∩[0,1]\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon}\in(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})\cap[0,1] be chosen so that 𝕥∈[𝕩ε−ε,𝕩ε]\mathbbm{t}\in[\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon,\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon}]. Let x1<…<xkx_{1}<\ldots<x_{k} denote the vertices of the boundary ∂𝒢ε\partial\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, in numerical order. Let 𝔭⁡(xk)\mathfrak{p}(x_{k}) denote the probability that simple random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, started from 𝕩ε\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon}, first hits ∂𝒢ε\partial\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} in the arc {x1,…,xk}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\}. Then the boundary vertices x1,…,xkx_{1},\ldots,x_{k} are mapped (counterclockwise) respectively to z1=e2​i​π​𝔭​(x1),…,zk=e2​i​π​𝔭​(xk)z_{1}=e^{2i\pi\mathfrak{p}(x_{1})},\ldots,z_{k}=e^{2i\pi\mathfrak{p}(x_{k})}. This makes it so that the harmonic measure from 𝕩ε\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon} approximates Lebesgue measure on ∂𝔻\partial\mathbbm{D}. As for the interior vertices, if x∈𝒱​𝒢εx\in\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}, let ψε:𝒱​𝒢ε→ℂ\psi^{\varepsilon}:\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}\to\mathbbm{C} denote the unique function which is discrete harmonic on 𝒱​𝒢ε∖∂𝒢ε\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\partial\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} and whose boundary values are given by ψε​(xi)=zi\psi^{\varepsilon}(x_{i})=z_{i}. This gives an embedding of the vertices of the graph (into the unit disk 𝔻\mathbbm{D}, by an argument similar to the maximum principle). A theorem of Tutte [Tut63] then guarantees that if the edges of the graph are drawn as straight lines then the edges can overlap but not cross.

SLE/LQG embedding.

One of the reasons the mated-CRT maps (either in finite or infinite volume) are convenient is that, due to the main result of [DMS21], they admit an elegant alternative description given by a certain type of γ\gamma-LQG surface (represented by a random distribution hh in a portion D⊂ℂD\subset\mathbbm{C} of the complex plane), decorated by an independent space-filling version of a Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) curve η\eta with parameter κ=16/γ2∈(4,∞)\kappa=16/\gamma^{2}\in(4,\infty). The notion of LQG surfaces will be described in greater details in Section 2.2, but let us nevertheless describe the embedding as succinctly as possibly, deferring the definitions to that section. See Figure 3 for an illustration.

We start with the infinite volume case, which is slightly easier to explain. In that case, D=ℂD=\mathbbm{C} and hh is the random distribution corresponding to a so-called γ\gamma-quantum cone. Since the law of hh is locally absolutely continuous with respect to that of a Gaussian free field one can define a volume measure μh\mu_{h} which is a version of the LQG measure (or Gaussian multiplicative chaos) associated to hh. One way to define this measure is as follows. For z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, let hε​(z)h_{\varepsilon}(z) be the average of hh over the circle of radius ε\varepsilon centered at zz. Then for any open set A⊂ℂA\subset\mathbbm{C},

μh​(A)=limε→0∫Aεγ2/2​eγ​hε​(z)​𝑑z\mu_{h}(A)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{A}\varepsilon^{\gamma^{2}/2}e^{\gamma h_{\varepsilon}(z)}dz (1.4)

in probability (see, e.g., [DS11, Ber17]). In fact the convergence was shown to be a.s. in [SW16].

The curve η\eta mentioned above is in the whole-plane case a whole-plane space-filling SLEκ from ∞\infty to ∞\infty, sampled independently from hh. When κ≥8\kappa\geq 8, i.e. when γ≤2\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}, whole-plane SLEκ is already space-filling and η\eta is then nothing but an ordinary whole-plane SLE from ∞\infty to ∞\infty. However, when κ∈(4,8)\kappa\in(4,8) ordinary SLE is not space-filling and the construction is more complicated, see [MS17, Section 1.2.3] and Section 2.2.2. This choice of (h,η)(h,\eta) corresponds to the setting of the whole-plane mating of trees theorem [DMS21, Theorem 1.9].

Let us now describe the disk case, which is slightly more involved. In this case, D=𝔻D=\mathbbm{D} is the unit disk and hh is the random distribution corresponding to a type of quantum surface known as a quantum disk with unit area and unit boundary length. Such a surface does not normally come with a specified marked point either on the boundary or in the bulk, but we add a marked point on the boundary by sampling from the boundary length measure (the appropriate analogue of (1.4) restricted to the boundary).

The curve η\eta is a space-filling SLEκ loop from the marked boundary point to itself (with loops being filled in clockwise). Such a curve is obtained as the limit of a chordal space-filling SLEκ between two boundary points xx and yy, as y→xy\to x; see Section 2.2.2 for more details. This setup corresponds essentially to the (finite volume) mating of trees theorem proved by Ang and Gwynne [AG21, Theorem 1.1], with two unessential differences: one is that the loops of η\eta are filled counterclockwise in [AG21] (corresponding to the Brownian pair (L,R)(L,R) ending on the RR axis instead of the LL axis as is the case here). The second is that the paper [AG21] describes the situation corresponding to unit boundary length (but random area). The corresponding mating of trees theorem for the case we need here is naturally obtained by conditioning on the total area, whose law is described in [AG21, Theorem 1.2].

In both setups, since the curve η\eta is space-filling, it can be reparametrized by μh\mu_{h}-area: in any time interval of length tt, the curve covers an area of mass tt. The LQG embedding of mated-CRT planar maps is then as follows. Each vertex x∈𝒱​𝒢εx\in\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon} corresponds to a cell η⁡([x−ε,x])\eta([x-\varepsilon,x]) with appropriate modifications for the last cell if ε\varepsilon is not of the form 1/n1/n for some n≥1n\geq 1. Two cells are declared adjacent if their intersection is nonempty and contains a nontrivial curve11 1 When κ≥8\kappa\geq 8, this second condition is in fact not necessary. On the other hand, when κ∈(4,8)\kappa\in(4,8), an SLEκ curve is self-touching, resulting in pinch points for the cells formed by the space-filling curve. On either side of such a pinch point could be two different cells, but our definition ensures that these are nevertheless not declared adjacent, even though they intersect at the pinch point.. It is not hard to see via the mating of trees theorems mentioned earlier (Theorem 1.9 in [DMS21] and Theorem 1.1 in [AG21]) that this gives an alternative and equivalent construction of the mated-CRT planar maps in the respective setups. Concretely, this gives an a priori embedding of the mated-CRT planar map into the domain DD (either the whole plane or the disk) obtained by sending each vertex xx to a point of the corresponding cell.

This embedding is extremely useful to carry out concrete computations on the mated-CRT planar maps. Furthermore, it is closely related to the Tutte embedding: indeed, one of the main results of [GMS21] implies that the Tutte embedding converges uniformly to the SLE embedding. More precisely, if ψε\psi^{\varepsilon} denotes the Tutte embedding of the mated-CRT map with the disk topology, as above, then

maxx∈𝒱​𝒢ε⁡|ψε​(x)−η⁡(x)|→0\max_{x\in\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}}|\psi^{\varepsilon}(x)-\eta(x)|\to 0 (1.5)

in probability; see (3.3) in Section 3.4 of [GMS21].

Convergence of the random walk modulo time parametrization.

Most of the work in [GMS21] goes into proving that that the random walk on the mated-CRT map converges to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization under the LQG embedding discussed above. More precisely, it is shown in [GMS21, Theorem 3.4] that for each compact set K⊂ℂK\subset\mathbbm{C}, the Prokhorov distance between the following two probability measures converges to zero in probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, uniformly over all z∈Kz\in K:

  • •

    The law of standard planar Brownian motion started from zz, viewed modulo time parametrization;

  • •

    The conditional law given (h,η)(h,\eta) of the random walk on the mated-CRT map under the LQG embedding with cell size ε\varepsilon, started from the (a.s. unique) vertex x∈𝒱​𝒢εx\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} such that z∈η⁡([x−ε,x])z\in\eta([x-\varepsilon,x]), extended to be a continuous curve by piecewise linear interpolation, and viewed modulo time parametrization.

See [GMS21, Section 2.1.2] for a discussion of the topology on curves modulo time parametrization. The proof of the above convergence result is based on a general scaling limit result for random walks in planar random environments which are in some sense “translation invariant modulo scaling” [GMS18, Theorem 3.10].

Due to the relationship between random walk and discrete harmonic functions, the convergence of random walk on the mated-CRT map to Brownian motion implies that, under the LQG embedding, discrete harmonic functions on the mated-CRT map approximate their continuum counterparts when ε\varepsilon is small. This, in turn, allows one to show that the Tutte embedding is close to the LQG embedding, in the sense of (1.5).

This paper will build on the result of [GMS21] to get convergence of the parametrized walk on the mated-CRT map. Let us now discuss the limiting object.

Liouville Brownian motion.

Let hh be either field considered in the preceding section, i.e., a γ\gamma-quantum cone with circle average embedding or a unit quantum disk. Along with an area measure μh\mu_{h} on DD, it is possible to associate to the field hh a diffusion XX, called Liouville Brownian motion. We give a few more details now. Let z∈Dz\in D, let BzB^{z} denote a standard planar Brownian motion in DD started from zz and let τ\tau denote its exit time from DD. By definition22 2 In fact, the works [Ber15, GRV16] focus on slightly different versions of the field hh where instead of a γ\gamma-quantum cone or quantum disk, hh is a Dirichlet GFF. The finiteness of this last integral can be checked by splitting the disk into dyadic annuli and considering the contribution of each annulus. τ1/2=inf{t>0:|Bϕ−1​(t)|≥1/2},\tau_{1/2}=\inf\{t>0:|B_{\phi^{-1}(t)}|\geq 1/2\},

Xtz=Bϕ−1​(t​m0)z.X^{z}_{t}=B^{z}_{\phi^{-1}(tm_{0})}. (1.6)

1.3 Main results

Our main result will come in two versions, corresponding respectively to the whole plane and disk setups. We start with the whole-plane case. In this case, we work only with the SLE/LQG embedding since the Tutte embedding is harder to define if we do not have a boundary. Let (h,η)(h,\eta) denote the γ\gamma-quantum cone decorated by an independent space-filling SLE describing the SLE/LQG embedding of the whole plane mated-CRT planar maps (𝒢ε)ε>0(\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon>0} with parameter γ\gamma, as described above. We assume that hh is the circle-average embedding of the γ\gamma-quantum cone.

For z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, let Xz,ε:ℕ0→𝒱​𝒢εX^{z,\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{N}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} be the simple random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} started from xx, where x∈𝒱​𝒢ε=ε​ℤx\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} is chosen so that zz belongs to the cell η⁡([x−ε,x])\eta([x-\varepsilon,x]) (there is a.s. a unique such xx for each fixed z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}; for the atypical points for which there are multiple possibilities, we arbitrarily choose the smallest possible value of xx). We extend the domain of definition of the embedded walk ℕ0∋j↦η⁡(Xjz,ε)\mathbbm{N}_{0}\ni j\mapsto\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{j}) from ℕ0\mathbbm{N}_{0} to [0,∞)[0,\infty) by piecewise linear interpolation. Also let

OPENmε:=(median exit time of η⁡(X0,ε) from B1/2CLOSE)m_{\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{median exit time of $\eta(X^{0,\varepsilon})$ from $B_{1/2}$}}}\right) (1.7)

where B1/2B_{1/2} is the Euclidean ball of radius 1/21/2 centered at 0. Note that this is an annealed median, i.e., we are not conditioning on (h,η)(h,\eta) and so mεm_{\varepsilon} is deterministic. In this whole plane setup, our main result is the following theorem.

Theorem 1.2.

For each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, the conditional law of the embedded, linearly interpolated walk (η⁡(Xmε​tz,ε))t≥0(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t}))_{t\geq 0} given (Lt,Rt)t∈ℝ(L_{t},R_{t})_{t\in\mathbbm{R}} (equivalently, given (h,η)(h,\eta)) converges in probability to the rescaled law of γ\gamma-Liouville Brownian motion started from zz associated with hh, defined in (1.6), with respect to the Prokhorov topology induced by the local uniform metric on curves [0,∞)→ℂ[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}. In fact, the convergence occurs uniformly over all points zz in any compact subset of ℂ\mathbbm{C}.

Remark 1.3.

Our proof shows that there is a constant C>1C>1 depending only on γ\gamma such that the time scaling constants mεm_{\varepsilon} of (1.7) satisfy

C−1​ε−1≤mε≤C​ε−1,for all sufficiently small ε>0.C^{-1}\varepsilon^{-1}\leq m_{\varepsilon}\leq C\varepsilon^{-1},\quad\text{for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$.} (1.8)

We do not know that ε​mε\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon} converges, so we do not get convergence in Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 when we scale time by 1/ε1/\varepsilon instead of by mεm_{\varepsilon}. See, however, Section 1.4.

We now give our theorem statement in the disk case. The theorem is similar to the whole-plane case except that we state it for the more intrinsic Tutte embedding (rather than the a priori LQG embedding, although the result is also valid for this latter embedding). Let (h,η)(h,\eta) denote the quantum disk decorated by an independent space-filling SLE describing the SLE/LQG embedding of the mated-CRT maps (𝒢ε)ε>0(\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon>0} with the disk topology and parameter γ\gamma, as described above. We assume that the marked point for hh (equivalently, the starting point for η\eta) is 1. Let ψε:𝒱​𝒢ε→ℂ\psi^{\varepsilon}:\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}\to\mathbbm{C} be the Tutte embedding of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, as defined in Section 1.2. For z∈𝔻z\in\mathbbm{D} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, let Xz,ε:ℕ0→𝒱​𝒢εX^{z,\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{N}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} be the simple random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} started from xx, where x=x⁡(z,ε)∈𝒱​𝒢ε=ε​ℤ∩[0,1]x=x(z,\varepsilon)\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\cap[0,1] is chosen to be a vertex such that zz is closest to ψε​(x)\psi^{\varepsilon}(x). In case of ties, pick xx arbitrarily among the possible choices. We extend the domain of definition of the embedded walk ℕ0∋j↦ψ⁡(Xjz,ε)\mathbbm{N}_{0}\ni j\mapsto\psi(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{j}) from ℕ0\mathbbm{N}_{0} to [0,∞)[0,\infty) by piecewise linear interpolation. Let mεm_{\varepsilon} be as in (1.7) (note that we define mεm_{\varepsilon} in terms of the whole-plane mated-CRT map in both the whole-plane and disk settings).

Theorem 1.4.

For each z∈𝔻z\in\mathbbm{D}, consider the conditional law of the embedded, linearly interpolated walk (ψε​(Xmε​tz,ε))t≥0(\psi^{\varepsilon}(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t}))_{t\geq 0}, given (Lt,Rt)t∈[0,1](L_{t},R_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} (equivalently, given (h,η)(h,\eta)). As ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, these laws converge in probability to the rescaled law of γ\gamma-Liouville Brownian motion started from zz associated with hh, defined in (1.6), stopped upon leaving the unit disk 𝔻\mathbbm{D}, with respect to the Prokhorov topology induced by the local uniform metric on curves [0,∞)→ℂ[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}. In fact, the convergence occurs uniformly over all points zz in any compact subset of 𝔻¯∖{1}\overline{\mathbbm{D}}\setminus\{1\}.

Due to (1.5), Theorem 1.4 is equivalent to the analogous statement with the SLE/LQG embedding in place of the Tutte embedding. Note that we only claim uniform convergence on compact subsets of 𝔻¯∖{1}\overline{\mathbbm{D}}\setminus\{1\} in Theorem 1.4, not uniform convergence on all of 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbbm{D}}. We know that the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} converges to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization uniformly over all starting points in 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbbm{D}} [GMS21, Theorem 3.4] (in the quenched sense). We expect that the result of Theorem 1.4 also holds uniformly over all z∈𝔻¯z\in\overline{\mathbbm{D}}, but in order to prove this one would need some arguments to prevent the walk started near the marked point 11 from getting “stuck” and staying in a small neighborhood of 11 for an unusually long time without hitting ∂𝔻\partial\mathbbm{D}.

As we explain below, our proof of Theorem 1.2 relies on the one hand on proving a tightness result for the conditional law of {η⁡(Xmε​tz,ε)}t≥0\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t})\}_{t\geq 0} given (h,η)(h,\eta), and on the other hand on a characterization statement for the subsequential limits, which is stated below as Theorem 1.5. Our proof of convergence to Liouville Brownian motion is restricted to mated-CRT maps and does not apply in full to other natural models of random planar maps such as the UIPT. Nevertheless, several aspects of our proof might be useful in this more general setting. In particular, the following characterization of Liouville Brownian motion is of independent interest and may be useful for identifying (subsequential) limits of random walk on other models of conformally embedded random planar maps. We state this result somewhat informally, deferring the actual necessary definitions and full statement to Section 7 and in particular Proposition 7.10.

Theorem 1.5.

Let hh be the random distribution associated with the circle average embedding of a γ\gamma-quantum cone. Suppose that we are given a coupling of hh and a random continuous function P={Pz:z∈ℂ}P=\{P_{z}:z\in\mathbbm{C}\} which takes each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} to a (random) element PzP_{z} of the space Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})) of probability measures on random continuous paths in ℂ\mathbbm{C} started from zz. Suppose that the following conditions hold:

  • •

    Conditional on (h,P)(h,P), a.s. for each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} the process with the law PzP_{z} is Markovian;

  • •

    For each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, PzP_{z} has the law of a (random) time-change of a standard Brownian motion starting from zz;

  • •

    PP leaves the Liouville measure μ=μh\mu=\mu_{h} associated to hh invariant.

Then there is a (possibly random) constant cc such that for each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, PzP_{z} coincides with the law of (Xc​tz,t≥0)(X^{z}_{ct},t\geq 0), where XzX^{z} is a Liouville Brownian motion associated with hh, starting from zz.

1.4 Outline

Most of the paper is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.2. See Section 7.4 for an explanation of how one deduces Theorem 1.4 from Theorem 1.2 using (1.5) and a local absolute continuity argument. It is shown in [GMS21, Theorem 3.4] that, in the setting of Theorem 1.2, the conditional law of {η⁡(Xmε​tz,ε)}t≥0\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t})\}_{t\geq 0} given (h,η)(h,\eta) converges in probability to the law of Brownian motion started from zz with respect to the Prokhorov topology induced by the metric on curves in ℂ\mathbbm{C} modulo time parametrization. It is also shown there that the convergence is uniform over zz in any compact subset of ℂ\mathbbm{C}. We need to show that the walk in fact converges uniformly to γ\gamma-LBM.

Most of the work in the proof goes into proving an appropriate tightness result, which says that the conditional law of {η⁡(Xmε​tz,ε)}t≥0\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t})\}_{t\geq 0} given (h,η)(h,\eta) admits subsequential limits as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 (Proposition 6.1). This is done in Sections 3 through 6 and requires us to establish many new estimates for the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, building on the results of [GMS21, GMS19]. The identification of the subsequential limit, summarized in Theorem 1.5, is carried out in Section 7. A crucial role is played in particular by the notion of Revuz measure associated to a Positive Additive Continuous Functional (PCAF) for general Markov processes.

Before outlining the proof, we make some general comments about our arguments.

  • •

    Only a few main results from each section (usually stated at the beginning of the section) are used in subsequent sections. So, the different sections can to a great extent be read independently of each other.

  • •

    Our proofs give quantitative estimates for random walk on the mated-CRT map which are stronger than what is strictly necessary to prove convergence to Liouville Brownian motion. Such estimates include up-to-constants bounds for exit times from Euclidean balls (Propositions 4.1 and 5.1), bounds for the Green’s function (Lemmas 4.4, 5.4, and 5.6), and modulus of continuity estimates for random walk paths (Proposition 6.5) and for the law of the walk as a function of its starting point (Proposition 6.12).

  • •

    For most of the proof of Theorem 1.2, we will scale time by 1/ε1/\varepsilon instead of by mεm_{\varepsilon}, i.e., we will work with (η⁡(Xt/εz,ε))t≥0(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon}))_{t\geq 0}. We switch to scaling time by mεm_{\varepsilon} at the very end of the proof, in Section 7.3, for reasons which will be explained at the end of this outline.

In order to establish tightness of (η⁡(Xt/εz,ε))t≥0(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon}))_{t\geq 0}, we need up-to-constants estimates for the conditional law given (h,η)(h,\eta) of the exit time of the (embedded) random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} from a Euclidean ball. Moreover, these estimates need to hold uniformly over all Euclidean balls contained in any given compact subset of ℂ\mathbbm{C}. Moments of exit times from Euclidean balls can be expressed as sums involving the discrete Green’s function for random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} stopped upon exiting the ball. Hence we need to prove up-to-constants estimates for the discrete Green’s function.

The results of [GMS19] allow us to bound the discrete Dirichlet energies of discrete harmonic functions on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, which leads to bounds for effective resistances (equivalently, for the values of the discrete Green’s function on the diagonal). The main task in the proof of tightness is to transfer from these estimates to bounds for the behavior of the Green’s function off the diagonal. Section 3 contains the two key estimates which allow us to do this.

  • •

    Lemma 3.4 says that for any finite graph GG and any vertex sets A⊂B⊂𝒱⁡(G)A\subset B\subset\mathcal{V}(G), the following is true. The maximum (resp. minimum) value on the boundary ∂A\partial A of the Green’s function for random walk killed upon exiting BB is bounded below (resp. above) by the effective resistance from AA to BB.

  • •

    Proposition 3.8 is a Harnack-type inequality which says that the maximum and minimum values of the discrete Green’s function on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} on the boundary of a Euclidean ball differ by at most a constant factor.

Combined, these two estimates reduce the problem of estimating the Green’s function to the problem of estimating effective resistances, which we can do (with a non-trivial amount of work) using tools from [GMS19].

In Sections 4 and 5, we use the ideas discussed above to establish a lower (resp. upper) bound for the Green’s function, which in turn leads lower (resp. upper) bounds for the exit times of the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} from Euclidean balls. In Section 6, we use these estimates to establish the tightness of the conditional law of {η⁡(Xt/εz,ε)}t≥0\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon})\}_{t\geq 0} given (h,η)(h,\eta). The arguments involved in these steps are non-trivial, but we do not outline them here; see the beginnings of the individual sections and subsections for outlines.

In Section 7, we show that the subsequential limit must be LBM as follows. Since we already know the convergence of the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization, every subsequential limit of the conditional law of {η⁡(Xt/εz,ε)}t≥0\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon})\}_{t\geq 0} given (h,η)(h,\eta) is a probability measure on curves X^z\widehat{X}^{z} in ℂ\mathbbm{C} which are time-changed Brownian motions, with a continuous time change function. Our estimates show that the time change function is in fact strictly increasing. Furthermore, it can be checked using the Markov property for random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} that X^z\widehat{X}^{z} is Markovian (Lemma 7.4). Finally, since the counting measure on vertices of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} weighted by their degree is reversible for the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, it is easily seen that the γ\gamma-LQG measure μh\mu_{h} is invariant (in fact, reversible) for X^z\widehat{X}^{z}.

The properties of the subsequential limit process described in the preceding paragraph are all also known to hold for Liouville Brownian motion [GRV16, GRV14, Ber15]. It turns out that these properties are in fact sufficient to uniquely characterize LBM up to a time change of the form t↦c​tt\mapsto ct for a deterministic c>0c>0 which does not depend on the starting point. This is a consequence of a general proposition (Proposition 7.10, which is a generalization of Theorem 1.5), which says that two Markovian time changed Brownian motions with a common invariant measure agree in law modulo such a time change. In our setting, the two Markovian time changed Brownian motions are the subsequential limit process and the LBM and the common invariant measure is the LQG measure.

As explained in Section 7.2, Proposition 7.10 is a (in our view surprisingly simple) consequence of known results in general Markov process theory. In particular, the time change function for a time changed Brownian motion is a positive continuous additive functionals (PCAF) of the Brownian motion with the standard parametrization. The Revuz measure associated with the PCAF is an invariant measure for the time changed Brownian motion, and is in fact the unique such invariant measure up to multiplication by a deterministic constant. Since the Revuz measure uniquely determines the PCAF, this shows that two different time changed Brownian motions with the same invariant measure must agree in law modulo a linear time change, as required.

The above argument shows that for any sequence of positive ε\varepsilon’s tending to zero, there is a subsequence ℰ\mathcal{E} and a deterministic33 3 We are glossing over a technicality here — as explained in Section 7.3, some argument is needed to show that the constant cc is deterministic rather than just a random variable which is determined by (h,η)(h,\eta) and the limiting law on random paths. constant c>0c>0 which may depend on ℰ\mathcal{E} along which {η⁡(Xt/εz,ε)}t≥0\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon})\}_{t\geq 0} converges in law to LBM started from zz pre-composed with the linear time change t↦c​tt\mapsto ct (in the quenched sense). This does not yet give Theorem 1.2 since cc can depend on the subsequence. To get around this, we need to scale time by mεm_{\varepsilon} instead of by 1/ε1/\varepsilon. Indeed, by the definition (1.7), the median exit time of the process {η⁡(Xmε​tz,ε)}t≥0\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t})\}_{t\geq 0} from B1/2B_{1/2} is equal to 1, so all of the possible subsequential limits of the laws of this process must be LBM with the same linear time change.

Appendix A contains some basic estimates for the γ\gamma-LQG measure and for space-filling SLE cells which are used in our proofs. The proofs in this appendix are routine and do not use any of the other results in the paper, so are collected here to avoid distracting from the main ideas of the argument.

2.1 Basic notation

We write ℕ={1,2,3,…}\mathbbm{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\} and ℕ0=ℕ∪{0}\mathbbm{N}_{0}=\mathbbm{N}\cup\{0\}.

For a<ba<b, we define the discrete interval [a,b]ℤ:=[a,b]∩ℤ[a,b]_{\mathbbm{Z}}:=[a,b]\cap\mathbbm{Z}.

For a graph GG, we write 𝒱⁡(G)\mathcal{V}(G) and ℰ⁡(G)\mathcal{E}(G) for its vertex and edge sets, respectively.

For z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and r>0r>0, we write Br​(z)B_{r}(z) for the Euclidean ball of radius rr centered at zz. We abbreviate Br=Br​(0)B_{r}=B_{r}(0).

If f:(0,∞)→ℝf:(0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{R} and g:(0,∞)→(0,∞)g:(0,\infty)\rightarrow(0,\infty), we say that f⁡(ε)=Oε​(g⁡(ε))f(\varepsilon)=O_{\varepsilon}(g(\varepsilon)) (resp. f⁡(ε)=oε​(g⁡(ε))f(\varepsilon)=o_{\varepsilon}(g(\varepsilon))) as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 if f⁡(ε)/g⁡(ε)f(\varepsilon)/g(\varepsilon) remains bounded (resp. tends to zero) as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. We similarly define O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) and o⁡(⋅)o(\cdot) errors as a parameter goes to infinity.

If f,g:(0,∞)→[0,∞)f,g:(0,\infty)\rightarrow[0,\infty), we say that f⁡(ε)⪯g⁡(ε)f(\varepsilon)\preceq g(\varepsilon) if there is a constant C>0C>0 (independent from ε\varepsilon and possibly from other parameters of interest) such that f⁡(ε)≤C​g​(ε)f(\varepsilon)\leq Cg(\varepsilon). We write f⁡(ε)≍g⁡(ε)f(\varepsilon)\asymp g(\varepsilon) if f⁡(ε)⪯g⁡(ε)f(\varepsilon)\preceq g(\varepsilon) and g⁡(ε)⪯f⁡(ε)g(\varepsilon)\preceq f(\varepsilon).

Let {Eε}ε>0\{E^{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0} be a one-parameter family of events. We say that EεE^{\varepsilon} occurs with

  • •

    polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 if there is a p>0p>0 (independent from ε\varepsilon and possibly from other parameters of interest) such that ℙ⁡[Eε]≥1−Oε​(εp)\mathbbm{P}[E^{\varepsilon}]\geq 1-O_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon^{p}).

  • •

    superpolynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 if ℙ⁡[Eε]≥1−Oε​(εp)\mathbbm{P}[E^{\varepsilon}]\geq 1-O_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon^{p}) for every p>0p>0.

We will often specify any requirements on the dependencies on rates of convergence in O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) and o⁡(⋅)o(\cdot) errors, implicit constants in ⪯\preceq, etc., in the statements of lemmas/propositions/theorems, in which case we implicitly require that errors, implicit constants, etc., appearing in the proof satisfy the same dependencies.

2.2 Background on Liouville quantum gravity and SLE

Throughout this paper we fix the LQG parameter γ∈(0,2)\gamma\in(0,2) and the corresponding SLE parameter κ=16/γ2>4\kappa=16/\gamma^{2}>4.

2.2.1 Liouville quantum gravity

We will give some relatively brief background on LQG. We will in particular focus on quantum cones (which are the main types of quantum surfaces considered in this paper) and also briefly discuss quantum disks. The following definition is taken from [DS11, She16, DMS21].

Definition 2.1.

A γ\gamma-Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) surface is an equivalence class of pairs (D,h)(D,h), where D⊂ℂD\subset\mathbbm{C} is an open set and hh is a distribution on DD (which will always be taken to be a realization of a random distribution which locally looks like the Gaussian free field), with two such pairs (D,h)(D,h) and (D~,h~)(\widetilde{D},\widetilde{h}) declared to be equivalent if there is a conformal map f:D~→Df:\widetilde{D}\rightarrow D such that

h~=h∘f+Q​log⁡|f′|forQ=2γ+γ2.\widetilde{h}=h\circ f+Q\log|f^{\prime}|\quad\text{for}\quad Q=\frac{2}{\gamma}+\frac{\gamma}{2}. (2.1)

More generally, for k∈ℕk\in\mathbbm{N} a γ\gamma-LQG surface with kk marked points is an equivalence class of k+2k+2-tuples (D,h,x1,…,xk)(D,h,x_{1},\dots,x_{k}) where x1,…,xk∈D∪∂Dx_{1},\dots,x_{k}\in D\cup\partial D, with the equivalence relation defined as in (2.1) except that the map ff is required to map the marked points of one surface to the corresponding marked points of the other.

We think of different elements of the same equivalence class in Definition 2.1 as representing different parametrizations of the same surface. If (D,h,x1,…,xk)(D,h,x_{1},\dots,x_{k}) is a particular equivalence class representative of a quantum surface, we call hh an embedding of the surface into (D,x1,…,xk)(D,x_{1},\dots,x_{k}).

Suppose now that hh is a random distribution on DD which can be coupled with a GFF on DD in such a way that their difference is a.s. a continuous function. Following [DS11, Section 3.1], we can then define for each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and ε>0\varepsilon>0 the circle average hε​(z)h_{\varepsilon}(z) of hh over ∂Bε​(z)\partial B_{\varepsilon}(z). It is shown in [DS11, Proposition 3.1] that (z,ε)↦hε​(z)(z,\varepsilon)\mapsto h_{\varepsilon}(z) a.s. admits a continuous modification. We will always assume that this process has been replaced by such a modification.

One can define the γ\gamma-LQG area measure μh\mu_{h} on DD, which is defined to be the a.s. limit

μh=limε→0εγ2/2​eγ​hε​(z)​d​z\mu_{h}=\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}\varepsilon^{\gamma^{2}/2}e^{\gamma h_{\varepsilon}(z)}\,dz

with respect to the local Prokhorov distance on DD as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 along powers of 2 [DS11]. One can similarly define a boundary length measure νh\nu_{h} on certain curves in DD, including ∂D\partial D [DS11] and SLEκ¯{}_{\underline{\kappa}}-type curves for κ¯=γ2\underline{\kappa}=\gamma^{2} which are independent from hh [She16]. If hh and h~\widetilde{h} are related by a conformal map as in (2.1), then f∗​μh~=μhf_{*}\mu_{\widetilde{h}}=\mu_{h} and f∗​νh~=νhf_{*}\nu_{\widetilde{h}}=\nu_{h}. Hence μh\mu_{h} and νh\nu_{h} are intrinsic to the LQG surface — they do not depend on the choice of parametrization. The measures μh\mu_{h} and νh\nu_{h} are a special case of a more general theory of regularized random measures called Gaussian multiplicative chaos which originates in work of Kahane [Kah85]. See [Ber17] for an elementary proof of convergence (and independence of the limit with respect to the regularization procedure) and [RV14a] for a survey of this theory.

The main type of LQG surface which we will be interested in in this paper is the γ\gamma-quantum cone, which is the surface appearing in the SLE/LQG embedding of the mated-CRT map. The γ\gamma-quantum cone is a doubly marked LQG surface (ℂ,h,0,∞)(\mathbbm{C},h,0,\infty) introduced in [DMS21, Definition 4.10]. Roughly speaking, the γ\gamma-quantum cone is the surface obtained by starting with a general γ\gamma-LQG surface, sampling a point zz uniformly from the γ\gamma-LQG area measure, then “zooming in” near the marked point and re-scaling so that the μh\mu_{h}-mass of the unit disk remains of constant order [DMS21, Proposition 4.13(ii) and Lemma A.10]. This surface can be described explicitly as follows.

Definition 2.2 (Quantum cone).

The γ\gamma-quantum cone is the LQG surface (ℂ,h,0,∞)(\mathbbm{C},h,0,\infty) with the distribution hh defined as follows. Let BB be a standard linear Brownian motion and let B^\widehat{B} be a standard linear Brownian motion conditioned so that B^t+(Q−γ)​t>0\widehat{B}_{t}+(Q-\gamma)t>0 for all t>0t>0 (here Q=2/γ+γ/2Q=2/\gamma+\gamma/2, as in (2.1)). Let At=Bt−α​tA_{t}=B_{t}-\alpha t for t≥0t\geq 0 and let At=B^−t+γ​tA_{t}=\widehat{B}_{-t}+\gamma t for t<0t<0. The circle average process of hh centered at the origin satisfies he−t​(0)=Ath_{e^{-t}}(0)=A_{t} for each t∈ℝt\in\mathbbm{R}. The “lateral part” h−h|⋅|(0)h-h_{|\cdot|}(0) is independent from {he−t​(0)}t∈ℝ\{h_{e^{-t}}(0)\}_{t\in\mathbbm{R}} and has the same law as h~−h~|⋅|(0)\widetilde{h}-\widetilde{h}_{|\cdot|}(0), where h~\widetilde{h} is a whole-plane GFF.

By Definition 2.1, one can get another embedding of the γ\gamma-quantum cone by replacing hh by h(a⋅)+Qlog|a|h(a\cdot)+Q\log|a| for any a∈ℂ∖{0}a\in\mathbbm{C}\setminus\{0\}. The particular embedding hh appearing in Definition 2.2 is called the circle average embedding and is characterized by the condition that sup{r>0:hr​(0)+Q​log⁡r=0}=1\sup\{r>0:h_{r}(0)+Q\log r=0\}=1. The circle average embedding is especially convenient to work with since for this embedding, h|𝔻h|_{\mathbbm{D}} agrees in law with the corresponding restriction of a whole-plane GFF plus −γlog|⋅|-\gamma\log|\cdot|, normalized so that its circle average over ∂𝔻\partial\mathbbm{D} is 0. Indeed, this is essentially immediate from Definition 2.2 since the process AtA_{t} has no conditioning for t>0t>0.

Since we can only compare hh to the whole-plane GFF on the unit disk 𝔻\mathbbm{D}, for many of our estimates we will restrict attention to a Euclidean ball of the form BρB_{\rho} for ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1). It is possible to transfer these estimates to larger Euclidean balls using the scale invariance property of the γ\gamma-quantum cone, which is proven in [DMS21, Proposition 4.13(i)].

Lemma 2.3.

Let hh be the circle average embedding of a γ\gamma-quantum cone. For b>0b>0, define

Rb:=sup{r>0:hr(0)+Qlogr=1γlogb}.R_{b}:=\sup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{r>0:h_{r}(0)+Q\log r=\frac{1}{\gamma}\log b}}\right\}. (2.2)

Then hb:=h(Rb⋅)+QlogRb−1γlogb=𝑑hh^{b}:=h(R_{b}\cdot)+Q\log R_{b}-\frac{1}{\gamma}\log b\overset{d}{=}h.

Lemma 2.3 says that the law of hh is invariant under the operation of scaling areas by a constant (i.e., adding 1γ​log⁡b\frac{1}{\gamma}\log b to hh), then re-scaling space and applying the LQG coordinate change formula (2.1) so that the new field is embedded in the same way as hh.

In addition to the γ\gamma-quantum wedge we will also have occasion to consider the quantum disk, which appears in Theorem 1.4. To define the quantum disk, one first defines an infinite measure ℳdisk\mathcal{M}^{\operatorname{disk}} on doubly quantum surfaces (𝔻,h,−1,1)(\mathbbm{D},h,-1,1) using the Bessel excursion measure. We will not need the precise definition here, so we refer to [DMS21, Section 4.5] for details. The infinite measure ℳdisk\mathcal{M}^{\operatorname{disk}} assigns finite mass to quantum surfaces with boundary length νh​(∂𝔻)≥L\nu_{h}(\partial\mathbbm{D})\geq L for any L>0L>0. By considering the regular conditional law of ℳdisk\mathcal{M}^{\operatorname{disk}} given {νh​(∂𝔻)=L,μh​(𝔻)=A}\{\nu_{h}(\partial\mathbbm{D})=L,\mu_{h}(\mathbbm{D})=A\} for any L,A>0L,A>0, one defines the doubly marked quantum disk with boundary length LL and area AA. We define the singly marked quantum disk or the unmarked quantum disk by forgetting one or both of the marked boundary points. By Proposition [DMS21, Proposition A.8], the marked points of a quantum disk are uniform samples from the LQG boundary length measure. That is, if (𝔻,h)(\mathbbm{D},h) is an unmarked quantum disk (with some specified area and boundary length) and conditional on hh we sample x,yx,y independently from the probability measure νh/L\nu_{h}/L, then (𝔻,h,x)(\mathbbm{D},h,x) is a single marked quantum disk and (𝔻,h,x,y)(\mathbbm{D},h,x,y) is a doubly marked quantum disk.

2.2.2 Space-filling SLEκ

The Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLEκ) for κ>0\kappa>0 is a one-parameter family of random fractal curves originally defined by Schramm in [Sch00]. SLEκ curves are simple for κ∈(0,4]\kappa\in(0,4], self-touching, but not space-filling or self-crossing, for κ∈(4,8)\kappa\in(4,8), and space-filling but still not self-crossing for κ≥8\kappa\geq 8 [RS05]. One can consider SLEκ curves between two marked boundary points of a simply connected domain (chordal), from a boundary point to an interior point (radial), or between two points in ℂ∪{∞}\mathbbm{C}\cup\{\infty\} (whole-plane). We refer to [Law05] or [Wer04] for an introduction to SLE.

We first consider the whole-plane space-filling SLEκ from ∞\infty to ∞\infty, which was introduced in [MS17, Sections 1.2.3 and 4.3]. This is a random space-filling curve η\eta in ℂ\mathbbm{C} which travels from ∞\infty to ∞\infty which fills all of ℂ\mathbbm{C} and never enters the interior of its past. Moreover, its law is invariant under spatial scaling: for any r>0r>0, r​ηr\eta agrees in law with η\eta viewed as curves modulo time parametrization. This is essentially the only information about space-filling SLEκ which is needed to understand this paper — we do not use any detailed information about the geometry of the curve. However, we briefly describe how space-filling SLEκ is defined (without details) to give the reader some more intuition about what this curve is. See [GHS19b, Section 3.6] for a detailed review of space-filling SLEκ.

When κ≥8\kappa\geq 8, in which case ordinary SLEκ is already space-filling, whole-plane SLEκ from ∞\infty to ∞\infty describes the local behavior of an ordinary chordal SLEκ curve near a typical interior point. For any a<ba<b, the set η⁡([a,b])\eta([a,b]) has the topology of a closed disk and its boundary is the union of four SLEκ¯{}_{\underline{\kappa}}-type curves for κ¯=16/κ\underline{\kappa}=16/\kappa which intersect only at their endpoints.

When κ∈(4,8)\kappa\in(4,8), the definition of space-filling SLEκ is more involved. Roughly speaking, chordal space-filling SLEκ can be obtained by starting with an ordinary chordal SLEκ curve and iteratively “filling in” the bubbles which it disconnects from its target point by SLEκ-type curves. It is shown in [MS17] that the curve one obtains after countably many iterations is space-filling and continuous when parameterized so that it traverses one unit of Lebesgue measure in one unit of time. The whole-plane space-filling SLEκ from ∞\infty to ∞\infty for κ∈(4,8)\kappa\in(4,8) describes the local behavior of the chordal version near a typical interior point, as in the case κ≥8\kappa\geq 8.

The topology of the curve is much more complicated for κ∈(4,8)\kappa\in(4,8) than for κ≥8\kappa\geq 8. For a<ba<b, neither the interior of the set η⁡([a,b])\eta([a,b]) nor its complement ℂ∖η⁡([a,b])\mathbbm{C}\setminus\eta([a,b]) is connected. Rather, each of these sets consists of a countable union of domains with the topology of the open disk (or the punctured plane in the case of the unbounded connected component of ℂ∖η⁡([a,b])\mathbbm{C}\setminus\eta([a,b]). The boundary of η⁡([a,b])\eta([a,b]) is the union of four SLEκ¯{}_{\underline{\kappa}}-type curves for κ¯=16/κ\underline{\kappa}=16/\kappa, but these curves typically intersect each other.

If D⊂ℂD\subset\mathbbm{C} is a simply connected domain and a∈∂Da\in\partial D, we can similarly define the clockwise space-filling SLEκ loop in DD based at aa. This is a random curve in DD from aa to aa which is the limit of chordal space-filling SLE from aa to bb in DD as a→ba\rightarrow b from the counterclockwise direction. See Section A.3 for details.

2.3 Mated-CRT map setup

Throughout most of this paper we will work with the following setup. Let (ℂ,h,0,∞)(\mathbbm{C},h,0,\infty) be a γ\gamma-quantum cone with the circle average embedding. Let η\eta be a whole-plane space-filling SLEκ with κ=16/γ2\kappa=16/\gamma^{2} sampled independently from hh and then parametrized so that η⁡(0)=0\eta(0)=0 and μh​(η⁡([a,b]))=b−a\mu_{h}(\eta([a,b]))=b-a for every a<ba<b. We define the cells

Hxε:=η⁡([x−ε,x]),∀ε>0,∀x∈ε​ℤ.H_{x}^{\varepsilon}:=\eta([x-\varepsilon,x]),\quad\forall\varepsilon>0,\quad\forall x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}. (2.3)

For ε>0\varepsilon>0, we let 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} be the mated-CRT map associated with (h,η)(h,\eta), i.e., 𝒱​𝒢ε=ε​ℤ\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} and two distinct vertices x,y∈𝒱​𝒢εx,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} are connected by one (resp. two) edges if and only if Hxε∩HyεH_{x}^{\varepsilon}\cap H_{y}^{\varepsilon} has one (resp. two) connected component which are not singletons. For z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, we define

OPENxzε:=(smallest x∈ε​ℤ such that z∈HxεCLOSE)x_{z}^{\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{smallest $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ such that $z\in H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$}}}\right) (2.4)

and we note that for a fixed z∈ℂ∖{0}z\in\mathbbm{C}\setminus\{0\}, xzεx_{z}^{\varepsilon} is in fact the only x∈ε​ℤx\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} for which z∈Hxεz\in H_{x}^{\varepsilon} (this is related to the fact that the boundaries of the cells of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} have zero Lebesgue measure). For a set D⊂ℂD\subset\mathbbm{C}, we define

𝒢ε(D):=(subgraph of 𝒢ε induced by {x∈ε​ℤ:Hxε∩D≠∅}).\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D):=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{subgraph of $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ induced by $\{x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}:H_{x}^{\varepsilon}\cap D\not=\emptyset\}$}}}\right). (2.5)

We write XεX^{\varepsilon} for the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}. For x∈𝒱​𝒢εx\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, we define

OPENℙ¯xε:=(conditional law given (h,η) of Xε started from X0ε=xCLOSE)\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{conditional law given $(h,\eta)$ of $X^{\varepsilon}$ started from $X_{0}^{\varepsilon}=x$}}}\right) (2.6)

and we write 𝔼¯xε\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon} for the corresponding expectation. For D⊂ℂD\subset\mathbbm{C}, we define

OPENτDε:=(first exit time of Xε from 𝒢ε​(D)CLOSE).\tau_{D}^{\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{first exit time of $X^{\varepsilon}$ from $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$}}}\right). (2.7)

Since h|B1h|_{B_{1}} agrees in law with the corresponding restriction of a whole-plane GFF plus γlog|⋅|−1\gamma\log|\cdot|^{-1}, it will be convenient in most of our arguments to restrict attention to a proper subdomain of B1B_{1}. Consequently, throughout the paper we fix ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and work primarily in BρB_{\rho}.

We will frequently need the following estimate for the Euclidean diameters of space-filling SLE cells.

Lemma 2.4 (Cell diameter estimates).

Fix a small parameter ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1). With polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, the Euclidean diameters of the cells of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} which intersect BρB_{\rho} satisfy

ε2(2−γ)2+ζ≤diam⁡Hxε≤ε2(2+γ)2−ζ,∀x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(Bρ).\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{(2-\gamma)^{2}}+\zeta}\leq\operatorname{diam}H_{x}^{\varepsilon}\leq\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{(2+\gamma)^{2}}-\zeta},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}). (2.8)
Proof.

The upper bound for cell diameters is proven in [GMS19, Lemma 2.7]. To get the lower bound, use Lemma A.1 with δ=ε2(2−γ)2+ζ\delta=\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{(2-\gamma)^{2}}+\zeta}, which implies that with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, each Euclidean ball of radius ε2(2−γ)2+ζ\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{(2-\gamma)^{2}}+\zeta} contained in 𝔻\mathbbm{D} has μh\mu_{h}-mass at most ε\varepsilon. If this is the case then no such Euclidean ball can contain one of the cells HxεH_{x}^{\varepsilon} (since each such cell has μh\mu_{h}-mass ε\varepsilon). ∎

3 Green’s function, effective resistance, and Harnack inequalities

3.1 Definitions of Dirichlet energy, Green’s function, and effective resistance

In this subsection we review some mostly standard notions in the theory of electrical networks and fix some notation.

Definition 3.1.

For a graph GG and a function f:𝒱⁡(G)→ℝf:\mathcal{V}(G)\to\mathbbm{R}, we define its Dirichlet energy to be the sum over unoriented edges

Energy⁡(f;G):=∑{x,y}∈ℰ⁡(G)(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))2,\operatorname{Energy}(f;G):=\sum_{\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{E}(G)}(f(x)-f(y))^{2},

with edges of multiplicity mm counted mm times.

Definition 3.2.

For a graph GG, a set of vertices V⊂𝒱⁡(G)V\subset\mathcal{V}(G), and two vertices x,y∈Gx,y\in G, we define the Green’s function for random walk on GG killed upon exiting VV by

GrV(x,y):=𝔼x[number of times that X hits y before leaving V]\operatorname{Gr}_{V}(x,y):=\mathbbm{E}_{x}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{number of times that $X$ hits $y$ before leaving $V$}}}\right] (3.1)

where 𝔼x\mathbbm{E}_{x} denotes the expectation for random walk on GG started from xx. Note that GrV⁡(x,y)=0\operatorname{Gr}_{V}(x,y)=0 if either xx or yy is not in VV. We also define the normalized Green’s function

grV⁡(x,y):=GrVG⁡(x,y)deg⁡(y).\operatorname{gr}_{V}(x,y):=\frac{\operatorname{Gr}_{V}^{G}(x,y)}{\operatorname{deg}(y)}. (3.2)

By, e.g., [LP16, Proposition 2.1], the function grV⁡(x,⋅)\operatorname{gr}_{V}(x,\cdot) is the voltage function when a unit of current flows from xx to VV. In particular, grV⁡(x,⋅)\operatorname{gr}_{V}(x,\cdot) is discrete harmonic on 𝒱⁡(G)∖(V∪{x})\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus(V\cup\{x\}).

To define effective resistance, we view a graph GG as an electrical network where each edge has unit resistance. For a vertex x∈𝒱⁡(G)x\in\mathcal{V}(G) and a set Z⊂𝒱⁡(G)Z\subset\mathcal{V}(G) with x∉Zx\notin Z, the effective resistance from xx to ZZ in GG is defined (using Definition 3.2) by

OPENℛ⁡(x↔ZCLOSE):=gr𝒱⁡(G)∖Z⁡(x,x),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x\leftrightarrow Z}}\right):=\operatorname{gr}_{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus Z}(x,x), (3.3)

i.e., OPENℛ​(x↔ZCLOSE)\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x\leftrightarrow Z}}\right) is the expected number of times that random walk started at xx returns to xx before hitting ZZ, divided by the degree of xx. For two disjoint vertex sets W,Z⊂𝒱⁡(G)W,Z\subset\mathcal{V}(G), we define ℛ⁡(W↔Z)\mathcal{R}(W\leftrightarrow Z) to be the effective resistance from w¯\overline{w} to ZZ in the graph G¯\overline{G} obtained from GG by identifying all of the vertices of WW to a single vertex w¯\overline{w}.

There are several equivalent definitions of effective resistance which will be useful for our purposes.

  1. 1.

    Dirichlet’s principle. Let 𝔣=𝔣Z,x:𝒱⁡(G)→[0,1]\mathfrak{f}=\mathfrak{f}_{Z,x}:\mathcal{V}(G)\rightarrow[0,1] be the function such that 𝔣⁡(x)=1\mathfrak{f}(x)=1, 𝔣|Z≡0\mathfrak{f}|_{Z}\equiv 0, and 𝔣\mathfrak{f} is discrete harmonic on 𝒱⁡(G)∖(Z∪{x})\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus(Z\cup\{x\}). Then (see, e.g., [LP16, Exercise 2.13])

    OPENℛG​(x↔ZCLOSE)=1Energy⁡(𝔣,G).\mathcal{R}^{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x\leftrightarrow Z}}\right)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{Energy}(\mathfrak{f};G)}. (3.4)
  2. 2.

    Thomson’s principle. A unit flow from xx to ZZ in GG is a function θ\theta from oriented edges e=(y,z)e=(y,z) of GG to ℝ\mathbbm{R} such that θ⁡(y,z)=−θ⁡(z,y)\theta(y,z)=-\theta(z,y) for each oriented edge (y,z)(y,z) of GG and

    ∑z∈𝒱⁡(G)z∼yθ⁡(y,z)=0∀y∈𝒱⁡(G)∖({x}∪Z)and∑z∈𝒱⁡(G)z∼xθ⁡(x,z)=1.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in\mathcal{V}(G)\\ z\sim y\end{subarray}}\theta(y,z)=0\quad\forall y\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus(\{x\}\cup Z)\quad\operatorname{and}\quad\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in\mathcal{V}(G)\\ z\sim x\end{subarray}}\theta(x,z)=1.

    One has (see, e.g., [LPW09, Theorem 9.10] or [LP16, Page 35])

    ℛG(x↔V)=inf{∑e∈ℰ⁡(G)[θ(e)]2:θ is a unit flow from x to Z}.\mathcal{R}^{G}(x\leftrightarrow V)=\inf\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}(G)}[\theta(e)]^{2}:\text{$\theta$ is a unit flow from $x$ to $Z$}}}\right\}. (3.5)
Notation 3.3.

In the case when G=𝒢εG=\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} is the mated-CRT map, we will typically include a superscript ε\varepsilon in the above notations, so, e.g., ℛε\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon} denotes effective resistance on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}. We will commonly apply the above definitions in the case when the vertex sets V,Z,WV,Z,W are of the form 𝒱​𝒢ε​(A)\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(A) for some set A⊂ℂA\subset\mathbbm{C}. To lighten notation we will simply write AA instead of 𝒱​𝒢ε​(A)\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(A). So, for example, GrAε\operatorname{Gr}_{A}^{\varepsilon} denotes the Green’s function for the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} killed upon exiting 𝒢ε​(A)\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(A).

3.2 Comparison of Green’s function and effective resistance

The results of [GMS19, GM21] give us good control on effective resistances in the mated-CRT map. In this subsection we will prove a general lemma which allows us to convert estimates for effective resistance to estimates for the Green’s function.

To state the lemma, we first introduce some notation. For a graph GG and a set A⊂𝒱⁡(G)A\subset\mathcal{V}(G), we write

∂A:={x∈A:∃y∈𝒱⁡(G)∖A with x∼y}.\partial A:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{x\in A:\text{$\exists y\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A$ with $x\sim y$}}}\right\}. (3.6)

We also write

OPENA¯:=(subgraph of G induced by A∪∂(𝒱⁡(G)∖A)CLOSE).\overline{A}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{subgraph of $G$ induced by $A\cup\partial(\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A)$}}}\right). (3.7)

The following lemma bounds the maximum and minimum of the Green’s function on ∂A\partial A in terms of effective resistances. It will be used in conjunction with Lemma 3.9 to get a uniform bound for the Green’s function on ∂A\partial A.

Lemma 3.4.

Let GG be a finite graph and let A⊂B⊂𝒱⁡(G)A\subset B\subset\mathcal{V}(G) be a finite sets of vertices. Let x∈Ax\in A and define (using the notation of Definition 3.2)

a:=miny∈∂AgrB(x,y),b:=maxy∈∂AgrB(x,y),δ:=max{|grB(x,u)−grB(x,v)|:u,v∈B,u∼v}.a:=\min_{y\in\partial A}\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,y),\quad b:=\max_{y\in\partial A}\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,y),\quad\delta:=\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{|\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,u)-\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,v)|:u,v\in B,u\sim v}}\right\}. (3.8)

Then for any x∈Ax\in A,

OPENa2a+δ≤ℛ⁡(A↔𝒱⁡(G)∖BCLOSE)≤b+δ.\frac{a^{2}}{a+\delta}\leq\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(A\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B}}\right)\leq b+\delta. (3.9)

Lemma 3.4 is a discrete version of [Gri99, Proposition 4.1], and is proven in a similar manner. It can be checked that the error term δ\delta in Lemma 3.4 is at most 1; see Lemma 3.7. This is the only bound for δ\delta which is needed for our purposes. To prove Lemma 3.4, we need some preparatory lemmas.

Lemma 3.5.

Let GG be a graph, let x∈Gx\in G, and let A⊂𝒱⁡(G)A\subset\mathcal{V}(G) be a finite set of vertices with x∈Ax\in A. If θ\theta is a unit flow from xx to Z⊂𝒱⁡(G)∖AZ\subset\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A, then

∑{θ(u,v):u∈A,v∈𝒱(G)∖A,u∼v}=1.\sum\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\theta(u,v):u\in A,v\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A,u\sim v}}\right\}=1.
Proof.

Since θ\theta is a unit flow, we have ∑v∼xθ⁡(x,v)=1\sum_{v\sim x}\theta(x,v)=1 and for any y∈A∖{x}y\in A\setminus\{x\}, ∑v∼yθ⁡(y,v)=0\sum_{v\sim y}\theta(y,v)=0. Therefore,

∑u∈A∑v∈𝒱⁡(G)v∼uθ⁡(u,v)=1.\sum_{u\in A}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in\mathcal{V}(G)\\ v\sim u\end{subarray}}\theta(u,v)=1.

We can break up the double sum on the left into two parts: the sum over the pairs (u,v)∈A×A(u,v)\in A\times A with u∼vu\sim v and the sum over the pairs (u,v)∈A×(𝒱⁡(G)∖A)(u,v)\in A\times(\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A) with u∼vu\sim v. The first sum is zero since θ⁡(u,v)=−θ⁡(v,u)\theta(u,v)=-\theta(v,u) for every u,v∈Au,v\in A. Therefore the second sum is equal to 1. ∎

Lemma 3.6 (Discrete Green’s identity).

Let GG be a graph, let A⊂𝒱⁡(G)A\subset\mathcal{V}(G) be a finite set of vertices, let f,𝔤:𝒱⁡(G)→ℝf,\mathfrak{g}:\mathcal{V}(G)\rightarrow\mathbbm{R} and suppose that 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is discrete harmonic on 𝒱⁡(G)∖A\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A. Then

∑{x,y}∈ℰ⁡(G)(f(x)−f(y))(𝔤(x)−𝔤(y))=−∑x∈Af(x)Δ𝔤(x),\sum_{\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{E}(G)}(f(x)-f(y))(\mathfrak{g}(x)-\mathfrak{g}(y))=-\sum_{x\in A}f(x)\Delta\mathfrak{g}(x), (3.10)

where Δ\Delta is the discrete Laplacian and the sum is over all unoriented edges of GG.

Proof.

Write ℰ→\mathcal{E}^{\shortrightarrow} for the set of oriented edges of GG. We have

∑{x,y}∈ℰ⁡(G)(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))​(𝔤⁡(x)−𝔤⁡(y))\displaystyle\sum_{\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{E}(G)}(f(x)-f(y))(\mathfrak{g}(x)-\mathfrak{g}(y))

3.3 Harnack inequality for the mated-CRT map

Lemma 3.4 gives an upper (resp. lower) bound for the minimum (resp. maximum) value of the Green’s function on ∂A\partial A in terms of effective resistances. It is of course much more useful to have an upper (resp. lower) bound for the maximum (resp. minimum) value of the Green’s function on ∂A\partial A. Hence we need a Harnack-type estimate which allows us to compare the maximum and minimum values of the Green’s function on ∂A\partial A. In this subsection we will prove such an estimate for the mated-CRT map 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} in the case when AA is the set of vertices which intersect a Euclidean ball.

Throughout this subsection we assume the setup and notation of Section 2.3. In particular we recall that for z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, xzε∈𝒱​𝒢εx_{z}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} is chosen so that zz is contained in the cell HxzεεH_{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon} and for D⊂ℂD\subset\mathbbm{C}, 𝒢ε​(D)\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D) is the subgraph of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} induced by the vertex set {xzε:z∈D}\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}:z\in D\}. We also recall that ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) is fixed.

Proposition 3.8 (Harnack inequality on a circle).

There exists β=β⁡(γ)>0\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0 and C=C⁡(ρ,γ)>0C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0 such that the following holds with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. Simultaneously for every z∈Bρz\in B_{\rho}, every s∈[εβ,13​dist⁡(z,∂Bρ)𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸]s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})}}\right], and every function 𝔣:𝒱​𝒢ε→[0,∞)\mathfrak{f}:\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow[0,\infty) which is discrete harmonic on 𝒱​𝒢ε​(B3​s​(z))∖{xzε}\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{3s}(z))\setminus\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\},

maxy∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(∂Bs​(z))⁡𝔣⁡(y)≤C​miny∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(∂Bs​(z))⁡𝔣⁡(y).\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))}\mathfrak{f}(y)\leq C\min_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))}\mathfrak{f}(y). (3.20)

The reason why we do not require that 𝔣\mathfrak{f} is discrete harmonic at the center point xzεx_{z}^{\varepsilon} is that we eventually want to apply Proposition 3.8 with 𝔣\mathfrak{f} equal to the normalized Green’s function grUε⁡(xzε,⋅)\operatorname{gr}_{U}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},\cdot) for B3​s​(z)⊂U⊂BρB_{3s}(z)\subset U\subset B_{\rho} (recall Notation 3.3). The key input in the proof of Proposition 3.8 is the following coupling lemma for random walks on a graph with different starting points, which follows from Wilson’s algorithm and is a variant of [GMS19, Lemma 3.12].

Lemma 3.9.

Let GG be a connected graph and let A⊂𝒱⁡(G)A\subset\mathcal{V}(G) be a set such that the simple random walk started from any vertex of GG a.s. hits AA in finite time. For x∈𝒱⁡(G)x\in\mathcal{V}(G), let XxX^{x} be the simple random walk started from xx and let τx\tau^{x} be the first time XxX^{x} hits AA. For x,y∈𝒱⁡(G)∖Ax,y\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A, there is a coupling of XxX^{x} and XyX^{y} such that a.s.

ℙ[Xxτx=Xyτy|Xy|[0,τy]]≥ℙ[Xx disconnects y from A before time τx].\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X^{x}_{\tau^{x}}=X^{y}_{\tau^{y}}\,\Big|\,X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}}}\right]\geq\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$X^{x}$ disconnects $y$ from $A$ before time $\tau^{x}$}}}\right]. (3.21)
Proof.

The lemma is a consequence of Wilson’s algorithm. Let TT be the uniform spanning tree of GG with all of the vertices of AA wired to a single point. For x∈𝒱⁡(G)x\in\mathcal{V}(G), let LxL^{x} be the unique path in TT from xx to AA. For a path PP in GG, write LE⁡(P)\operatorname{LE}(P) for its chronological loop erasure. By Wilson’s algorithm [Wil96], we can generate the union Lx∪LyL^{x}\cup L^{y} in the following manner.

  1. 1.

    Run XyX^{y} until time τy\tau^{y} and generate the loop erasure LE⁡(Xy|[0,τy])\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}).

  2. 2.

    Conditional on Xy|[0,τy]X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}, run XxX^{x} until the first time τ~x\widetilde{\tau}^{x} that it hits either LE⁡(Xy|[0,τy])\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}) or AA.

  3. 3.

    Set Lx∪Ly=LE⁡(Xy|[0,τy])∪LE⁡(Xx|[0,τ~x])L^{x}\cup L^{y}=\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]})\cup\operatorname{LE}(X^{x}|_{[0,\widetilde{\tau}^{x}]}).

Note that Ly=LE⁡(Xy|[0,τy])L^{y}=\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}) in the above procedure. Applying the above procedure with the roles of xx and yy interchanged shows that Lx​=𝑑​LE⁡(Xx|[0,τx])L^{x}\overset{d}{=}\operatorname{LE}(X^{x}|_{[0,\tau^{x}]}). When we construct Lx∪LyL^{x}\cup L^{y} as above, the points where LxL^{x} and LyL^{y} hit AA coincide provided XxX^{x} hits LE⁡(Xy|[0,τy])\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}) before AA. The conditional probability given Xy|[0,τy]X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]} that XxX^{x} hits LE⁡(Xy|[0,τy])\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}) before AA is at least the unconditional probability that XxX^{x} disconnects yy from AA before time τx\tau^{x}. We thus obtain a coupling of LE⁡(Xx|[0,τx])\operatorname{LE}(X^{x}|_{[0,\tau^{x}]}) and LE⁡(Xy|[0,τy])\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}) such that the conditional probability given Xy|[0,τy]X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]} that these two loop erasures hit AA at the same point is at least ℙ[Xx disconnects y from A before time τx]\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$X^{x}$ disconnects $y$ from $A$ before time $\tau^{x}$}}}\right]. We now obtain (3.21) by observing that XτxxX^{x}_{\tau^{x}} is the same as the point where LE⁡(Xx|[0,τx])\operatorname{LE}(X^{x}|_{[0,\tau^{x}]}) first hits AA, and similarly with yy in place of xx. ∎

Lemma 5.4 only provides an upper bound for GrBρε⁡(x,y)\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y) in the case when |η⁡(x)−η⁡(y)|≥εβ|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\geq\varepsilon^{\beta}. 5.4 Proof of Proposition 5.1

The following estimate is the main input in the proof of Proposition 5.1.

Lemma 5.8.

There are constants α=α⁡(γ)>0\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)>0 and C=C⁡(ρ,γ)>0C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0 such that with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, it holds simultaneously for every Borel set D⊂BρD\subset B_{\rho} and every x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D) that

OPEN∑y∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)GrDε⁡(x,y)≤C​ε−1​∫Bεα​(D)log⁡(1|η⁡(x)−w|CLOSE)+1​d​μh​(w)+ε−1+α.\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq C\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|\eta(x)-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}. (5.38)
Proof.

Note that the Green’s function is increasing in the domain, so for any D⊂BρD\subset B_{\rho},

GrDε⁡(x,y)≤GrBρε⁡(x,y),∀x,y∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D).\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y),\quad\forall x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D). (5.39)

Fix β,ζ>0\beta,\zeta>0, to be chosen later in a manner depending only on γ\gamma. For a Borel set D⊂BρD\subset B_{\rho} and x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D), we break the sum on the left side of (5.38) into two pieces:

YD,xnear\displaystyle Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{near}} :={y∈𝒱𝒢ε(D):|η(x)−η(y)|<εβ}\displaystyle:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D):|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|<\varepsilon^{\beta}}}\right\}
YD,xtypical\displaystyle Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{typical}} :=𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)∖YD,xnear.\displaystyle:=\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)\setminus Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{near}}.

Let us first bound the sum over YD,xnearY_{D,x}^{\operatorname{near}}. By Lemma 5.6, it holds with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 that

maxx,y∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(Bρ)⁡GrBρε⁡(x,y)≤ε−ζ.\max_{x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})}\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq\varepsilon^{-\zeta}. (5.40)

Since the cells of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} have μh\mu_{h}-mass ε\varepsilon, it is easily seen from Lemmas A.1 and 2.4 that there exists α0=α0​(β,γ)>0\alpha_{0}=\alpha_{0}(\beta,\gamma)>0 such that with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, we have supz∈Bρ#​𝒱​𝒢ε​(Bεβ​(z))≤ε−1+α0\sup_{z\in B_{\rho}}\#\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\varepsilon^{\beta}}(z))\leq\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha_{0}}, which implies that

≤6ε−1∫Bεα1​(D)fx(w)dμh(w)+ε−1+α1by Lemma A.5\displaystyle\leq 6\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha_{1}}}(D)}f_{x}(w)\,d\mu_{h}(w)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha_{1}}\quad\text{by Lemma~\ref{lem-cell-sum-deg}}

We now prove an elementary lemma for general graphs which will allow us to deduce moment bounds for exit times of the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} from Lemma 5.8.

Lemma 5.9.

Let GG be a graph, let B⊂𝒱⁡(G)B\subset\mathcal{V}(G), and let x∈Bx\in B. Let τB\tau_{B} be the exit time from BB of the simple random walk on GG started from xx. Then for each N∈ℕN\in\mathbbm{N},

𝔼[τBN]≤N!∑y1,…,yN∈BGrB(x,y1)∏n=2NGrB(yn−1,yn).\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B}^{N}}}\right]\leq N!\sum_{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\in B}\operatorname{Gr}_{B}(x,y_{1})\prod_{n=2}^{N}\operatorname{Gr}_{B}(y_{n-1},y_{n}). (5.46)

We have

τB=∑y∈B∑j=0∞𝟙(j<τB,Xj=y).\tau_{B}=\sum_{y\in B}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\mathbbm{1}_{(j<\tau_{B},\,X_{j}=y)}.
