≤N!∑y1,…,yN∈B∑0≤j1≤⋯≤jN<∞ℙ[jN<τB,Xj1=y1,…,XjN=yN].\displaystyle\leq N!\sum_{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\in B}\sum_{0\leq j_{1}\leq\dots\leq j_{N}<\infty}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{N}<\tau_{B},\,X_{j_{1}}=y_{1},\dots,X_{j_{N}}=y_{N}}}\right]. (5.47)

For y∈By\in B, let XyX^{y} denote the simple random walk on GG started from yy and let τBy\tau_{B}^{y} be its exit time from BB (so that X=XxX=X^{x} and τB=τBx\tau_{B}=\tau_{B}^{x}). By NN applications of the strong Markov property, we obtain

ℙ[jN<τB,Xj1=y1,…,XjN=yN]=ℙ[j1<τB,Xj1=y1]∏n=2Nℙ[jn−jn−1<τByn−1,Xyn−1jn−jn−1=yj].\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{N}<\tau_{B},\,X_{j_{1}}=y_{1},\dots,X_{j_{N}}=y_{N}}}\right]=\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{1}<\tau_{B},\,X_{j_{1}}=y_{1}}}\right]\prod_{n=2}^{N}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{n}-j_{n-1}<\tau_{B}^{y_{n-1}},X^{y_{n-1}}_{j_{n}-j_{n-1}}=y_{j}}}\right]. (5.48)

Note that we allow jn=jn−1j_{n}=j_{n-1} for some n∈[1,N]ℤn\in[1,N]_{\mathbbm{Z}}, in which case the nnth factor in the product on the right side of (5.48) is either zero or one according to whether yn=yn−1y_{n}=y_{n-1}. By (5.48), the right side of (5.47) equals

N!∑y1,…,yN∈B∑0≤j1≤⋯≤jN<∞ℙ[j1<τB,Xj1=y1]∏n=2Nℙ[jn−jn−1<τByn−1,Xyn−1jn−jn−1=yn].\displaystyle N!\sum_{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\in B}\sum_{0\leq j_{1}\leq\dots\leq j_{N}<\infty}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{1}<\tau_{B},\,X_{j_{1}}=y_{1}}}\right]\prod_{n=2}^{N}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{n}-j_{n-1}<\tau_{B}^{y_{n-1}},X^{y_{n-1}}_{j_{n}-j_{n-1}}=y_{n}}}\right]. (5.49)

Summing over jNj_{N}, then over jN−1j_{N-1}, …\dots, then over j1j_{1} gives (5.46). ∎

6 Tightness

For z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, let Xz,ε:ℕ0→𝒱​𝒢εX^{z,\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{N}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} denote the simple random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} started from the vertex xzε∈𝒱​𝒢εx_{z}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}. Let X^z,ε:[0,∞)→ℂ\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C} be the process t↦η⁡(Xt/εz,ε)t\mapsto\eta(X_{t/\varepsilon}^{z,\varepsilon}), extended from ε​ℕ0\varepsilon\mathbbm{N}_{0} to [0,∞)[0,\infty) by piecewise linear interpolation.

We want to establish a tightness result for the random functions

Pε:z↦{Conditional law of t↦X^tz,ε given (h,η)}P^{\varepsilon}:z\mapsto\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\text{Conditional law of $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t}$ given $(h,\eta)$}}}\right\} (6.1)

from ℂ\mathbbm{C} to the space of probability measures on continuous paths [0,∞)→ℂ[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}. To state our tightness result we need to specify metrics on various spaces.

  • •

    The space C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}) of continuous paths X:[0,∞)→B¯ρX:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\overline{B}_{\rho} is equipped with the local uniform metric

    𝕕Unif(X,X′)=∫0∞e−T∧{supt∈[0,T]|Xt−Xt′|}dT,\mathbbm{d}_{\operatorname{Unif}}(X,X^{\prime})=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-T}\wedge\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|X_{t}-X_{t}^{\prime}|}}\right\}\,dT, (6.2)

    so that Xn→XX^{n}\rightarrow X if and only if Xn→XX^{n}\rightarrow X uniformly on each compact subset of [0,∞)[0,\infty).

  • •

    The space OPENProb⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)CLOSE)\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right) of probability measures on C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}) is equipped with the Prokhorov metric 𝕕Prok\mathbbm{d}_{\operatorname{Prok}} induced by the metric 𝕕Unif\mathbbm{d}_{\operatorname{Unif}} on C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}).

  • •

    The space of functions P:ℂ→Prob(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)CLOSE)P:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right) is equipped with the L∞L^{\infty} metric

    OPEN𝕕∞​(P,P′)=supz∈ℂ𝕕Prok​(Pz,Pz′CLOSE),\mathbbm{d}_{\infty}(P,P^{\prime})=\sup_{z\in\mathbbm{C}}\mathbbm{d}_{\operatorname{Prok}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(P_{z},P^{\prime}_{z}}}\right), (6.3)

    so that Pn→PP^{n}\rightarrow P if and only if Pzn→PzP^{n}_{z}\rightarrow P_{z} uniformly on each compact subset of ℂ\mathbbm{C} with respect to the above Prokhorov topology on OPENProb⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)CLOSE)\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right).

The main result of this subsection is the following proposition.

Proposition 6.1.

The laws of the random functions (6.1) for ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) are tight with respect to the topology specified just above. If PP is any subsequential limit in law of these functions, then a.s. PP is continuous and the following is true. If z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and X^z\widehat{X}^{z} is a path with the law PzP_{z}, then a.s. X^z\widehat{X}^{z} does not stay at a single point for a positive interval of time.

Fix ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1). Since most of our estimates only apply for cells of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} which intersect BρB_{\rho}, we will first prove a tightness statement when we stop our walks upon exiting BρB_{\rho}. For z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, let τ^z,ε\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon} be the first time that X^z,ε\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon} hits a point η⁡(x)∈η⁡(ε​ℤ)\eta(x)\in\eta(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}) whose corresponding cell η⁡([x−ε,x])\eta([x-\varepsilon,x]) is disjoint from BρB_{\rho}. We define

Pρ,⋅ε:z↦{Conditional law of t↦X^t∧τ^z,εz,ε given (h,η)}.P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}:z\mapsto\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\text{Conditional law of $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}$ given $(h,\eta)$}}}\right\}. (6.4)

Note that Pρ,zεP_{\rho,z}^{\varepsilon} assigns probability 1 to the constant path at xzεx_{z}^{\varepsilon} if zz is not contained in a cell of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} which intersects BρB_{\rho}.

Proposition 6.2.

The laws of the random functions (6.4) for ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) are tight with respect to the topology specified just above Proposition 6.1. If Pρ,⋅P_{\rho,\cdot} is any subsequential limit in law of these functions, then a.s. PP is continuous and the following is true. If z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and X^z\widehat{X}^{z} is a path with the law Pρ,zP_{\rho,z}, then a.s. X^z\widehat{X}^{z} does not stay at a single point for a positive interval of time before it exits BρB_{\rho}.

Most of this section is devoted to the proof of Proposition 6.2. We will deduce Proposition 6.1 from Proposition 6.2 and a scaling argument in Section 6.4.

For proving tightness results, it is convenient to work with the space

𝒞:=C[ℂ,Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)CLOSE)]\mathcal{C}:=C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{C},\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)}}\right] (6.5)

of continuous functions OPENℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)CLOSE)\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right), rather than the space of all functions OPENℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)CLOSE)\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right) (e.g., so that we can use the Arzéla-Ascoli theorem). So, we will approximate the function Pρ,⋅εP_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon} of (6.4) by a continuous function P~ρ,⋅ε∈𝒞\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{C} which satisfies P~ρ,η⁡(x)ε=Pρ,η⁡(x)ε\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon}=P_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon} for each x∈ε​ℤx\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}. One way to do this is as follows. For each x∈ε​ℤx\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}, choose rxε>0r_{x}^{\varepsilon}>0 such that the Euclidean neighborhood of the cell Brxε​(Hxε)B_{r_{x}^{\varepsilon}}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}) does not contain η⁡(y)\eta(y) for any y∈ε​ℤ∖{x}y\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\setminus\{x\}. Choose a partition of unity {ϕxε}x∈ε​ℤ\{\phi_{x}^{\varepsilon}\}_{x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}} subordinate to the open cover {Brxε​(Hxε)}x∈ε​ℤ\{B_{r_{x}^{\varepsilon}}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})\}_{x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}} of ℂ\mathbbm{C}. Then set P~ρ,zε=∑x∈ε​ℤPρ,η⁡(x)ε​ϕxε​(z)\widetilde{P}_{\rho,z}^{\varepsilon}=\sum_{x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}}P_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon}\phi_{x}^{\varepsilon}(z).

To prove Proposition 6.2, we need a compactness criterion, which follows easily from the Prokhorov theorem and the Arzéla-Ascoli theorem.

Lemma 6.3.

Let 𝒦⊂𝒞\mathcal{K}\subset\mathcal{C}. Then 𝒦\mathcal{K} is pre-compact (i.e., the closure of 𝒦\mathcal{K} is compact) if the following conditions are satisfied.

  1. 1.

    (Equicontinuity of laws) For each L>1L>1, there exists δ=δ⁡(L)>0\delta=\delta(L)>0 such that for each P=(Pz)z∈ℂ∈𝒦P=(P_{z})_{z\in\mathbbm{C}}\in\mathcal{K} and each z,w∈BL​(0)z,w\in B_{L}(0) with |z−w|≤δ|z-w|\leq\delta, the Prokhorov distance between the laws PzP_{z} and PwP_{w} is at most 1/L1/L.

  2. 2.

    (Equicontinuity of paths) For each L>0L>0 and each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, there exists δ=δ⁡(z,L)>0\delta=\delta(z,L)>0 such that for each P=(Pw)w∈ℂ∈𝒦P=(P_{w})_{w\in\mathbbm{C}}\in\mathcal{K}, the following is true. If X:[0,∞)→ℂX:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C} is sampled from the law PzP_{z}, then with probability at least 1−1/L1-1/L,

    |Xs−Xt|≤1/L,∀s,t∈[0,L]with|s−t|≤δ.|X_{s}-X_{t}|\leq 1/L,\quad\forall s,t\in[0,L]\quad\text{with}\quad|s-t|\leq\delta.
Proof.

By the Arzéla-Ascoli theorem for continuous functions into the complete metric space Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})), 𝒦\mathcal{K} is pre-compact provided condition 1 holds and for each fixed z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, the set {Pz}P∈𝒦\{P_{z}\}_{P\in\mathcal{K}} is a pre-compact subset of Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})).

By the Prokhorov theorem, {Pz}P∈𝒦\{P_{z}\}_{P\in\mathcal{K}} is pre-compact provided that for each ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1), there is a pre-compact subset 𝒦ζ′=𝒦ζ′​(z)\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}=\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}(z) of C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}) such that for each P∈𝒦P\in\mathcal{K}, we have Pz​[𝒦ζ′]≥1−ζP_{z}[\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}]\geq 1-\zeta. By the Arzéla-Ascoli theorem, 𝒦ζ′\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta} is pre-compact provided there is a uniform modulus of continuity for all of the functions in 𝒦ζ′\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}.

We now assume condition 2 and check that {Pz}P∈𝒦\{P_{z}\}_{P\in\mathcal{K}} is pre-compact using the criterion of the preceding paragraph. To this end, fix ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1) and for k∈ℕk\in\mathbbm{N} let δk\delta_{k} be as in condition 2 for L=2k/ζL=2^{k}/\zeta. By a union bound over all k∈ℕk\in\mathbbm{N}, we get that if P∈𝒦P\in\ \mathcal{K} and XX is sampled from PzP_{z} then it holds with probability at least 1−ζ1-\zeta that

|Xs−Xt|≤ζ/2k,∀s,t∈[0,2k/ζ]with|s−t|≤δk,∀k∈ℕ.|X_{s}-X_{t}|\leq\zeta/2^{k},\quad\forall s,t\in[0,2^{k}/\zeta]\quad\text{with}\quad|s-t|\leq\delta_{k},\quad\forall k\in\mathbbm{N}. (6.6)

The set 𝒦ζ′\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta} of X∈C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)X\in C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}) for which (6.6) holds and X0=zX_{0}=z is a pre-compact subset of C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}), which verifies the condition of the preceding paragraph. ∎

The proof of the tightness part of Proposition 6.2 is divided into two steps, based on the two conditions of Lemma 6.3. First we prove equicontinuity of paths in Section 6.1, then we prove equicontinuity of laws in Section 6.2. In Section 6.3, we prove an estimate for the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} which will help us verify the last part of Proposition 6.1 (i.e., that the subsequential limiting path does not stay at a point for a positive time interval). In Section 6.4 we deduce Proposition 6.1 from Proposition 6.2 via a scaling argument. Throughout this section, we will use the following terminology.

Definition 6.4.

We say that ψ:[0,∞)→[0,∞)\psi:[0,\infty)\rightarrow[0,\infty) is a superpolynomial function if ψ⁡(0)=0\psi(0)=0 and limδ→0δ−p​ψ​(δ)=0\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\delta^{-p}\psi(\delta)=0 for every p>0p>0.

We do not require the superpolynomial functions appearing in different proposition / lemma statements to be the same.

6.1 Equicontinuity of paths

The main result of this subsection is the following estimate.

Proposition 6.5 (Equicontinuity of paths).

Let χ>2​(2+γ)2−γ\chi>\frac{2(2+\gamma)}{2-\gamma}. There is a superpolynomial function ψ\psi, depending only on ρ,χ,γ\rho,\chi,\gamma, such that probability tending to 1 as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, it holds simultaneously for each z∈Bρz\in B_{\rho} that the following is true. With conditional probability at least 1−ψ⁡(δ)1-\psi(\delta) given (h,η)(h,\eta),

|X^sz,ε−X^tz,ε|≤2​δ,∀s,t∈[0,τ^z,ε]with|s−t|≤δχ.|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{s}-\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t}|\leq 2\delta,\quad\forall s,t\in[0,\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}]\quad\text{with}\quad|s-t|\leq\delta^{\chi}. (6.7)

Once Theorem 1.2 is established, Proposition 6.5 implies that a.s. Liouville Brownian motion is locally Hölder continuous with any exponent less than 2−γ2​(2+γ)\frac{2-\gamma}{2(2+\gamma)}. This bound is not optimal: indeed, it follows from [GRV16, Corollary 2.14] that Liouville Brownian motion is Hölder continuous with any exponent less than 12​(1+γ/2)2\frac{1}{2(1+\gamma/2)^{2}}. Note in particular that this exponent does not degenerate as γ\gamma approaches 2. The proof in [GRV16] relies on the study of negative moments for the exit time from a ball, which in turn relies on the a priori knowledge of the multifractal spectrum of Liouville Brownian motion. Such tools are not directly available here and we instead use a “worst-case scenario” approach which leads to a suboptimal (but still finite) exponent.

To prove Proposition 6.5 we want to use our lower bound for the exit times of the walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} from Euclidean balls (Proposition 4.1) to say that X^z,ε\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon} is very unlikely to travel a long Euclidean distance in a short amount of time. The main difficulty is that Proposition 6.5 only gives a lower bound for the conditional expectation of the exit time given (h,η)(h,\eta). This by itself is far from good enough to get a modulus of continuity estimate for X^z,ε\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}, so we need to use additional arguments to get a better lower bound for exit times.

The first step of the proof, carried out in Lemma 6.6, is to use Proposition 4.1 together with our upper bound for moments of exit times from Euclidean balls (Proposition 5.1) and the Payley-Zygmund inequality to say the following. Let c>0c>0 be the constant from Proposition 4.1. If δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) is fixed and ε>0\varepsilon>0 is small, then with high probability it holds uniformly over all x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(Bρ)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}) and all r∈[δ,dist⁡(η⁡(x),∂BρCLOSE)]r\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\delta,\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right] that

ℙ[Exit time of X^η⁡(x),ε from Br​(η​(x))≥12μh(Bc​r​(η​(x))CLOSE)|h,η]\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{Exit time of $\widehat{X}^{\eta(x),\varepsilon}$ from $B_{r}(\eta(x))$}\geq\frac{1}{2}\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{cr}(\eta(x))}}\right)\,|\,h,\eta}}\right] (6.8)

is bounded below by an explicit quantity depending on μh|Br​(η​(x))\mu_{h}|_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}.

Using basic “worst-case” estimates for the LQG measure, the above bound can be made more explicit. In particular, fix a large constant ℓ>1\ell>1 to be chosen later. Then when ε\varepsilon and δ\delta are small, it holds with high probability over (h,η)(h,\eta) that

ℙ[Exit time of X^z,ε from Bδℓ​(z)≳δ(2+γ)2​ℓ/2|h,η]≳δℓ​γ2/2\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{Exit time of $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ from $B_{\delta^{\ell}}(z)$}\gtrsim\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2}\,|\,h,\eta}}\right]\gtrsim\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2} (6.9)

uniformly over all x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(Bρ−δℓ)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta^{\ell}}), where here ≳\gtrsim denotes inequality up to a multiplicative error of order δζ\delta^{\zeta}, where ζ>0\zeta>0 can be made as small as we like (see Lemma 6.7).

At first glance, the bound (6.9) still seems to be far from a modulus of continuity estimate for X^z,ε\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon} since it only gives a lower bound for exit times which holds with probability at least δℓ​γ2/2\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2}, not with probability close to 1. To get around this difficulty, we exploit the (quenched) convergence of X^z,ε\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon} to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization, which was proven in [GMS21]. Indeed, using a basic Brownian motion estimate (Lemma 6.8) and the aforementioned convergence, we can show that when ε\varepsilon and δ\delta are small the following is true with extremely high conditional probability given (h,η)(h,\eta). If z∈Bρz\in B_{\rho}, then the walk X^z,ε\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon} has to travel Euclidean distance δℓ\delta^{\ell} at least N≈δ−2​(ℓ−1)N\approx\delta^{-2(\ell-1)} times before exiting the ball of radius δ\delta centered at its starting point. More precisely, if TT is the exit time of X^z,δ\widehat{X}^{z,\delta} from Bδ​(z)B_{\delta}(z), then typically there are of order N≈δ−2​(ℓ−1)N\approx\delta^{-2(\ell-1)} times 0=τ0<τ1<⋯<τN<T0=\tau_{0}<\tau_{1}<\dots<\tau_{N}<T such that X^τnz,ε−X^τn−1z,ε≥δℓ\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\tau_{n}}-\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\tau_{n-1}}\geq\delta^{\ell} for each n=1,…,Nn=1,\dots,N (Lemma 6.9). This is related to the fact that Brownian motion has linear quadratic variation.

The estimate (6.9) tells us that (ignoring small multiplicative errors) under the conditional law given (h,η)(h,\eta), each of the time intervals [τn−1,τn][\tau_{n-1},\tau_{n}] has probability at least δℓ​γ2/2\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2} to have length at least δ(2+γ)2​ℓ/2\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2}. Since there are of order δ−2​(ℓ−1)\delta^{-2(\ell-1)} such intervals, and using the Markov property of the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, we get that the probability that at least one of these intervals has length at least δ(2+γ)2​ℓ/2\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2} is at least

OPEN1−(1−δℓ​γ2/2CLOSE)δ−2​(ℓ−1).1-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2}}}\right)^{\delta^{-2(\ell-1)}}. (6.10)

If we choose ℓ>4/(4−γ2)\ell>4/(4-\gamma^{2}), so that 2​(ℓ−1)>ℓ​γ2/22(\ell-1)>\ell\gamma^{2}/2, then (6.10) is of the form 1−ψ⁡(δ)1-\psi(\delta) for a superpolynomial function ψ\psi. We therefore get that when ε>0\varepsilon>0 is small, it holds uniformly over all x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(Bρ−δ)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta}) that

ℙ[Exit time of X^z,ε from Bδ​(z)≳δ(2+γ)2​ℓ/2|h,η]≥1−ψ(δ);\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{Exit time of $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ from $B_{\delta}(z)$}\gtrsim\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2}\,|\,h,\eta}}\right]\geq 1-\psi(\delta); (6.11)

see Lemma 6.11. Once (6.11) is established, it is a simple matter to conclude the proof of Proposition 6.5 using the Markov property and a union bound. We remind the reader that this only holds with high probability over (h,η)(h,\eta) because the bound (6.9) only holds with high probability.

We now proceed with the details of the above argument. For convenience we will mostly phrase our estimates in terms of the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} instead of in terms of the embedded, linearly interpolated walk X^z,ε\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon} as in the outline above. We start with the Payley-Zygmund argument mentioned above.

Fix p>1p>1 and let α=α⁡(γ)\alpha=\alpha(\gamma) be as in Proposition 5.1. Continuing with the outline above, we now want to use the convergence of random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization to argue that the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} has to have at least δ−2​(ℓ−1)\delta^{-2(\ell-1)} increments during which it travels Euclidean distance δℓ\delta^{\ell} before it can travel Euclidean distance δ\delta. We start with the desired Brownian motion estimate.

Lemma 6.8.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a standard planar Brownian motion started from 0. For r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), let σ0​(r):=0\sigma_{0}(r):=0 and inductively let σk​(r)\sigma_{k}(r) for k∈ℕk\in\mathbbm{N} be the first time t≥σk−1​(r)t\geq\sigma_{k-1}(r) for which |ℬt−ℬσk−1​(r)|≥r|\mathcal{B}_{t}-\mathcal{B}_{\sigma_{k-1}(r)}|\geq r. For each ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1), there is a superpolynomial function ψ\psi such that

ℙ[ℬ first exits B1​(0) before time σ⌊r−(2−ζ)⌋​(r)]≤ψ(r)and\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\mathcal{B}$ first exits $B_{1}(0)$ before time $\sigma_{\lfloor r^{-(2-\zeta)}\rfloor}(r)$}}}\right]\leq\psi(r)\quad\text{and} (6.21)
ℙ[ℬ first exits B1​(0) after time σ⌊r−(2+ζ)⌋​(r)]≤ψ(r).\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\mathcal{B}$ first exits $B_{1}(0)$ after time $\sigma_{\lfloor r^{-(2+\zeta)}\rfloor}(r)$}}}\right]\leq\psi(r). (6.22)
Proof.

By Brownian scaling, the rescaled increments OPENr−2​(σk​(r)−σk−1​(r)CLOSE)r^{-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sigma_{k}(r)-\sigma_{k-1}(r)}}\right) are i.i.d., and each has the same law as the exit time σ1​(1)\sigma_{1}(1) of ℬ\mathcal{B} from B1​(0)B_{1}(0). Using the strong Markov property of Brownian motion, it is easily seen that there are universal constants c0,c1,c2>0c_{0},c_{1},c_{2}>0 such that or each A>1A>1, each k∈ℕk\in\mathbbm{N}, and each r>0r>0,

ℙ[σk(r)−σk−1(r)>Ar2]=ℙ[σ1(1)>A]≤c0e−c1​Aand\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{k}(r)-\sigma_{k-1}(r)>Ar^{2}}}\right]=\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{1}(1)>A}}\right]\leq c_{0}e^{-c_{1}A}\quad\text{and} (6.23)
ℙ[σk(r)−σk−1(r)≥r2]≥c2.\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{k}(r)-\sigma_{k-1}(r)\geq r^{2}}}\right]\geq c_{2}. (6.24)

Proof of (6.21). By expanding σK​(r)N\sigma_{K}(r)^{N} as a sum over KNK^{N} products of NN increments and applying (6.23), we get that for each K∈ℕK\in\mathbbm{N} and each N∈ℕN\in\mathbbm{N},

𝔼[σK(r)N]⪯r2​NKN,\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{K}(r)^{N}}}\right]\preceq r^{2N}K^{N}, (6.25)

with the implicit constant depending only on NN. By setting K=⌊r−(2−ζ)⌋K=\lfloor r^{-(2-\zeta)}\rfloor in (6.25) and applying the Chebyshev inequality, we get

ℙ[σ⌊r−(2−ζ)⌋(r)>rζ/2]⪯rζ​N/2,∀N∈ℕ.\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{\lfloor r^{-(2-\zeta)}\rfloor}(r)>r^{\zeta/2}}}\right]\preceq r^{\zeta N/2},\quad\forall N\in\mathbbm{N}. (6.26)

On the other hand, by a Gaussian tail bound, Brownian scaling, and the reflection principle,

with a universal implicit constant. Combining (6.26) and (6.27) and sending N→∞N\rightarrow\infty gives (6.21) for an appropriate choice of ψ\psi.

Proof of (6.22). By (6.24), r−2​σk​(r)r^{-2}\sigma_{k}(r) stochastically dominates a binomial random variable with kk trials and success probability c2c_{2}. By a standard binomial concentration inequality, ℙ[σ⌊r−(2−ζ)⌋(r)<r−ζ/2]\mathbbm{P}[\sigma_{\lfloor r^{-(2-\zeta)}\rfloor}(r)<r^{-\zeta/2}] decays faster than any positive power of rr as r→0r\rightarrow 0. Combining the two preceding sentences gives (6.22). ∎

The events considered in Lemma 6.8 do not depend on the time parametrization of the Brownian motion ℬ\mathcal{B}, so we can transfer the conclusion of Lemma 6.8 to a statement for random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} using the convergence modulo time parametrization established in [GMS21].

6.2 Equicontinuity of laws

In this section we establish the other part of the compactness criterion of Lemma 6.3 for the function Pρ,⋅εP_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon} of (6.4).

Proposition 6.12 (Equicontinuity of laws).

There exists ξ=ξ⁡(ρ,γ)>0\xi=\xi(\rho,\gamma)>0, and A=A⁡(ρ,γ)>0A=A(\rho,\gamma)>0 such that the following is true with probability tending to 1 as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 and then δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0. For each z,w∈Bρz,w\in B_{\rho} with |z−w|≤δ|z-w|\leq\delta, the Prokhorov distance (w.r.t. the local Skorokhod metric) between the conditional laws given (h,η)(h,\eta) of the stopped processes t↦X^t∧τ^z,εz,εt\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}} and t↦X^t∧τ^w,εw,εt\mapsto\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}} is at most A​δξA\delta^{\xi}.

Unlike for the exponent χ\chi of Proposition 6.5, our proof of Proposition 6.12 does not give an explicit expression for the exponent ξ\xi. We note that a similar continuity result is obtained for Liouville Brownian motion in [GRV16, Proposition 2.19] which allows the authors to a.s. start Liouville Brownian motion from any given point.

The basic idea of the proof of Proposition 6.5 (which differs somewhat from [GRV16]) is that if |z−w|<δ|z-w|<\delta then the embedded, linearly interpolated walk X^z,ε\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon} is likely to disconnect ww from ∂Bρ\partial B_{\rho} before leaving Bδ​(z)B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z) (similar estimates are proven in Section 3). We can then use Lemma 3.9 to couple X^z,ε\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon} and X^w,ε\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon} in such a way that they agree after their exit times from Bδ​(z)B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z) with high probability (see Lemma 6.13). Both of these exit times are likely to be small (Corollary 5.2), so the uniform modulus of continuity estimate of Proposition 6.5 tells us that under such a coupling, the uniform distance between t↦X^t∧τ^z,εz,εt\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}} and t↦X^t∧τ^w,εw,εt\mapsto\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}} is small.

Lemma 6.13.

There exists ξ=ξ⁡(ρ,γ)>0\xi=\xi(\rho,\gamma)>0, and A=A⁡(ρ,γ)>0A=A(\rho,\gamma)>0 such that for each δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), it holds with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 that the following is true. For each z∈Bρz\in B_{\rho} and each x,y∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(Bδ​(z))x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta}(z)), the total variation distance between the conditional laws given (h,η)(h,\eta) of the following two random variables is at most A​δξA\delta^{\xi}:

    The first vertex of 𝒢ε​(∂Bδ​(z))\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z)) hit by a random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} started from yy.

Furthermore, if x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(Bρ∖Bρ−δ)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}\setminus B_{\rho-\delta}), then it holds with probability at least 1−A​δξ1-A\delta^{\xi} that the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} started from xx exits 𝒢ε​(Bρ)\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}) before hitting 𝒱​𝒢ε​(∂Bδ​(η⁡(x)))\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(\eta(x))).

Proof.

Let ρ′=(1+ρ)/2∈(ρ,1)\rho^{\prime}=(1+\rho)/2\in(\rho,1). Proof of Proposition 6.2.

Define Pρ,⋅ε:ℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})) as in (6.4) and let P~ρ,⋅ε\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon} be a continuous approximation of Pρ,⋅εP_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon} as in the discussion just after (6.5). Since Pρ,η⁡(x)ε=P~ρ,η⁡(x)εP_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon}=\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon} for each x∈ε​ℤx\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} it is easily seen that if εn→0\varepsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0 is a sequence along which P~ρ,⋅εn\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon_{n}} converges in law, then also Pρ,⋅εnP_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon_{n}} converges in law to the same limit. Therefore, to prove tightness for Pρ,⋅εP_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon} we only need to prove tightness for P~ρ,⋅ε\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}. The subsequential limits will be continuous since continuity is preserved under uniform convergence.

By the Prokhorov theorem, we need to show that for each ζ>0\zeta>0, there is a compact subset 𝒦ζ\mathcal{K}_{\zeta} of the space 𝒞\mathcal{C} of continuous functions ℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})) such that for each small enough ε>0\varepsilon>0, we have ℙ[P~ρ,⋅ε∈𝒦ζ]≥1−ζ\mathbbm{P}[\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{K}_{\zeta}]\geq 1-\zeta. As a consequence of Lemma 6.3, it suffices to establish the following.

  1. 1.

    (Equicontinuity of laws) For each L>1L>1, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that for each small enough ε>0\varepsilon>0, it holds with (annealed) probability at least 1−1/L1-1/L that for each z,w∈Bρz,w\in B_{\rho} with |z−w|≤δ|z-w|\leq\delta, the Prokhorov distance between the laws Pρ,zεP_{\rho,z}^{\varepsilon} and Pρ,wεP_{\rho,w}^{\varepsilon} is at most 1/L1/L.

  2. 2.

    (Equicontinuity of paths) For each z∈Bρz\in B_{\rho} and each L>1L>1, there exists δ=δ⁡(z,L)>0\delta=\delta(z,L)>0 such that for each small enough ε>0\varepsilon>0, the following is true. With (annealed) probability at least 1−1/L1-1/L,

    |X^sz,ε−X^sz,ε|≤1/L,∀s,t∈[0,τ^z,ε]with|s−t|≤δ.|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{s}-\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{s}|\leq 1/L,\quad\forall s,t\in[0,\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}]\quad\text{with}\quad|s-t|\leq\delta.

While this seems very similar to the statement of Lemma 6.3, there is in fact a difference: the compactness criterion of that lemma require us to check the equicontinuity of laws and paths conditions with quenched probability at least 1−ζ1-\zeta (i.e., conditioned on hh and η\eta), whereas we claim here it suffices to check these conditions with annealed (i.e., unconditional) probability. That this is sufficient follows from a dyadic argument similar to the one in the proof of Lemma 6.3: in particular, we apply the conditions with L=2k/ζL=2^{k}/\zeta for k∈ℕk\in\mathbbm{N}, then take a union bound over kk.

Recall that for z∉Bρz\notin B_{\rho}, Pρ,zεP_{\rho,z}^{\varepsilon} is simply the point mass at the constant t↦xzεt\mapsto x_{z}^{\varepsilon}, which is why we only need to consider z∈Bρz\in B_{\rho}. Conditions 1 and 2 follow from Propositions 6.12 and 6.5, respectively. Finally, the last assertion of the proposition (that X^z\widehat{X}^{z} does not stay at a single point for a positive interval of time until after exiting BρB_{\rho}) is immediate from Proposition 6.14. ∎

7 Identifying the subsequential limit

We equip the space of distributions on ℂ\mathbbm{C} with the usual weak topology (whereby convergence of distributions is equivalent to convergence of the integrals against all smooth compactly supported text functions). We also equip the space of continuous curves ℝ→ℂ\mathbbm{R}\rightarrow\mathbbm{C} with the local uniform topology. We know from Proposition 6.1 that the laws of the functions Pε:ℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))P^{\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})) of (6.1) are tight. By the Prokhorov theorem also the joint laws of (h,η,Pε)(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon}) as ε\varepsilon varies are tight.

Before we explain the main ideas behind the identification of (h,η,P)(h,\eta,P), we point out that a priori we do not even know that PP is determined by (h,η)(h,\eta). To explain what is the issue, note first that if we used the known tightness of PεP^{\varepsilon} given (h,η)(h,\eta), then any subsequential limit PP of the family of laws PεP^{\varepsilon} could only be random insofar as (h,η)(h,\eta) is random: i.e., PP would necessarily be determined by (h,η)(h,\eta). However, this approach would force us to deal with possibly random subsequences ε\varepsilon along which the convergence to PP occurs and would add a serious layer of complication to our arguments. Instead, we prefer to work with the law of the triplet (h,η,Pε)(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon}) which is also tight and consider a subsequential limit (h,η,P)(h,\eta,P). The trade-off, however, is that we do not know a priori that PP, viewed as a random variable in the space 𝒞\mathcal{C} of continuous functions from ℂ\mathbbm{C} to Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})), is measurable with respect to (h,η)(h,\eta): indeed, it is straightforward to construct examples of random variables (X,Yn)(X,Y_{n}) converging to (X,Y)(X,Y) in distribution with YnY_{n} measurable with respect to XX, but YY not measurable with respect to XX. This lack of a priori measurability will require specific arguments in various places (especially in Section 7.3).

We want to show that if (h,η,P)(h,\eta,P) is a subsequential limit of these joint laws, then PzP_{z} is the law of the γ\gamma-Liouville Brownian motion associated with hh started from zz for each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, up to a linear time-change. To do this, we first establish some basic properties (such as the Markov property) of any subsequential limit in Section 7.1. These properties are easy consequences of basic properties of random walk on random planar maps. We then prove a general uniqueness criterion for Markovian time-changed Brownian motions in Section 7.2 (using general theory of Markov processes). This criterion will show that PzP_{z} for z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} is the law as that of Liouville Brownian motion pre-composed with the linear time change t↦c​tt\mapsto ct for some random c>0c>0 which does not depend on cc, but which may depend on (h,η,P)(h,\eta,P). In Section 7.3 we will argue that cc is a.s. equal to a deterministic constant. Then, we will change the time scaling in order to eliminate the dependence of this constant on the choice of subsequence, as discussed at the end of Section 1.4. This will complete the proof of Theorem 1.2. Finally, in Section 7.4 we will explain how to deduce the disk version of the theorem statement, Theorem 1.4, from Theorem 1.2.

We now record some definitions which will play a fundamental role in this section. In each definition, we let P:ℂ→Prob(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)CLOSE)∈𝒞P:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)\in\mathcal{C} be a function from ℂ\mathbbm{C} to the set of probability measures on continuous paths [0,∞)→ℂ[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C} such that PzP_{z} for each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} is supported on paths started from zz. We recall that the topology on the space of such functions PP is defined in Section 6.

Definition 7.1.

We say that PP is Markovian if the following is true. Let z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and let XzX^{z} be sampled from PzP_{z}. For each s≥0s\geq 0, the conditional law of Xs+⋅zX_{s+\cdot}^{z} given Xz|[0,s]X^{z}|_{[0,s]} is a.s. equal to PXsP_{X_{s}}.

Definition 7.2.

We say that PP defines a time-changed Brownian motion if the following is true. Let z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and let XzX^{z} be sampled from PzP_{z}. Then there is a standard planar Brownian motion ℬ\mathcal{B} started from zz and a continuous, strictly increasing process u↦τuu\mapsto\tau_{u} with τ0=0\tau_{0}=0 such that a.s. Xuz=ℬτuX^{z}_{u}=\mathcal{B}_{\tau_{u}} for each u≥0u\geq 0. We say that PP defines a Markovian time changed Brownian motion if also PP is Markovian.

Definition 7.3.

We say that a measure μ\mu on ℂ\mathbbm{C} is invariant for PP if for every Borel set A⊂ℂA\subset\mathbbm{C},

∫ℂPz[Xt∈A]dμ(z)=μ(A)\int_{\mathbbm{C}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X_{t}\in A}}\right]d\mu(z)=\mu(A) (7.1)

We say that μ\mu is reversible for PP if for every pair of Borel sets A,B⊂ℂA,B\subset\mathbbm{C},

∫BPz[Xt∈A]dμ(z)=∫APw[Xt∈B]dμ(w).\int_{B}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X_{t}\in A}}\right]d\mu(z)=\int_{A}P_{w}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X_{t}\in B}}\right]d\mu(w). (7.2)

We note that if μ\mu is reversible for PP, then μ\mu is stationary for PP: just take B=ℂB=\mathbbm{C} in (7.2).

7.1 Properties of subsequential limits

Let (h,η,P)(h,\eta,P) be distributed according to a subsequential scaling limit of the joint law of (h,η,Pε)(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon}) as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. Note that PP is a continuous function ℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})). In this section we will establish some properties for PP which are known to also hold for Liouville Brownian motion due to results in [GRV16]. The key behind these properties is the a priori continuity in the starting point zz of the laws PzP_{z}. More precisely, we show that PP defines a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion and the LQG measure μh\mu_{h} is reversible for PP. The proof of the first statement uses only the Markov property for random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} and the fact that Pε→PP^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P in law w.r.t. the local uniform (in zz) topology. The proof of the second statement uses the fact that the counting measure on vertices of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, weighted by their degree, is reversible for the random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}; the fact that this measure converges weakly to μh\mu_{h} under the SLE/LQG embedding (Corollary A.6); and the aforementioned convergence Pε→PP^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P.

Lemma 7.4.

Almost surely, the random function PP defines a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion in the sense of Definition 7.2.

To check the Markov property for PP in proof of Lemma 7.4, we will use the following criterion for the convergence of conditional laws (see, e.g., [GP20, Lemma 4.3]).

Lemma 7.5.

Let (Xn,Yn)(X_{n},Y_{n}) be a sequence of pairs of random variables taking values in a product of separable metric spaces ΩX×ΩY\Omega_{X}\times\Omega_{Y} and let (X,Y)(X,Y) be another such pair of random variables such that (Xn,Yn)→(X,Y)(X_{n},Y_{n})\rightarrow(X,Y) in law. Suppose further that there is a family of probability measures {Py:y∈ΩY}\{P_{y}:y\in\Omega_{Y}\} on ΩX\Omega_{X}, indexed by ΩY\Omega_{Y}, such that for each bounded continuous function f:ΩX→ℝf:\Omega_{X}\rightarrow\mathbbm{R}, y↦𝔼Py​(f)y\mapsto\mathbbm{E}_{P_{y}}(f) is a measurable function of y∈ΩYy\in\Omega_{Y} and

OPENOPEN(𝔼[f(Xn)|Yn],Yn)→(𝔼PY​(f),YCLOSE)in law.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[f(X_{n})\,|\,Y_{n}}}\right],Y_{n}}}\right)\rightarrow\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbbm{E}_{P_{Y}}(f),Y}}\right)\quad\text{in law}. (7.3)

Then PYP_{Y} is a regular conditional law of XX given YY.

Proof.

This elementary lemma (stated and proved in [GP20, Lemma 4.3]) is a straightforward consequence of the uniqueness of the conditional distribution as a probability kernel (see [Kal02, Theorem 6.5] and preceding definitions) since the assumption that y↦𝔼Py​(f)y\mapsto\mathbbm{E}_{P_{y}}(f) is measurable guarantees that (y,B)↦Py​(B)(y,B)\mapsto P_{y}(B) for y∈ΩYy\in\Omega_{Y} and BB a Borel set in ΩX\Omega_{X} is a probability kernel. ∎

The proof of Lemma 7.4 also involves the topology on curves viewed modulo time parametrization, which we now briefly recall. If β1:[0,Tβ1]→ℂ\beta_{1}:[0,T_{\beta_{1}}]\rightarrow\mathbbm{C} and β2:[0,Tβ2]→ℂ\beta_{2}:[0,T_{\beta_{2}}]\rightarrow\mathbbm{C} are continuous curves defined on possibly different time intervals, we set

𝕕CMP(β1,β2CLOSE):=infϕsupt∈[0,Tβ1]|β1(t)−β2(ϕ(t))|\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}}}\right):=\inf_{\phi}\sup_{t\in[0,T_{\beta_{1}}]}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|\beta_{1}(t)-\beta_{2}(\phi(t))}}\right| (7.4)

where the infimum is over all increasing homeomorphisms ϕ:[0,Tβ1]→[0,Tβ2]\phi:[0,T_{\beta_{1}}]\rightarrow[0,T_{\beta_{2}}] (the CMP stands for “curves modulo parameterization”). It is shown in [AB99, Lemma 2.1] that 𝕕CMP\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}} induces a complete metric on the set of curves viewed modulo time parameterization.

Since we will be working with curves defined for infinite time, we will use a local variant of the metric 𝕕CMP\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}. Suppose β1:[0,∞)→ℂ\beta_{1}:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C} and β2:[0,∞)→ℂ\beta_{2}:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C} are two curves. For r>0r>0, let T1,rT_{1,r} (resp. T2,rT_{2,r}) be the first exit time of β1\beta_{1} (resp. β2\beta_{2}) from the ball Br​(0)B_{r}(0) (or 0 if the curve starts outside Br​(0)B_{r}(0)). We define

OPENOPEN𝕕locCMP​(β1,β2CLOSE):=∫1∞e−r​(1∧𝕕CMP​(β1|[0,T1,r],β2|[0,T2,r]CLOSE))​𝑑r,\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}_{\operatorname{loc}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}}}\right):=\int_{1}^{\infty}e^{-r}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1\wedge\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1}|_{[0,T_{1,r}]},\beta_{2}|_{[0,T_{2,r}]}}}\right)}}\right)\,dr, (7.5)

so that 𝕕locCMP​(βn,β)→0\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}_{\operatorname{loc}}(\beta^{n},\beta)\rightarrow 0 if and only if for Lebesgue a.e. r>0r>0, βn\beta^{n} stopped at its first exit time from Br​(0)B_{r}(0) converges to β\beta stopped at its first exit time from Br​(0)B_{r}(0) with respect to the metric (7.4). We note that the definition (7.4) of OPEN𝕕CMP​(β1|[0,T1,r],β2|[0,T2,r]CLOSE)\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1}|_{[0,T_{1,r}]},\beta_{2}|_{[0,T_{2,r}]}}}\right) makes sense even if one or both of T1,rT_{1,r} or T2,rT_{2,r} is infinite, provided we allow OPEN𝕕CMP​(β1|[0,T1,r],β2|[0,T2,r]CLOSE)=∞\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1}|_{[0,T_{1,r}]},\beta_{2}|_{[0,T_{2,r}]}}}\right)=\infty (this doesn’t pose a problem due to the 1∧1\wedge in (7.5)).

Lemma 7.6.

Almost surely, the γ\gamma-LQG measure μh\mu_{h} is reversible for PP (Definition 7.3).

The idea of the proof of Lemma 7.6 is as follows. The measure on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} which assigns mass degε⁡(x)\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x) to each vertex xx is reversible for the simple random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, and under the embedding x↦η⁡(x)x\mapsto\eta(x) this measure converges in law to μh\mu_{h} (see Corollary A.6). We want to pass this through to the limit to get Lemma 7.6. The next lemma is the main technical input in the proof of Lemma 7.6. It gives us the convergence statements necessary to pass the reversibility of random walk on 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} through to the limit.

For the statement of the lemma, we will use the following notation. For a set A⊂ℂA\subset\mathbbm{C} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, let

Aε:=⋃x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(A)HxεA^{\varepsilon}:=\bigcup_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(A)}H_{x}^{\varepsilon} (7.6)

be the union of the space-filling SLE cells which intersect AA.

Lemma 7.7.

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} be a sequence of ε\varepsilon-values tending to zero along which (h,η,Pε)→(h,η,P)(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P) in law. Let t>0t>0, let U,V⊂ℂU,V\subset\mathbbm{C} be bounded open sets, and define VεV^{\varepsilon} as in (7.6). For each δ>0\delta>0, it holds with probability tending to 1 as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 that

∑x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(U)ℙ¯xε[ηε(X⌊t/ε⌋ε)∈Vε]degε(x)≤6∫U¯Pz[X^t∈V¯]dμh(z)+δ\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(U)}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\eta^{\varepsilon}(X_{\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}^{\varepsilon})\in V^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\leq 6\int_{\overline{U}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in\overline{V}}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)+\delta (7.7)

and

(7.8)
Proof.

Let us now make this more precise. By Corollary A.6, as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 the measure μhε\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon} converges in probability to 6​μh6\mu_{h} w.r.t. the local Prokhorov topology. μhεε→μhandPε→P,as ℰ∋ε→0.\mu_{h^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow\mu_{h}\quad\text{and}\quad P^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P,\quad\text{as $\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$}. (7.10)

By the definition of the topology for PP from Section 6, the Prokhorov distance between PzεP_{z}^{\varepsilon} and PzP_{z} converges to zero uniformly on a neighborhood of U¯\overline{U}. We can now prove the following weaker version of Lemma 7.6.

The inequality of Lemma 7.8 could be converted into an equality if we knew that μh​(∂V)=0\mu_{h}(\partial V)=0 and ∫V¯Pz[X^t∈∂U]dμh(z)=0\int_{\overline{V}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in\partial U}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)=0. This is achieved by means of the following lemma.

Lemma 7.9.

Let A,U⊂ℂA,U\subset\mathbbm{C} be deterministic bounded sets such that AA is closed with zero Lebesgue measure and UU is open. For each t>0t>0, a.s.

μh(A)=0and∫UPz[X^t∈A]dμh(z)=0.\mu_{h}(A)=0\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{U}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in A}}\right]\,d\mu_{h}(z)=0. (7.18)

The statement that μh​(A)=0\mu_{h}(A)=0 a.s. follows from this and straightforward absolute continuity considerations.
