∫UPz[X^t∈A]dμh(z)\displaystyle\int_{U}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in A}}\right]\,d\mu_{h}(z) ≤∫UPz[X^t∈Bδ(A)]dμh(z)\displaystyle\leq\int_{U}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in B_{\delta}(A)}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)
≤∫Bδ​(A)¯Pz[X^t∈U¯]dμh(z)\displaystyle\leq\int_{\overline{B_{\delta}(A)}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in\overline{U}}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)
≤μh​(Bδ​(A)¯).\displaystyle\leq\mu_{h}(\overline{B_{\delta}(A)}). (7.19)

Since μh​(A)=0\mu_{h}(A)=0 and Bδ​(A)¯\overline{B_{\delta}(A)} decreases to AA as δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0 (since AA is closed) we can send δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0 in (7.19) to conclude the proof. ∎

Proof of Lemma 7.6.

Fix t>0t>0. We need to show that a.s. for any two Borel sets A,B⊂ℂA,B\subset\mathbbm{C},

∫APz[X^t∈B]dμh(z)=∫BPz[X^t∈A]dμh(z).\int_{A}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in B}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)=\int_{B}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in A}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z). (7.20)

By Lemmas 7.8 and 7.9, (7.20) holds a.s. if A,BA,B are fixed open sets whose boundaries have zero Lebesgue measure. In fact, these lemmas (applied with UU and VV equal to the interiors of AA and BB) imply that (7.20) holds a.s. if A,BA,B are fixed Borel sets such that ∂A\partial A and ∂B\partial B have zero Lebesgue measure, A¯\overline{A} is equal to closure of the interior of AA, and B¯\overline{B} is equal to closure of the interior of BB.

We now fix R>0R>0 and show that a.s. (7.20) holds for all Borel sets A,B⊂BR​(0)A,B\subset B_{R}(0). We do this using the monotone class theorem. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the collection of subsets of BR​(0)B_{R}(0) which can be expressed in terms of finite unions and intersections of sets of the form Br​(z)B_{r}(z) or BR​(0)∖Br​(z)B_{R}(0)\setminus B_{r}(z) for r∈ℚ∩(0,∞)r\in\mathbbm{Q}\cap(0,\infty) and z∈ℚ2z\in\mathbbm{Q}^{2}. Then 𝒜\mathcal{A} has the following properties. It is countable; it is closed under finite unions and intersections; it generates the Borel σ\sigma-algebra of BR​(0)B_{R}(0); we have BR​(0)∖A∈𝒜B_{R}(0)\setminus A\in\mathcal{A} for each A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}; the boundary of each A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} has zero Lebesgue measure; and for each A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} the closure A¯\overline{A} is also equal to the closure of the interior of AA. From this, we infer that a.s. (7.20) holds simultaneously for each A,B∈𝒜A,B\in\mathcal{A}.

Due to the monotone convergence theorem, for each fixed AA the set of Borel sets BB for which (7.20) holds is closed under increasing unions and intersections. By two applications of the monotone class theorem (one for each of AA and BB), we get that a.s. (7.20) holds for all Borel sets A,B⊂BR​(0)A,B\subset B_{R}(0). Sending R→∞R\rightarrow\infty now concludes the proof. ∎

7.2 Time-changed Brownian motions are determined by invariant measures

We now have two random functions OPENℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)CLOSE)\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right) which each define a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion, namely the subsequential limit PP above and the function which takes z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} to the law of Liouville Brownian motion w.r.t. hh started from zz. These functions have a common reversible measure, namely the γ\gamma-LQG measure. We want to show that these two functions are a.s. the same up to a global linear time change.

Proposition 7.10.

Let P1,P2P^{1},P^{2} be two continuous mappings 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁ℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ)𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right) which each define a Markovian time changed Brownian motion. Assume that there is a non-zero measure μ\mu which is invariant for both P1P^{1} and P2P^{2}. There is a determinsitic constant c>0c>0 such that the following is true. For each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, a process with the law Pz1P_{z}^{1} can be obtained by composing a process with the law Pz2P_{z}^{2} by the linear time change t↦c​tt\mapsto ct.

We note that Proposition 7.10, applied under the conditional law given hh, immediately implies Theorem 1.5 since the conditional law of LBM given hh is a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion which leaves the LQG measure μh\mu_{h} invariant [GRV16].

Proposition 7.10 is a consequence of results in the general theory of positive continuous additive functionals of Brownian motion. To explain how the proposition is proven, we will need to review some of this theory.

In what follows, for z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} we let ℙz\mathbbm{P}_{z} be the law of standard planar Brownian motion ℬ\mathcal{B} started from zz.

Definition 7.11.

A positive continuous additive functional (PCAF) of ℬ\mathcal{B} is a process t↦𝒜tt\mapsto\mathcal{A}_{t}, defined for all possible choices of starting points for ℬ\mathcal{B}, which is adapted to the filtration generated by ℬ\mathcal{B} (completed by null events), such that the following is true. Almost surely, 𝒜0=0\mathcal{A}_{0}=0 and 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} is continuous and non-decreasing in tt. Furthermore, for each s,t≥0s,t\geq 0, a.s.

𝒜s+t=𝒜t+𝒜s∘θt\mathcal{A}_{s+t}=\mathcal{A}_{t}+\mathcal{A}_{s}\circ\theta_{t} (7.21)

where θt\theta_{t} is the shift operator on the state space for ℬ\mathcal{B} defined by θt(ℬ)=ℬt+⋅\theta_{t}(\mathcal{B})=\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}.

Definition 7.11 is related to Proposition 7.10 by the following lemma.

Lemma 7.12.

Suppose that P:ℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))P:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})) is continuous and defines a Markovian time changed Brownian motion as in Definition 7.1. Write ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}} for a process with the law PzP_{z} for some starting point z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}. Let u↦τuu\mapsto\tau_{u} be the time change used to get from standard Brownian motion to ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}}, as in Definition 7.2, and for t≥0t\geq 0 let 𝒜t=τ−1(t):=inf{u≥0:τu=t}\mathcal{A}_{t}=\tau^{-1}(t):=\inf\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{u\geq 0:\tau_{u}=t}}\right\}. Then 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a PCAF for the Brownian motion ℬt=ℬ^𝒜t\mathcal{B}_{t}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}.

For the proof of Lemma 7.12, we need the following elementary fact.

Lemma 7.13.

Suppose that P:ℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))P:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})) is continuous and defines a Markovian time changed Brownian motion. Then PP is strongly Markovian, i.e., if ℬ^z\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z} is sampled from PzP_{z} then for each stopping time σ\sigma for ℬ^z\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}, the conditional law of ℬ^σ+⋅z\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\sigma+\cdot}^{z} given ℬ^z|[0,σ]\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}|_{[0,\sigma]} is Pℬ^σzP_{\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{\sigma}}.

Proof.

If σ\sigma takes on only countably many possible values, the Markov property at time σ\sigma is immediate from the case of a deterministic time. Due to the continuity of z↦Pzz\mapsto P_{z} and the a.s. continuity of a process with the law PP, we can approximate a general stopping time by a sequence of stopping times which take on only countably many possible values to get the result in general. ∎

Proof of Lemma 7.12.

Since u↦τuu\mapsto\tau_{u} is continuous, strictly increasing, and satisfies τ0=0\tau_{0}=0, the same is also true for 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and furthermore τ𝒜t=𝒜τt=t\tau_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}=\mathcal{A}_{\tau_{t}}=t, whence ℬt=ℬ^𝒜t\mathcal{B}_{t}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}} for any t≥0t\geq 0. The time 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} is the smallest u≥0u\geq 0 for which the quadratic variation of ℬ^|[0,u]\widehat{\mathcal{B}}|_{[0,u]} is tt. This implies in particular that 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} is a stopping time for ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}}.

Before arguing that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is adapted, we will first check that for 0≤a<b≤∞0\leq a<b\leq\infty,

OPENOPENσ⁡({ℬ^𝒜a+u}u∈[0,𝒜b−𝒜a]CLOSE)=σ⁡(ℬ|[a,b],{𝒜t−𝒜a}t∈[a,b]CLOSE).\sigma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\{\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+u}\}_{u\in[0,\mathcal{A}_{b}-\mathcal{A}_{a}]}}}\right)=\sigma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathcal{B}|_{[a,b]},\{\mathcal{A}_{t}-\mathcal{A}_{a}\}_{t\in[a,b]}}}\right). (7.22)

Indeed, for any t∈[a,b]t\in[a,b] we have that 𝒜t−𝒜a\mathcal{A}_{t}-\mathcal{A}_{a} is the first time that the quadratic variation of the process ℬ^𝒜a+⋅\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+\cdot} reaches t−at-a, and ℬt=ℬ^𝒜t\mathcal{B}_{t}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}. This shows that the left σ\sigma-algebra in (7.22) contains the right σ\sigma-algebra. For the reverse inclusion, we now observe that for each u∈[0,𝒜b−𝒜a]u\in[0,\mathcal{A}_{b}-\mathcal{A}_{a}] we have ℬ^𝒜a+u=ℬτ𝒜a+u\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+u}=\mathcal{B}_{\tau_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+u}} and τ𝒜a+u=inf{t≥a:𝒜t−𝒜a=u}\tau_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+u}=\inf\{t\geq a:\mathcal{A}_{t}-\mathcal{A}_{a}=u\}.

By (7.22) (applied with (a,b)=(0,t)(a,b)=(0,t) and with (a,b)=(t,∞)(a,b)=(t,\infty)) and Lemma 7.13 (applied with σ=𝒜t\sigma=\mathcal{A}_{t}), we get that the pairs (ℬt+⋅,𝒜t+⋅−𝒜t)(\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot},\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t}) and (ℬ|[0,t],𝒜|[0,t])(\mathcal{B}|_{[0,t]},\mathcal{A}|_{[0,t]}) are conditionally independent given ℬ^𝒜t\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}, equivalently, given ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t}.

We will now argue that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a.s. determined by ℬ\mathcal{B}. Indeed, it follows from the above that if we condition on ℬ\mathcal{B} then the process 𝒜\mathcal{A} is continuous with conditionally independent increments. It follows that the conditional law of 𝒜\mathcal{A} given ℬ\mathcal{B} is that of a Gaussian process: indeed, it is easy to see from the independence of the increments that the centered process is a continuous martingale with deterministic quadratic variation, conditionally on ℬ\mathcal{B}. But, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is non-negative, so the conditional law of 𝒜\mathcal{A} given ℬ\mathcal{B} must be a point mass at some ℬ\mathcal{B}-measurable continuous increasing function. That is, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a.s. determined by ℬ\mathcal{B} (which implies that also τ=𝒜−1\tau=\mathcal{A}^{-1} and ℬ^⋅=ℬτ⁡(⋅)\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\cdot}=\mathcal{B}_{\tau(\cdot)} are a.s. determined by ℬ\mathcal{B}) .

Since (ℬt+⋅,𝒜t+⋅−𝒜t)(\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot},\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t}) and (ℬ|[0,t],𝒜|[0,t])(\mathcal{B}|_{[0,t]},\mathcal{A}|_{[0,t]}) are conditionally independent given ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t}, it follows that 𝒜|[0,t]\mathcal{A}|_{[0,t]} is a.s. determined by ℬ|[0,t]\mathcal{B}|_{[0,t]} and that 𝒜t+⋅−𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t} is a.s. determined by ℬ|[t,∞)\mathcal{B}|_{[t,\infty)}. In particular, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is adapted to the natural filtration of ℬ\mathcal{B} completed by null events and 𝒜t+⋅−𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t} is a.s. given by a functional of the shifted process ℬt+⋅\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}. Hence for each t,s≥0t,s\geq 0 there is a measurable function Ft,sF_{t,s} from continuous paths in ℂ\mathbbm{C} to [0,∞)[0,\infty) such that a.s. Ft,s(ℬt+⋅)=𝒜t+s−𝒜tF_{t,s}(\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot})=\mathcal{A}_{t+s}-\mathcal{A}_{t}, i.e.,

𝒜t+s=𝒜t+Ft,s∘θt.\mathcal{A}_{t+s}=\mathcal{A}_{t}+F_{t,s}\circ\theta_{t}. (7.23)

We need to check that the functional Ft,sF_{t,s} does not depend on tt. The process ℬt+⋅\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot} is obtained by parameterizing ℬ^𝒜t+⋅\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot} by its quadratic variation, so the functional which takes in ℬ^𝒜t+⋅\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot} and outputs ℬt+⋅\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot} does not depend on tt. Since ℬt+⋅\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot} a.s. determines 𝒜t+⋅−𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t}, it follows that ℬt+⋅\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot} a.s. determines ℬ^𝒜t+⋅\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot}, i.e., there is a measurable functional which takes in ℬt+⋅\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot} and a.s. outputs ℬ^𝒜t+⋅\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot}. Since the functional which takes in ℬ^𝒜t+⋅\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot} and outputs ℬt+⋅\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot} does not depend on tt, it follows that the functional which goes in the opposite direction can be taken to not depend on tt either. Since ℬ^𝒜t+⋅\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot} determines 𝒜t+⋅−𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t} in a manner which does not depend on tt, we get that ℬt+⋅\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot} a.s. determines 𝒜t+⋅−𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t} in a manner which does not depend on tt, i.e., Ft,sF_{t,s} does not depend on tt. In particular, Ft,s=F0,sF_{t,s}=F_{0,s} is the functional which a.s. takes ℬ\mathcal{B} to 𝒜s\mathcal{A}_{s}. By (7.23), 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a PCAF. ∎

PCAFs are in bijective correspondence with so-called Revuz measures, defined as follows.

Definition 7.14.

A Revuz measure is a measure μ\mu on ℂ\mathbbm{C} such that μ⁡(A)=0\mu(A)=0 for each set AA which is polar for the Brownian motion ℬ\mathcal{B} (i.e., it is a.s. never hit by ℬ\mathcal{B}).

From [FOT11, Theorem 5.1.3] (here the Hunt process in the theorem statement is planar Brownian motion), we know that there is a bijective correspondence between PCAFs and Revuz measures. For each PCAF 𝒜\mathcal{A} there exists a unique Revuz measure μ\mu such that for any two bounded continuous functions f,g:ℂ→[0,∞)f,g:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow[0,\infty),

∫ℂ𝔼z[∫0tf(Bs)d𝒜s]g(z)dz=∫0t∫ℂ∫ℂps(z,w)f(w)g(z)dμ(w)dzds\int_{\mathbbm{C}}\mathbbm{E}_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\int_{0}^{t}f(B_{s})\,d\mathcal{A}_{s}}}\right]g(z)\,dz=\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbbm{C}}\int_{\mathbbm{C}}p_{s}(z,w)f(w)g(z)\,d\mu(w)\,dz\,ds (7.24)

and for every Revuz measure μ\mu there exists a unique PCAF 𝒜\mathcal{A} for which (7.24) holds. Here, d​𝒜sd\mathcal{A}_{s} is interpreted as a Lebesgue-Stieljes measure. We call μ\mu the Revuz measure of 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

For a PCAF 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we can define the time-changed process

ℬ^u:=ℬτu,whereτu:=inf{t≥0:𝒜t=u}.\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{u}:=\mathcal{B}_{\tau_{u}},\quad\text{where}\quad\tau_{u}:=\inf\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{t\geq 0:\mathcal{A}_{t}=u}}\right\}. (7.25)

Then the law of ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}} for varying choices of starting points defines a Markovian time changed Brownian motion in the sense of Definition 7.1. By [FOT11, Theorem 6.2.1(i)], the Revuz measure of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is reversible (hence invariant) for ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}}. In fact, the Revuz measure of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the only invariant measure for ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}}, up to multiplication by a deterministic constant, as shown by the following lemma.

Lemma 7.15.

Let PP define a Markovian time changed Brownian motion and assume that z↦Pzz\mapsto P_{z} is continuous. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the corresponding PCAF as in Lemma 7.12 and let μ\mu be the Revuz measure of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Then any other invariant measure for PP is a deterministic constant multiple of μ\mu.

To prove Lemma 7.15, we will use a general criterion for the uniqueness of invariant measures for Markov processes; see, e.g., [RY99, Chapter X, Section 3]. One of the hypotheses of this criterion involves the resolvent associated with PP, which is the operator Rλ:L∞​(ℂ)→L∞​(ℂ)R^{\lambda}:L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C})\rightarrow L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C}) defined by

ℛλf(z)=∫0∞e−λ​tEz[f(ℬ^t)]dt,\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}E_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{t})}}\right]\,dt, (7.26)

where EzE_{z} denotes expectation w.r.t. PzP_{z}.

Lemma 7.16.

Let PP define a Markovian time changed Brownian motion and assume that z↦Pzz\mapsto P_{z} is continuous. If f∈L∞​(ℂ)f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C}), then ℛλ​f\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f is continuous. That is, PP is strongly Feller.

Proof.

The proof is based on the fact that hitting distributions of Brownian motion (i.e., harmonic measure) depend continuously on the starting point in the total variation sense. This allows us to show that if |z−w||z-w| is small then we can couple processes sampled from PzP_{z} and PwP_{w} so that they agree after leaving a small ball centered at zz. When the processes are coupled together in this way, it is not hard to check that for a fixed choice of f∈L∞​(ℂ)f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C}), it holds that |ℛλ​f​(z)−ℛλ​f​(w)||\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z)-\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(w)| is small. A similar argument is used to prove the strong Feller property for Liouville Brownian motion in [GRV14, Theorem 2.4].

Step 1: defining the coupling. Fix z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and ε>0\varepsilon>0. A path sampled from the law PzP_{z} a.s. does not stay constant for any non-trivial interval of time, so we can find δ0∈(0,1)\delta_{0}\in(0,1) such that

Pz[ℬ^ exits Bδ0​(z) before time ε]≥1−ε.P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ exits $B_{\delta_{0}}(z)$ before time $\varepsilon$}}}\right]\geq 1-\varepsilon. (7.27)

Since PwP_{w} depends continuously on ww in the Prokhorov distance, there exists δ1∈(0,δ0]\delta_{1}\in(0,\delta_{0}] such that

Pw[ℬ^ exits Bδ0​(z) before time 2​ε]≥1−2ε,∀w∈Bδ1(z).P_{w}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ exits $B_{\delta_{0}}(z)$ before time $2\varepsilon$}}}\right]\geq 1-2\varepsilon,\quad\forall w\in B_{\delta_{1}}(z). (7.28)

The harmonic measure on ∂Bδ0​(z)\partial B_{\delta_{0}}(z) as viewed from w∈Bδ0​(z)w\in B_{\delta_{0}}(z) (which is the same as that of Brownian motion and is therefore known explicitly) depends continuously on ww in the total variation sense. Therefore, we can find δ2∈(0,δ0]\delta_{2}\in(0,\delta_{0}] such that for any w∈Bδ2​(z)w\in B_{\delta_{2}}(z), we can find a coupling of ℬ^z∼Pz\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}\sim P_{z} and ℬ^w∼Pw\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}\sim P_{w} such that with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon, ℬ^z\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z} and ℬ^w\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w} exit Bδ0​(z)B_{\delta_{0}}(z) at the same point. Let TzT_{z} and TwT_{w} denote the exit times of ℬ^z\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z} and ℬ^w\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w} from Bδ0​(z)B_{\delta_{0}}(z), respectively. Then our coupling is such that ℙ[ℬ^Tzz=ℬ^Tww]≥1−ε\mathbbm{P}[\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{T_{z}}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{T_{w}}]\geq 1-\varepsilon. By the strong Markov property (Lemma 7.13) we can re-couple so that

ℙ[ℬ^zTz+s=ℬ^wTw+s,∀s≥0]≥1−ε.\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{T_{z}+s}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{T_{w}+s},\>\forall s\geq 0}}\right]\geq 1-\varepsilon. (7.29)

Henceforth fix such a coupling and let

E:={ℬ^zTz+s=ℬ^wTw+s,∀s≥0}∩{Tz∨Tw≤2ε},E:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{T_{z}+s}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{T_{w}+s},\>\forall s\geq 0}}\right\}\cap\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{T_{z}\vee T_{w}\leq 2\varepsilon}}\right\}, (7.30)

so that by (7.28) and (7.29) we have ℙ⁡[E]≥1−5​ε\mathbbm{P}[E]\geq 1-5\varepsilon.

Step 2: bounding the resolvent. Now fix f∈L∞​(ℂ)f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C}). By considering the positive and negative parts of ff separately, we can assume without loss of generality that f≥0f\geq 0. We have

ℛλ​f​(z)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z) =𝔼[∫0∞e−λ​tf(ℬ^zt)dt]\displaystyle=\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]
=𝔼[𝟙E∫0∞e−λ​tf(ℬ^zt)dt]+𝔼[𝟙Ec∫0∞e−λ​tf(ℬ^zt)dt]\displaystyle=\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E^{c}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]
=𝔼[𝟙E∫0Tze−λ​tf(ℬ^zt)dt]+𝔼[𝟙E∫0∞e−λ⁡(s+Tz)f(ℬ^zs+Tz)ds]+𝔼[𝟙Ec∫0∞e−λ​tf(ℬ^zt)dt]\displaystyle=\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\int_{0}^{T_{z}}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda(s+T_{z})}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{s+T_{z}})\,ds}}\right]+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E^{c}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]

and similarly with ww in place of zz. By subtracting the formulas for zz and ww and using the triangle inequality, we get

|ℛλ​f​(z)−ℛλ​f​(w)|\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z)-\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(w)| ≤𝔼[𝟙E(∫0Tze−λ​t​f​(ℬ^tz)​𝑑t+∫0Twe−λ​t​f​(ℬ^tw)​𝑑tCLOSE)]\displaystyle\leq\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\int_{0}^{T_{z}}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt+\int_{0}^{T_{w}}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{t})\,dt}}\right)}}\right]
+𝔼[𝟙E∫0∞|e−λ⁡(s+Tz)f(ℬ^zs+Tz)−e−λ⁡(s+Tw)f(ℬ^ws+Tw)|ds]\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|e^{-\lambda(s+T_{z})}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{s+T_{z}})-e^{-\lambda(s+T_{w})}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{s+T_{w}})}}\right|\,ds}}\right]
+𝔼[𝟙Ec∫0∞e−λ​t(f⁡(ℬ^tz)+f⁡(ℬ^tw)CLOSE)dt]\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E^{c}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})+f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{t})}}\right)\,dt}}\right] (7.31)

On EE, we have Tz∨Tw≤2​εT_{z}\vee T_{w}\leq 2\varepsilon, which implies that the first expectation on the right side of (7.31) is at most 4​ε​‖f‖∞4\varepsilon\|f\|_{\infty}. Furthermore, on EE we have f⁡(ℬ^s+Tzz)=f⁡(ℬ^s+Tww)f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{s+T_{z}})=f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{s+T_{w}}) for each s≥0s\geq 0, so the second expectation on the right side of (7.31) is equal to

𝔼[𝟙E|e−λ​Tz−e−λ​Tw|∫0∞e−λ​sf(ℬ^zs+Tz)ds],\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|e^{-\lambda T_{z}}-e^{-\lambda T_{w}}}}\right|\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda s}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{s+T_{z}})\,ds}}\right], (7.32)

which in turn is at most (1−e−2​λ​ε)​λ−1​‖f‖∞(1-e^{-2\lambda\varepsilon})\lambda^{-1}\|f\|_{\infty} since Tz∨Tw≤2​εT_{z}\vee T_{w}\leq 2\varepsilon on EE. Finally, since ℙ⁡[Ec]≤4​ε\mathbbm{P}[E^{c}]\leq 4\varepsilon the last term on the right side of (7.31) is at most 8​ε​λ−1​‖f‖∞8\varepsilon\lambda^{-1}\|f\|_{\infty}. Plugging the above estimates into (7.31) gives

|ℛλ​f​(z)−ℛλ​f​(w)|≤oε​(1)​‖f‖∞|\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z)-\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(w)|\leq o_{\varepsilon}(1)\|f\|_{\infty} (7.33)

where the oε​(1)o_{\varepsilon}(1) tends to zero as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 at a rate depending only on λ\lambda. Since ε>0\varepsilon>0 was arbitrary we infer that ℛλ​f\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f is continuous at zz. ∎

Proof of Lemma 7.15.

As discussed just after (7.25), the measure μ\mu is reversible, hence invariant, for PP. If ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}} is sampled from PzP_{z} for some z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, then ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}} is a time change of Brownian motion, so every open subset of ℂ\mathbbm{C} is recurrent for ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}}. Moreover, Lemma 7.16 says that PP is strongly Feller. By [RY99, Chapter X, Proposition 3.9], the process ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}} is Harris recurrent w.r.t. the measure μ\mu, i.e., each open set A⊂ℂA\subset\mathbbm{C} with μ⁡(A)>0\mu(A)>0 is recurrent for ℬ^\widehat{\mathcal{B}}. From this and the ergodic theorem for additive functionals of Brownian motion [RY99, Chapter X, Theorem 3.12] (see also [RY99, Chapter X, Exercise 3.14]) one obtains the uniqueness of the invariant measure for PP up to multiplication by a deterministic constant factor. ∎

Proof of Proposition 7.10.

Let 𝒜1\mathcal{A}^{1} and 𝒜2\mathcal{A}^{2} be the PCAFs associated with P1P^{1} and P2P^{2}, as in Lemma 7.12. Let μ1\mu^{1} and μ2\mu^{2} be the Revuz measures associated with these PCAFs. By the discussion just after (7.25), we know that μ1\mu^{1} (resp. μ2\mu^{2}) is invariant for P1P^{1} (resp. P2P^{2}). By Lemma 7.15, we know that each of P1P^{1} and P2P^{2} has a unique invariant measure, up to multiplication by a deterministic constant factor. Therefore, there are deterministic constants c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0 such that a.s. μ1=c1​μ\mu^{1}=c_{1}\mu and μ2=c2​μ\mu^{2}=c_{2}\mu. Since the Revuz measure uniquely determines the PCAF, we get that 𝒜1=(c1/c2)​𝒜2\mathcal{A}^{1}=(c_{1}/c_{2})\mathcal{A}^{2}. By the definitions of 𝒜1\mathcal{A}^{1} and 𝒜2\mathcal{A}^{2}, this implies Proposition 7.10. ∎

7.3 Proof of Theorem 1.2

As above, let (h,η,P)(h,\eta,P) be a subsequential limit of the joint laws of (h,η,Pε)(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon}) as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. Let us first record what we get from Proposition 7.10.

Lemma 7.17.

There is a random variable c>0c>0, which is measurable with respect to the σ\sigma-algebra generated by (h,η,P)(h,\eta,P) (completed by null sets), such that a.s. for each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} the law PzP_{z} is the same as the conditional law given hh of the Liouville Brownian motion started from zz pre-composed with the time change t↦c​tt\mapsto ct.

Proof.

By Lemma 7.4, PP defines a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion and by Lemma 7.6 the γ\gamma-LQG measure μh\mu_{h} is reversible, hence invariant, for PP. It is shown in [GRV16] that the same properties are a.s. true for the function PLBM:ℂ→Prob⁡(C⁡([0,∞),ℂ))P^{\operatorname{LBM}}:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})) which maps zz to the conditional law of LBM started from zz given hh. The lemma therefore follows from Proposition 7.10 applied under the conditional law given (h,η,P)(h,\eta,P). ∎

We claim the following.

Lemma 7.18.

The random variable c>0c>0 from Lemma 7.17 is a.s. equal to a deterministic constant.

We will prove Lemma 7.18 just below. We first assume the lemma and conclude the proof of Theorem 1.2.

Proof of Theorem 1.2, assuming Lemma 7.18.

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} be a sequence of ε\varepsilon-values tending to zero along which (h,η,Pε)→(h,η,P)(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P) in law. Lemmas 7.17 and 7.18 together imply that there is a deterministic constant c>0c>0 such that a.s. PzP_{z} for each z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} is the law of Liouville Brownian motion started from zz pre-composed with the time change t↦c​tt\mapsto ct. The constant cc may depend on the choice of subsequence ℰ\mathcal{E} (equivalently, cc may depend on the law of (h,η,P)(h,\eta,P)). We do not know how to rule this out so we get around the issue as follows.

Recall that, in the notation used in Section 6 and in the theorem statement, PεP^{\varepsilon} is the conditional law of (X^tz,ε)t≥0=(η(X⋅/εz,ε))t≥0(\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t})_{t\geq 0}=(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{\cdot/\varepsilon}))_{t\geq 0} given (h,η)(h,\eta). On the other hand, the theorem asserts that the conditional law of (η⁡(Xmε​tz,ε))t≥0(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t}))_{t\geq 0} given (h,η)(h,\eta) converges to the conditional law of LBM given hh, where mεm_{\varepsilon} is as in (1.7). Equivalently, ε​mε\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon} is the annealed median exit time of X^0,ε\widehat{X}^{0,\varepsilon} from B1/2B_{1/2}. Since X^0,ε\widehat{X}^{0,\varepsilon} converges in law as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 along ℰ\mathcal{E}, it follows that ε​mε\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon} converges to a constant 𝔪>0\mathfrak{m}>0 as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 along ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Let P^ε\widehat{P}^{\varepsilon} be the conditional law of (η⁡(Xmε​tz,ε))t≥0=(X^ε​mε​tz,ε)t≥0(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t}))_{t\geq 0}=(\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}t})_{t\geq 0} given (h,η)(h,\eta). From the convergence ε​mε→𝔪\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}\rightarrow\mathfrak{m} along ℰ\mathcal{E}, we infer that along ℰ\mathcal{E} the joint law of (h,η,P^ε)(h,\eta,\widehat{P}^{\varepsilon}) converges to the joint law of (h,η,P^)(h,\eta,\widehat{P}), where P^\widehat{P} is defined as follows. For z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C}, P^z\widehat{P}_{z} is the law of the path t↦X^𝔪​tzt\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z}_{\mathfrak{m}t} where X^z\widehat{X}^{z} is sampled from PzP_{z}. Equivalently, P^z\widehat{P}_{z} is the law of Liouville Brownian motion started from zz pre-composed with the time change t↦c​𝔪​tt\mapsto c\mathfrak{m}t.

By the definition of mεm_{\varepsilon}, the annealed median exit time of X^ε​mε​t0,ε\widehat{X}^{0,\varepsilon}_{\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}t} from B1/2B_{1/2} is 1, hence the annealed median exit time of a path with the law P^0\widehat{P}_{0} from B1/2B_{1/2} is 1. This fixes the value of the constant c​𝔪c\mathfrak{m} independently of the choice of subsequence. We therefore get that (h,η,P^ε)(h,\eta,\widehat{P}^{\varepsilon}) converges in law to (h,η,PLBM)(h,\eta,P^{\operatorname{LBM}}) as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, not just subsequentially, where here PzLBMP^{\operatorname{LBM}}_{z} for z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} is the conditional law given hh of (1.6), i.e., LBM with respect to hh started from zz pre-composed with the time-change t↦m0​tt\mapsto m_{0}t, where m0m_{0} is the median of the exit time of the B1/2B_{1/2} of this LBM. Since PLBMP^{\operatorname{LBM}} is a.s. determined by hh, it follows from an elementary fact in probability theory (analogous to the fact that convergence in distribution to a constant implies convergence in probability, see, e.g., [SS13, Lemma 4.5]) that in fact Pε→PLBMP^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P^{\operatorname{LBM}} in probability.

The bounds (1.8) for mεm_{\varepsilon} follow since we have show that for every sequence of ε\varepsilon’s tending to zero, there is a further subsequence along which ε​mε\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon} converges to a positive number. ∎

It remains to prove Lemma 7.18. Our argument will use the following minor generalization of Definition 2.1.

Definition 7.19.

A curve-decorated quantum surface is an equivalence class of triples (D,h,η)(D,h,\eta) where D⊂ℂD\subset\mathbbm{C} is open, hh is a distribution on DD, and η\eta is a curve in D¯\overline{D}, under the equivalence relation whereby two such triples (D,h,η)(D,h,\eta) and (D~,h~,η~)(\widetilde{D},\widetilde{h},\widetilde{\eta}) are equivalent if there is a conformal map ϕ:D~→h~\phi:\widetilde{D}\rightarrow\widetilde{h} which extends to a homeomorphism D~∪∂D~→D∪∂D\widetilde{D}\cup\partial\widetilde{D}\rightarrow D\cup\partial D (with ∂D~\partial\widetilde{D} and ∂D\partial D viewed as collections of prime ends) such that hh and h~\widetilde{h} are related as in (2.1) and ϕ∘η~=η\phi\circ\widetilde{\eta}=\eta. We similarly define a curve-decorated quantum surface with more than one curve.

The idea of the proof of Lemma 7.18 is as follows. Let a<u<ba<u<b and let X^\widehat{X} be a random curve sampled from the law Pη⁡(u)P_{\eta(u)} and stopped upon exiting η⁡([a,b])\eta([a,b]). It is easily seen that the constant cc is a.s. determined by the triple (η⁡([a,b]),h|η⁡([a,b]),X^)(\eta([a,b]),h|_{\eta([a,b])},\widehat{X}). Indeed, since the time parametrization of LBM is locally determined by the GFF, from this data we can see how we need to scale the time parametrization of X^\widehat{X} in order to get LBM w.r.t. hh (see Lemma 7.22). In fact, cc is a.s. determined by (η⁡([a,b]),h|η⁡([a,b]),X^)(\eta([a,b]),h|_{\eta([a,b])},\widehat{X}) viewed as a curve-decorated quantum surface since both LBM and the adjacency graph of cells obey the LQG coordinate change formula (by [Ber15, Theorem 1.4]).

If a<b<a~<b~a<b<\widetilde{a}<\widetilde{b}, then [DMS21, Theorem 1.9] tells us that the curve-decorated quantum surfaces corresponding to (η⁡([a,b]),h|η⁡([a,b]))(\eta([a,b]),h|_{\eta([a,b])}) and (η⁡([a~,b~]),h|η⁡([a~,b~]))(\eta([\widetilde{a},\widetilde{b}]),h|_{\eta([\widetilde{a},\widetilde{b}])}) are independent. If we knew that PP were in some sense locally determined by (h,η)(h,\eta), then we would be done: indeed, if we knew this then the preceding paragraph would tell us that cc is a.s. determined by each of two different independent random variables, which means that cc is independent from itself and hence a.s. constant. However, we do not know that PP is locally determined or even determined at all by (h,η)(h,\eta), even though PεP^{\varepsilon} is a.s. determined by (h,η)(h,\eta). This is because the property of one random variable being a.s. determined by another is not in general preserved under convergence in law. However, we know that PεP^{\varepsilon} is a.s. determined by (h,η)(h,\eta) and moreover independence is preserved under convergence in law. So, we can make the above argument precise by appealing to the subsequential convergence in law (h,η,Pε)→(h,η,P)(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P).

We now describe the framework in which we will prove the independence property needed to get Lemma 7.18. See Figure 4 for an illustration. Fix finite times a<u<ba<u<b. Let UU be the connected component of the interior of η⁡([a,b])\eta([a,b]) which contains η⁡(u)\eta(u) (such a component exists a.s. since a.s. η⁡(u)∉∂η⁡([a,b])\eta(u)\notin\partial\eta([a,b])). Due to the difference in topology for space-filling SLEκ in the phases κ≥8\kappa\geq 8 and κ∈(4,8)\kappa\in(4,8), when γ∈(0,2]\gamma\in(0,\sqrt{2}] the set UU is the entire interior of η⁡([a,b])\eta([a,b]) but for γ∈(2,2)\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2) a.s. UU is a proper subset of the interior of η⁡([a,b])\eta([a,b]). The domain UU is homeomorphic to the unit disk and there is a unique time interval [a′,b′][a^{\prime},b^{\prime}] for which η⁡([a′,b′])=U¯\eta([a^{\prime},b^{\prime}])=\overline{U}. Again, for γ∈(0,2]\gamma\in(0,\sqrt{2}] we have [a,b]=[a′,b′][a,b]=[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}] but this is a.s. not the case for γ∈(2,2)\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2). Also let X^\widehat{X} be sampled from the law Pη⁡(u)P_{\eta(u)} and let TT be the first exit time of X^\widehat{X} from UU.

We are interested in the curve(s)-decorated quantum surfaces (U,h,η|[a′,b′],X^|[0,T])(U,h,\eta|_{[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]},\widehat{X}|_{[0,T]}). We could just work directly with this curve-decorated quantum surface, but we find it more clear to instead specify a particular parametrization which depends only on the curve-decorated quantum surface (not on the original choice of equivalence class representative). Let ϕ:𝔻→U\phi:\mathbbm{D}\rightarrow U be the unique conformal map such that ϕ⁡(0)=η⁡(u)\phi(0)=\eta(u) and ϕ⁡(a′)=1\phi(a^{\prime})=1. Recalling (2.1), we define

h𝔻:=h∘ϕ+Qlog|ϕ′|,η𝔻:=ϕ−1∘η|[a′,b′],andX^𝔻:=ϕ−1∘X^|[0,T].h^{\mathbbm{D}}:=h\circ\phi+Q\log|\phi^{\prime}|,\quad\eta^{\mathbbm{D}}:=\phi^{-1}\circ\eta|_{[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]},\quad\text{and}\quad\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D}}:=\phi^{-1}\circ\widehat{X}|_{[0,T]}.

Then (𝔻,h𝔻,η𝔻,X^𝔻)=(U,h,η|[a′,b′],X^|[0,T])(\mathbbm{D},h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D}})=(U,h,\eta|_{[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]},\widehat{X}|_{[0,T]}) as curve-decorated quantum surfaces. We define

OPENP0𝔻:=(Pη⁡(u)-law of X^𝔻CLOSE),P^{\mathbbm{D}}_{0}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{$P_{\eta(u)}$-law of $\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D}}$}}}\right), (7.34)

so P0𝔻P^{\mathbbm{D}}_{0} is a random probability measure on curves in 𝔻\mathbbm{D} started from 0 and stopped upon hitting ∂𝔻\partial\mathbbm{D}. Our proof of Lemma 7.18 is based on the following three lemmas.

Lemma 7.20.

Let cc be the random variable from Lemma 7.17. In the setting described just above, a.s. P0𝔻P^{\mathbbm{D}}_{0} is the law of LBM with respect to hh started from 0 and stopped upon hitting ∂𝔻\partial\mathbbm{D}, pre-composed with the time change t↦c​tt\mapsto ct.

Proof.

This is immediate from the γ\gamma-LQG coordinate change formula for LBM [Ber15, Theorem 1.3] and for the adjacency graph of cells of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} (which follows from the coordinate change formula for the LQG area measure plus the conformal invariance of space-filling SLE). ∎

Lemma 7.21.

Let a<u<ba<u<b and a~<u~<b~\widetilde{a}<\widetilde{u}<\widetilde{b} be two triples of times and assume that b<a~b<\widetilde{a}. Define h𝔻,η𝔻,h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}}, and P0𝔻P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}} as above for a,u,ba,u,b and define h~𝔻,η~𝔻,\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}}, and P~0𝔻\widetilde{P}^{\mathbbm{D}}_{0} as above with a~,u~,b~\widetilde{a},\widetilde{u},\widetilde{b} in place of a,u,ba,u,b. Then the triples (h𝔻,η𝔻,P0𝔻)(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}) and (h~𝔻,η~𝔻,P~0𝔻)(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}) are independent.

Proof.

Fix a time 𝕤∈(b,a~)\mathbbm{s}\in(b,\widetilde{a}). By [DMS21, Theorem 1.9], the past / future curve-decorated quantum surfaces

OPENOPEN(η((−∞,𝕤]),h|η((−∞,𝕤]),η|(−∞,𝕤])and(η⁡([𝕤,∞)),h|η⁡([𝕤,∞)),η|[𝕤,∞)CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\eta((-\infty,\mathbbm{s}]),h|_{\eta((-\infty,\mathbbm{s}])},\eta|_{(-\infty,\mathbbm{s}]}}}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\eta([\mathbbm{s},\infty)),h|_{\eta([\mathbbm{s},\infty))},\eta|_{[\mathbbm{s},\infty)}}}\right) (7.35)

are independent. By definition, (h𝔻,η𝔻)(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}}) (resp. (h~𝔻,η~𝔻)(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}}) is determined by the first (resp. second) quantum surface in (7.35). Hence (h𝔻,η𝔻)(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}}) and (h~𝔻,η~𝔻)(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}}) are independent. We need to show that the independence continues to hold if we also include the random laws P0𝔻P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}} and P~0𝔻\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}.

The basic idea of the proof is that for each ε>0\varepsilon>0, the discrete analogs of the laws P0𝔻P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}} and P~0𝔻\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}} in the ε\varepsilon-mated-CRT map setting are determined by the first and second curve-decorated quantum surfaces in (7.35), respectively, so one has the desired independence statement with these discrete laws used in place of P0𝔻P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}} and P~0𝔻\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}. This will allow us to later use the fact that independence (unlike the condition that one random variable determines another) is preserved under taking limits in law.

Let us now define the discrete analogs of the laws P0𝔻P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}} and P~0𝔻\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}} which we will work with. Recalling the times a′,b′∈[a,b]a^{\prime},b^{\prime}\in[a,b] defined above, for ε>0\varepsilon>0 let 𝒯ε\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon} be the subgraph of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} induced by the vertex set [a′,b′]∩(ε​ℤ)[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}). Let ∂𝒯ε\partial\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon} be the set of vertices x∈𝒱​𝒯εx\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon} which are joined by an edge of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} to a vertex which is not in 𝒯ε\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}. By the Brownian motion definition of the mated-CRT map (1.2), for small enough ε>0\varepsilon>0 both 𝒯ε\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon} and ∂𝒯ε\partial\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon} are determined by the left/right boundary length process (L−L𝕤,R−R𝕤)|(−∞,𝕤](L-L_{\mathbbm{s}},R-R_{\mathbbm{s}})|_{(-\infty,\mathbbm{s}]}, which in turn is a.s. determined by the first curve-decorated quantum surface (7.35).

Let uε:=ε⁡⌈u/ε⌉u^{\varepsilon}:=\varepsilon\lceil u/\varepsilon\rceil, so that uε∈ε​ℤu^{\varepsilon}\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}. Conditional on (h,η)(h,\eta), let XεX^{\varepsilon} be a simple random walk on 𝒯ε\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon} stopped at the first time JεJ^{\varepsilon} that it hits ∂𝒯ε\partial\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}. Recalling the conformal map ϕ:𝔻→U\phi:\mathbbm{D}\rightarrow U above, for t∈[0,ε​Jε]∩(ε​ℤ)t\in[0,\varepsilon J^{\varepsilon}]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}), let X^t𝔻,ε:=ϕ−1​(η⁡(t/ε))\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}_{t}:=\phi^{-1}(\eta(t/\varepsilon)). We extend the definition of X^𝔻,ε\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} to all of [0,ε​Jε][0,\varepsilon J^{\varepsilon}] by piecewise linear interpolation at constant speed. Let P0𝔻,εP_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} be the conditional law of X^t𝔻,ε\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}_{t} given (h,η)(h,\eta). By the preceding paragraph and the definition of ϕ\phi, the law P0𝔻,εP_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} is a.s. determined by the first quantum surface in (7.35).

If we define P~0𝔻,ε\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} similarly but with a~,u~,b~\widetilde{a},\widetilde{u},\widetilde{b} in place of a,u,ba,u,b, then P~0𝔻,ε\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} is a.s. determined by the second quantum surface in (7.35). As a consequence, the triples (h𝔻,η𝔻,P0𝔻,ε)(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}) and (h~𝔻,η~𝔻,P~0𝔻,ε)(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}) are independent.

We now argue that if ℰ\mathcal{E} is a subsequence along which (h,η,Pε)→(h,η,P)(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P) in law, then we also have

(h𝔻,η𝔻,P0𝔻,ε,h~𝔻,η~𝔻,P~0𝔻,ε)→(h𝔻,η𝔻,P0𝔻,h~𝔻,η~𝔻,P~0𝔻)(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon},\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}) (7.36)

in law as ℰ∋ε→0\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, which concludes the proof since indepenendence is preserved under convergence of joint laws.

To get (7.36), we note that a process X^𝔻,ε\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} sampled from P0𝔻,εP_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} is almost the same as the process ϕ−1​(X^ε)\phi^{-1}(\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon}), where X^ε\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon} is sampled from Pη⁡(uε)εP_{\eta(u^{\varepsilon})}^{\varepsilon} and stopped at the first time it hits a point in η⁡(ε​ℤ∖[a′,b′])\eta(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\setminus[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]), except for the following minor difference. The process X^𝔻,ε\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} travels along straight line segments between the times when it hits points of ϕ−1​(η​(ε​ℤ))\phi^{-1}(\eta(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})), whereas the path ϕ−1​(X^ε)\phi^{-1}(\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon}) instead travels along paths whose images under ϕ\phi are straight line segments.

It is easily seen that the conformal map ϕ\phi can be extended to a homeomorphism U¯→𝔻¯\overline{U}\rightarrow\overline{\mathbbm{D}}: indeed, by the flow line construction of space-filling SLE [MS17, Section 1.2.3], ∂U\partial U is a finite union of SLEκ-type curves which intersect only at their endpoints. In particular, ∂U\partial U is a Jordan curve so the desired extension of ϕ\phi follows from [Pom92, Theorem 2.6]. By the above continuity and the preceding paragraph (note that ϕ\phi does not depend on ε\varepsilon), the Prokhorov distance between the law P0𝔻,εP_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} and the Pη⁡(hε)εP_{\eta(h^{\varepsilon})}^{\varepsilon}-law of ϕ−1​(X^ε)\phi^{-1}(\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon}) tends to zero in probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. On the other hand, it is easily seen from the convergence (h,η,Pε)→(h,η,P)(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P) in law that (7.36) holds if we replace P0𝔻,εP_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon} by the Pη⁡(uε)εP_{\eta(u^{\varepsilon})}^{\varepsilon}-law of ϕ−1​(X^ε)\phi^{-1}(\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon}), and we make the analogous replacement made for P~0𝔻,ε\widetilde{P}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}_{0}. Thus (7.36) holds. ∎

Lemma 7.22.

Let hh be a random distribution on a domain D⊂ℂD\subset\mathbbm{C} whose law is locally absolutely continuous w.r.t. the law of the GFF on DD. Let z∈Dz\in D and let XX be the Liouville Brownian motion w.r.t. hh, stopped at the first time that it exists DD. For any c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0 with c1≠c2c_{1}\not=c_{2}, the laws of (h,(Xc1​t)t≥0)(h,(X_{c_{1}t})_{t\geq 0}) and (h,(Xc2​t)t≥0)(h,(X_{c_{2}t})_{t\geq 0}) are mutually singular.

Proof.

Let BB be a standard planar Brownian motion started from zz and stopped when it exits DD, sampled independently from hh. By the definition of Liouville Brownian motion, there is a random σ⁡(h,B)\sigma(h,B)-measurable function ϕ:[0,∞)→[0,∞)\phi:[0,\infty)\rightarrow[0,\infty) such that (h,(Xt)t≥0)​=𝑑​(h,Bϕ−1​(t))t≥0(h,(X_{t})_{t\geq 0})\overset{d}{=}(h,B_{\phi^{-1}(t)})_{t\geq 0}. We have the following trivial elementary probability fact: if YY is a random variable and ff and gg are measurable functions such that ℙ[f(Y)≠g(Y)]=1\mathbbm{P}[f(Y)\not=g(Y)]=1, then the laws of (Y,f⁡(Y))(Y,f(Y)) and (Y,g⁡(Y))(Y,g(Y)) are mutually singular. To get the lemma, we apply this fact with Y=(h,B)Y=(h,B) and ff and gg given by the functionals which take (h,B)(h,B) to Bϕ−1​(c1​t)B_{\phi^{-1}(c_{1}t)} and Bϕ−1​(c2​t)B_{\phi^{-1}(c_{2}t)}, respectively. ∎

Remark 7.23.

The proof of Lemma 7.22 relies crucially on the fact that we are looking at the joint law of hh and the Liouville Brownian motion. At least for some choices of hh, the marginal laws of (Xc1​t)t≥0(X_{c_{1}t})_{t\geq 0} and (Xc2​t)t≥0(X_{c_{2}t})_{t\geq 0} are mutually absolutely continuous. Indeed, if hh is the restriction to DD of a zero-boundary GFF on a larger domain D′D^{\prime} with D¯⊂D′\overline{D}\subset D^{\prime}, then the laws of h+log⁡c1h+\log c_{1} and h+log⁡c2h+\log c_{2}, hence also the laws of (h+log⁡c1,(Xc1​t)t≥0)(h+\log c_{1},(X_{c_{1}t})_{t\geq 0}) and (h+log⁡c2,(Xc2​t)t≥0)(h+\log c_{2},(X_{c_{2}t})_{t\geq 0}) are mutually absolutely continuous (see, e.g., [MS16a, Proposition 3.4]).

Proof of Lemma 7.18.

Let c>0c>0 be as in Lemma 7.17 and assume the setup of Lemma 7.21. Due to Lemma 7.20 (applied to each of the triples a,u,ba,u,b and a~,u~,b~\widetilde{a},\widetilde{u},\widetilde{b}) followed by Lemma 7.22, we know that cc can a.s. be expressed as a measurable function of either of the two triples (h𝔻,η𝔻,P0𝔻)(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}) or (h~𝔻,η~𝔻,P~0𝔻)(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}). However, by Lemma 7.21 these two triples are independent from each other. Hence cc is independent from itself so cc must be a.s. equal to a deterministic constant. ∎

7.4 From whole plane to disk

In this short section we explain why Theorem 1.2 (convergence to Liouville Brownian motion in the whole plane case with the LQG embedding) implies Theorem 1.4 (convergence to Liouville Brownian motion in the disk case, under the Tutte embedding). The arguments in this section are quite close to (but more detailed than) [GMS21, Section 3.3], see in particular [GMS21, Lemma 3.6].

As recalled in Section 2.2, let (ℂ,h,0,∞)(\mathbbm{C},h,0,\infty) denote a γ\gamma-quantum cone (corresponding to a weight W=4−γ2W=4-\gamma^{2}, in the terminology of [DMS21]), and let η\eta be an independent space-filling SLEκ, with κ=16/γ2\kappa=16/\gamma^{2}, reparametrised by γ\gamma-quantum area, i.e., μh​(η⁡([s,t]))=t−s\mu_{h}(\eta([s,t]))=t-s for any s<ts<t. Then by [DMS21, Theorem 1.9], the quantum surface 𝒲\mathcal{W} obtained by restricting hh to the interior DD of η⁡([0,∞))\eta([0,\infty)), that is, 𝒲=(D,h|D,0,∞)\mathcal{W}=(D,h|_{D},0,\infty) has the distribution of a quantum wedge with weight W=2−γ2/2W=2-\gamma^{2}/2. Note that this corresponds to an α\alpha-quantum wedge where α=3​γ/2\alpha=3\gamma/2 (see Table 1.1 in [DMS21]), where α\alpha denotes the strength of the logarithmic singularity near 0 in a half-plane embedding. In particular, since α\alpha-quantum wedges are thick (have the topology of a half-plane) for α≤Q\alpha\leq Q, and are thin (given by a Poissonian chain of so-called “beads”) if α∈(Q,Q+γ/2)\alpha\in(Q,Q+\gamma/2), this means that 𝒲\mathcal{W} is thick for γ≤2\gamma\leq\sqrt{2} and thin if γ∈(2,2)\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2). Furthermore, given DD, in the thick case η\eta is simply an independent chordal space-filling SLEκ in DD from 0 to ∞\infty, reparametrised by its area, while in the thin case it is a concatenation of space-filling chordal SLEκ in each bead of 𝒲\mathcal{W}. Basically, the idea of the proof is to use the absolute continuity of the law of the quantum disk w.r.t. the law of 𝒲\mathcal{W} (or a single bead of 𝒲\mathcal{W} if γ∈(2,2)\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2)) away from their respective marked points.

Consider first the case γ≤2\gamma\leq\sqrt{2} so that 𝒲\mathcal{W} is a thick quantum wedge. Fix a large constant C>1C>1. We apply a conformal map D→ℍD\rightarrow\mathbbm{H} to get a new parametrization (ℍ,hC𝒲,−C,∞)(\mathbbm{H},h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C},-C,\infty) of the quantum surface 𝒲\mathcal{W}, chosen so that the two marked points are −C-C and ∞\infty and the νhC𝒲\nu_{h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}}-length of [−C,0][-C,0] is 1 (this last choice of normalization is somewhat arbitrary — 1 can be replaced by any number larger than 1/21/2). Let ηC𝒲\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C} be the image of η|[0,∞)\eta|_{[0,\infty)} under this conformal map, so that ηC𝒲\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C} is a chordal SLEκ from −C-C to ∞\infty in ℍ\mathbbm{H} parameterized by γ\gamma-LQG mass w.r.t. hC𝒲h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}. Recall that Liouville Brownian motion satisfies the quantum surface change of coordinates (2.1) by Theorem 1.4 in [Ber15]. From this and Theorem 1.2, we deduce the analog of Theorem 1.2 for (hC𝒲,ηC𝒲)(h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C},\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}): if we condition on (hC𝒲,ηC𝒲)(h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C},\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}), then the conditional law of the random walk on the adjacency graph of cells ηC𝒲​([x−ε,x])\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}([x-\varepsilon,x]) for x∈ε​ℕx\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{N}, stopped at the first time it hits a cell which intersects ∂ℍ\partial\mathbbm{H}, linearly interpolated and time changed appropriately, converges as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 to the law of Liouville Brownian motion w.r.t hC𝒲h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}} stopped upon hitting ∂ℍ\partial\mathbbm{H}. Moreover, the convergence is uniform over the choice of starting point in any compact subset of ℍ¯\overline{\mathbbm{H}}.

We now use an argument of absolute continuity between the above 3​γ2\frac{3\gamma}{2}-quantum wedge and a singly marked quantum disk 𝒟\mathcal{D} with unit area and unit boundary length. Let us choose a parametrization (ℍ,h𝒟,∞)(\mathbbm{H},h^{\mathcal{D}},\infty) of 𝒟\mathcal{D} so that the marked point is at ∞\infty and the νh\nu_{h}-lengths of (−∞,0](-\infty,0] and [0,∞)[0,\infty) are each equal to 1/21/2. Using the definitions of the quantum wedge and the quantum disk from [DMS21, Sections 4.2 and 4.5], it is easily verified that the law of the restriction of h𝒟h^{\mathcal{D}} to any fixed ball B=ℍ∩B⁡(0,R)B=\mathbbm{H}\cap B(0,R) centered at 0 with R<CR<C say, is absolutely continuous with respect to the law of the field hC𝒲h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C} (here it is important that we are considering the fields away from the marked points, since they have different logarithmic singularities at their respective marked points). Note, however, that the reverse absolute continuity statement is not true since, e.g., μhC𝒲​(B)\mu_{h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}}(B) can be greater than 1.

Let η𝒟\eta^{\mathcal{D}} be a space-filling SLEκ loop in 𝔻\mathbbm{D} based at ∞\infty, parametrized by μh𝒟\mu_{h^{\mathcal{D}}}-mass. Let ⪯C𝒲\preceq_{C}^{\mathcal{W}} (resp. ⪯𝒟\preceq^{\mathcal{D}}) be the total ordering on ℚ2∩B\mathbbm{Q}^{2}\cap B induced by ηC𝒲\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}} (resp. η𝒟\eta^{\mathcal{D}}). By Proposition A.10, we know that ⪯C𝒲→⪯𝒟\preceq_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}\rightarrow\preceq^{\mathcal{D}} in the total variation sense as C→∞C\rightarrow\infty. Note that ⪯C𝒲\preceq_{C}^{\mathcal{W}} determines each segment of ηC𝒲\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}} which is contained in BB viewed modulo time parameterization, as well as the order in which ηC𝒲\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}} traces these segments; a similar statement holds for η𝒟\eta^{\mathcal{D}}.

Let ℱC𝒲,ε\mathcal{F}_{C}^{\mathcal{W},\varepsilon} be the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the space-filling SLE cells η⁡([x−ε,x])\eta([x-\varepsilon,x]) for x∈ε​ℕx\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{N} which intersect BB. Note that ℱC𝒲,ε⊂σ⁡(hC𝒲,ηC𝒲)\mathcal{F}_{C}^{\mathcal{W},\varepsilon}\subset\sigma(h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}},\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}). We now combine the total variation convergence in the preceding paragraph with the absolute continuity in the paragraph before that, each applied with BB replaced by a slightly larger ball B′⊃BB^{\prime}\supset B (which contains all of the cells which intersect BB with probability tending to 1 as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0). We infer that there is an event ECεE_{C}^{\varepsilon} such that ℙ⁡[ECε]→1\mathbbm{P}[E_{C}^{\varepsilon}]\rightarrow 1 as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 and then C→∞C\rightarrow\infty, such that the following is true. For any p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), there exists q=q⁡(p)∈(0,1)q=q(p)\in(0,1) such that if F∈ℱC𝒲,εF\in\mathcal{F}_{C}^{\mathcal{W},\varepsilon} has probability at most qq and F~\widetilde{F} denotes the corresponding event defined with (h𝒟,η𝒟)(h^{\mathcal{D}},\eta^{\mathcal{D}}) in place of (hC𝒲,ηC𝒲)(h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}},\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}), then ℙ⁡[F~∩ECε]≤p\mathbbm{P}[\widetilde{F}\cap E_{C}^{\varepsilon}]\leq p.

Liouville Brownian motion started from z∈ℍz\in\mathbbm{H} leaves the upper half plane almost surely in finite time and its law depends continuously on its starting point. From this, we infer that for any fixed compact set K⊂ℍ¯K\subset\overline{\mathbbm{H}} we can choose the ball BB to be sufficiently large so that the infimum over all z∈Kz\in K of the probability that Liouville Brownian motion w.r.t. h𝒟h^{\mathcal{D}} started from zz hits ∂ℍ\partial\mathbbm{H} before leaving B¯\overline{B} is as close to 1 as we like. Due to this fact and the preceding paragraph, we see that the analog of Theorem 1.2 for (hC𝒲,ηC𝒲)(h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}},\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}) discussed above implies the corresponding analog of Theorem 1.2 for (h𝒟,η𝒟)(h^{\mathcal{D}},\eta^{\mathcal{D}}).

We now change coordinates back to 𝔻\mathbbm{D}. By a slight abuse of notation we do not change our notation for fields / curves, so that now h𝒟h^{\mathcal{D}} is a field on 𝔻\mathbbm{D} and η𝒟:[0,1]→𝔻¯\eta^{\mathcal{D}}:[0,1]\rightarrow\overline{\mathbbm{D}}. From the preceding paragraph and the invariance of LBM under LQG coordinate change [Ber15, Theorem 1.4], we infer that the statement of Theorem 1.4 holds (at least in the case γ≤2\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}) but with the SLE/LQG embedding x↦η𝒟​(x)x\mapsto\eta^{\mathcal{D}}(x) instead of the Tutte embedding. As we recalled in (1.5), the Tutte embedding ψε\psi_{\varepsilon} of the mated-CRT map associated with (h𝒟,η𝒟)(h^{\mathcal{D}},\eta^{\mathcal{D}}) satisfies

maxx∈𝒱​𝒢ε⁡|ψε​(x)−η𝒟​(x)|→0\max_{x\in\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}}|\psi_{\varepsilon}(x)-\eta^{\mathcal{D}}(x)|\to 0

in distribution; see (3.3) in Section 3.4 of [GMS21]. We thus obtain Theorem 1.4.

We now discuss the thin case where γ∈(2,2)\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2). The idea is to apply a similar argument except we restrict ourselves to a given bead of 𝒲\mathcal{W}. One issue with this is that it is not obvious how to describe the law of the bead containing a given point zz. However, since we assume the statement of Theorem 1.2 (which holds uniformly over an arbitrary compact set KK of the wedge embedded into ℍ\mathbbm{H}), the idea is to consider the first time that some bead of 𝒲\mathcal{W} has area greater than one, say. We then have a quenched invariance principle uniformly over points of the intersection of KK with this bead, and by choosing KK sufficiently large, we can ensure that with probability as close to one as desired, this intersection contains some given arbitrary compact set of the bead. Moreover, since the beads of 𝒲\mathcal{W} have a Poissonian structure, the first bead with area greater than one has a law which is mutually absolutely continuous w.r.t. the law of a doubly marked quantum disk conditioned to have area at least one away from their respective marked points [DMS21, Section 4.4] (for γ=8/3\gamma=\sqrt{8/3}, the beads are exactly quantum disks but for other values of γ\gamma they have different log singularities at the marked points). The proof in the case when γ∈(2,2)\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2) then follows from the same local absolute continuity argument as in the case when γ≤2\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}, except that we use this single bead instead of the whole of 𝒲\mathcal{W}.

Appendix A Appendix

In this appendix we prove some basic facts about the γ\gamma-LQG measure. The proofs of these facts are standard and do not use any of the other results described in the paper, so are collected here to avoid distracting from the main argument.

A.1 Basic estimates for the LQG area measure

Let γ∈(0,2)\gamma\in(0,2) and let hh be the circle average embedding of a γ\gamma-quantum cone, as in Definition 2.2. In this subsection we record some basic estimates for the γ\gamma-LQG measure μh\mu_{h} associated with hh.

Lemma A.1 (LQG mass of Euclidean balls).

Fix a small parameter ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1). With polynomially high probability as δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0,

δ(2+γ)2/2+ζ≤μh​(Bδ​(z))≤δ(2−γ)2/2−ζ,∀z∈B1−δ.\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}/2+\zeta}\leq\mu_{h}(B_{\delta}(z))\leq\delta^{(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\zeta},\quad\forall z\in B_{1-\delta}. (A.1)
Proof.

Let h0h^{0} be a whole-plane GFF with the additive constant chosen so that h10​(0)=0h^{0}_{1}(0)=0. It is shown in various places in the literature, e.g., [DG18, Lemma 3.8], that with polynomially high probability as δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0, one has

δ(2+γ)2/2+ζ≤μh0​(Bδ​(z))≤δ(2−γ)2/2−ζ,∀z∈𝔻.\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}/2+\zeta}\leq\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{\delta}(z))\leq\delta^{(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\zeta},\quad\forall z\in\mathbbm{D}. (A.2)

Now let h~:=h0−γlog|⋅|\widetilde{h}:=h^{0}-\gamma\log|\cdot|. Then h~|𝔻​=𝑑​h|𝔻\widetilde{h}|_{\mathbbm{D}}\overset{d}{=}h|_{\mathbbm{D}}. Hence it suffices to prove that with polynomially high probability as δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0, the bound (A.2) holds with h~\widetilde{h} in place of hh. The lower bound for μh0​(Bδ​(z))\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{\delta}(z)) in (A.2) with h~\widetilde{h} in place of hh is immediate from (A.2) since (h~−h0)|𝔻(\widetilde{h}-h^{0})|_{\mathbbm{D}} is a non-negative function. So, we only need to prove the upper bound. We do this using (A.2) and a union bound over exponential scales. The argument is entirely standard but we give the details for the sake of completeness.

For k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbbm{N}_{0}, let

h~k:=h~(e−k⋅)−h~e−k(0)andAk:=Be−k(0)∖Be−k−1(0).\widetilde{h}_{k}:=\widetilde{h}(e^{-k}\cdot)-\widetilde{h}_{e^{-k}}(0)\quad\text{and}\quad A_{k}:=B_{e^{-k}}(0)\setminus B_{e^{-k-1}}(0). (A.3)

By the scale invariance of the law of h0h^{0} modulo additive constant, h~k​=𝑑​h~\widetilde{h}_{k}\overset{d}{=}\widetilde{h}. The restriction of h~−h0=−γlog|⋅|\widetilde{h}-h^{0}=-\gamma\log|\cdot| to the annulus A0A_{0} is bounded above by a finite γ\gamma-dependent constant. We can therefore apply (A.2) with ek​δe^{k}\delta in place of δ\delta, followed by a union bound over all k∈[0,(1−ζ)​log⁡δ−1]ℤk\in[0,(1-\zeta)\log\delta^{-1}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}, to get that with polynomially high probability as δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0,

μh~k​(Bek​δ​(z))≤(ek​δ)(2−γ)2/2−ζ,∀z∈A0,∀k∈[0,(1−ζ)​log⁡δ−1]ℤ.\mu_{\widetilde{h}_{k}}(B_{e^{k}\delta}(z))\leq(e^{k}\delta)^{(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\zeta},\quad\forall z\in A_{0},\quad\forall k\in[0,(1-\zeta)\log\delta^{-1}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}. (A.4)

By the coordinate change formula for the LQG area measure [DS11, Proposition 2.1] and the definition of h~k\widetilde{h}_{k}, a.s.

μh~​(Bδ​(z))=eγ​h~e−k​(0)​e−γ​Q​k​μh~k​(Bek​δ​(ek​z))=eγ​he−k0​(0)​e−γ⁡(Q−γ)​k​μh~k​(Bek​δ​(ek​z)),∀δ>0,∀k∈ℕ.\mu_{\widetilde{h}}(B_{\delta}(z))=e^{\gamma\widetilde{h}_{e^{-k}}(0)}e^{-\gamma Qk}\mu_{\widetilde{h}_{k}}(B_{e^{k}\delta}(e^{k}z))=e^{\gamma h^{0}_{e^{-k}}(0)}e^{-\gamma(Q-\gamma)k}\mu_{\widetilde{h}_{k}}(B_{e^{k}\delta}(e^{k}z)),\quad\forall\delta>0,\quad\forall k\in\mathbbm{N}.

This is sufficient since ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1) is arbitrary. ∎

Lemma A.2.

Fix c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1). For each ζ>0\zeta>0, it holds with polynomially high probability as δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0 that

supz∈B1−δsupw∈Bδ​(z)μh​(Bδ​(z))μh​(Bc​δ​(w))≤δ−γ2/2−ζ.\sup_{z\in B_{1-\delta}}\sup_{w\in B_{\delta}(z)}\frac{\mu_{h}(B_{\delta}(z))}{\mu_{h}(B_{c\delta}(w))}\leq\delta^{-\gamma^{2}/2-\zeta}. (A.7)

See also [BGRV16, Theorem A.1] for a related (and in some ways more precise) statement.

Proof of Lemma A.2.

We first prove the lemma with hh replaced by a whole-plane GFF h0h^{0} with the additive constant chosen so that h10​(0)=0h^{0}_{1}(0)=0 and with B1−δB_{1-\delta} replaced by 𝔻\mathbbm{D}. For each w∈𝔻w\in\mathbbm{D}, the random variable μh0​(Bc​(w))\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{c}(w)) has negative moments of all orders which are bounded above by constants which depend on cc, but not on ww [RV14a, Theorem 2.12]. A union bound therefore shows that

ℙ[infz∈𝔻μh(Bc(w))≤δζ/2]=Oδ(δp),∀p>0.\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\inf_{z\in\mathbbm{D}}\mu_{h}(B_{c}(w))\leq\delta^{\zeta/2}}}\right]=O_{\delta}(\delta^{p}),\quad\forall p>0. (A.8)

Since μh0​(𝔻)\mu_{h^{0}}(\mathbbm{D}) has positive moments up to order 4/γ24/\gamma^{2} [RV14a, Theorem 2.11],

ℙ[μh0(𝔻)>δ−γ2/2−ζ/2]≤δ2+2​ζ/γ2+oδ​(1).\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mu_{h^{0}}(\mathbbm{D})>\delta^{-\gamma^{2}/2-\zeta/2}}}\right]\leq\delta^{2+2\zeta/\gamma^{2}+o_{\delta}(1)}. (A.9)

Therefore,

ℙ[supw∈𝔻μh0​(𝔻)μh0​(Bc​(w))>δ−γ2/2−ζ]≤δ2+2​ζ/γ2+oδ​(1).\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sup_{w\in\mathbbm{D}}\frac{\mu_{h^{0}}(\mathbbm{D})}{\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{c}(w))}>\delta^{-\gamma^{2}/2-\zeta}}}\right]\leq\delta^{2+2\zeta/\gamma^{2}+o_{\delta}(1)}. (A.10)

Due to the translation and scale invariance of the law of h0h^{0}, modulo additive constant, the law of supw∈Bδ​(z)μh0​(Bδ​(z))μh0​(Bc​δ​(w))\sup_{w\in B_{\delta}(z)}\frac{\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{\delta}(z))}{\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{c\delta}(w))} does not depend on zz or δ\delta. We may therefore apply (A.10) and take a union bound over Oδ​(δ−2)O_{\delta}(\delta^{-2}) points in 𝔻\mathbbm{D} to obtain that with polynomially high probability as δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0, the bound (A.7) with h0h^{0} in place of hh and 𝔻\mathbbm{D} in place of B1−δB_{1-\delta}. The lemma statement statement for hh follows from the preceding estimate for h0h^{0} via a multiscale argument as in the proof of Lemma A.1. ∎

A.2 Comparing sums over cells to integrals against LQG measure

Assume that we are in the setting of Section 2.3, so that hh is the circle average embedding of a γ\gamma-quantum cone, η\eta is a space-filling SLE16/γ2{}_{16/\gamma^{2}} sampled independently from hh and then parametrized by μh\mu_{h}-mass, 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} is the associated ε\varepsilon-mated CRT map, and Hxε:=η⁡([x−ε,x])H_{x}^{\varepsilon}:=\eta([x-\varepsilon,x]). We also recall the constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1). In this subsection we will give a quantitative version of the intuitively obvious statement that the counting measure on cells of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} approximates the γ\gamma-LQG measure when ε\varepsilon is small.

Lemma A.4.

There exists α=α⁡(γ)>0\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)>0 and β=β⁡(γ)>0\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0 such that with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, the following is true. If we let μh\mu_{h} be the γ\gamma-LQG area measure induced by hh, then

ε−1​∫Df⁡(z)​d​μh​(z)−ε−1+α≤∑x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)f⁡(wxε)≤ε−1​∫Bεα​(D)f⁡(z)​d​μh​(z)+ε−1+α\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{D}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)-\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}\leq\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha} (A.15)

simultaneously for every choice of DD and ff as above.

Proof.

Fix OPENq∈(0,2(2+γ)2CLOSE)q\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,\tfrac{2}{(2+\gamma)^{2}}}}\right) chosen in a manner depending only on γ\gamma and let β∈(0,q/2)\beta\in(0,q/2). By Lemma 2.4, it holds with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 that

OPENdiam⁡(HxεCLOSE)≤εq,∀x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(Bρ).\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\varepsilon^{q},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}). (A.16)

By a standard tail estimate for the γ\gamma-LQG measure (e.g., [GHS19a, Lemma A.3] together with the Chebyshev inequality), it holds with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 that

μh(Bρ+εqCLOSE)≤ε−q/2.\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{\rho+\varepsilon^{q}}}}\right)\leq\varepsilon^{-q/2}. (A.17)

Since ff is ε−β\varepsilon^{-\beta}-Lipschitz continuous and μh​(Hxε)=ε\mu_{h}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})=\varepsilon for each x∈𝒱​𝒢εx\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}, the bound (A.16) implies that for each x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D),

f⁡(wxε)=ε−1​∫Hxεf⁡(wxε)​d​μh​(z)\displaystyle f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})=\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})\,d\mu_{h}(z) ≤ε−1​∫Hxεf⁡(z)​d​μh​(z)+ε−β​diam⁡(Hxε)\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{-\beta}\operatorname{diam}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})
≤ε−1∫Hxεf(z)dμh(z)+εq−βby (A.16).\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{q-\beta}\quad\text{by~\eqref{eqn-cell-sum-diam}}. (A.18)

Similarly, we also have

f⁡(wxε)≥ε−1​∫Hxεf⁡(z)​d​μh​(z)−εq−β.f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})\geq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)-\varepsilon^{q-\beta}. (A.19)

By (A.16), for each x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D) we have Hxε⊂Bεq​(D)H_{x}^{\varepsilon}\subset B_{\varepsilon^{q}}(D) and the intersection of any two of these cells has zero μh\mu_{h}-mass. We can therefore sum (A.18) over all x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D) to get

∑x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)f⁡(wxε)\displaystyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon}) ≤ε−1​∫Bεq​(D)f⁡(z)​d​μh​(z)+εq−β​#​𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{q}}(D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{q-\beta}\#\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)
≤ε−1​∫Bεq​(D)f⁡(z)​d​μh​(z)+ε−1+q/2−β,\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{q}}(D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{-1+q/2-\beta}, (A.20)

where in the last line we used (A.17) and the fact that each cell HxεH_{x}^{\varepsilon} for x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D) is contained in BρB_{\rho} and has μh\mu_{h}-mass ε\varepsilon. This gives the upper bound in (A.15) with α=min⁡{q,q/2−β}\alpha=\min\{q,q/2-\beta\}.

Since DD is contained in the union of the cells HxεH_{x}^{\varepsilon} for x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D), we can similarly obtain the lower bound in (A.20) by summing (A.19) of all x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D). ∎

We will also need a variant of Lemma A.4 where we weight each cell by its degree, whose proof is somewhat more involved. The extra factor of 6 in this case comes from the fact that 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} is a planar triangulation, so it has average degree 6 (see e.g. e.g. [AHNR16] where the same factor 6 occurs for similar reasons).

Lemma A.5.

There exists α=α⁡(γ)>0\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)>0 and β=β⁡(γ)>0\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0 such that with polynomially high probability as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, the following is true. Let D⊂BρD\subset B_{\rho}, f:Bεα​(D)→ℝf:B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)\rightarrow\mathbbm{R}, and wxεw_{x}^{\varepsilon} for x∈𝒢ε​(D)x\in\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D) be as in Lemma A.4. Then

6​ε−1​∫D∖Bεα​(∂D)f⁡(z)​d​μh​(z)−ε−1+α≤∑x∈𝒱​𝒢ε​(D)fε​(wxε)​degε⁡(x)≤6​ε−1​∫Bεα​(D)f⁡(z)​d​μh​(z)+ε−1+α,6\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{D\setminus B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(\partial D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)-\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}\leq\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}f^{\varepsilon}(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\leq 6\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}, (A.21)

simultaneously for every choice of DD and ff as above.

We note that Lemma A.5 implies the following corollary.

Corollary A.6.

For ε>0\varepsilon>0, let μhε\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon} be the measure whose restriction to each cell HxεH_{x}^{\varepsilon} for x∈ε​ℤx\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} is equal to degε⁡(x)​μh|Hxε\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\mu_{h}|_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}. Then as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, we have μhε→6​μh\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow 6\mu_{h} in probability w.r.t. the vague topology.

Proof.

It is immediate from Lemma A.5 that μhε|Bρ→6​μh|Bρ\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon}|_{B_{\rho}}\rightarrow 6\mu_{h}|_{B_{\rho}} weakly. The corollary follows from this and the scale invariance property of the γ\gamma-quantum cone (Lemma 2.3). ∎

The idea of the proof of Lemma A.5 is as follows. Recall that a triangulation with boundary is a planar map 𝒯\mathcal{T} whose faces all have three edges, except for one special face called the external face. The perimeter Perim⁡(𝒯)\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}) is the degree of the external face. Due to the Euler characteristic formula, if 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a triangulation with boundary whose perimeter is much smaller than its total number of vertices #​𝒱​(𝒯)\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T}), then #​ℰ​(𝒯)\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T}) is close to 3​#​ℰ​(𝒯)3\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T}) (Lemma A.7), which implies that the sum of the degrees of the vertices of 𝒯\mathcal{T} is close to 6​#​𝒱​(𝒯)6\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T}).

Now assume for simplicity that ε−1/2\varepsilon^{-1/2} is an integer. We consider for each y∈ε1/2​ℤy\in\varepsilon^{1/2}\mathbbm{Z} the subgraph 𝒯yε\mathcal{T}_{y}^{\varepsilon} of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} induced by the set of vertices x∈(y−ε1/2,y]∩(εℤ)x\in(y-\varepsilon^{1/2},y]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}). Equivalently, this is the subgraph of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} induces by the vertices of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} whose corresponding cells are contained in the cell Hyε1/2H_{y}^{\varepsilon^{1/2}} of 𝒢ε1/2\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon^{1/2}}). Then 𝒯yε\mathcal{T}_{y}^{\varepsilon} is a triangulation with boundary, having ε−1/2\varepsilon^{-1/2} vertices in total (not just on its boundary). Furthermore, a basic Brownian motion estimates shows that the perimeter of 𝒯yε\mathcal{T}_{y}^{\varepsilon} is extremely unlikely to be much larger than ε−1/4\varepsilon^{-1/4} (Lemma A.8). Consequently, the sum of the degrees of the vetices of 𝒯yε\mathcal{T}_{y}^{\varepsilon} is typically of order 6ε−1/26\varepsilon^{-1/2}. Combining this with Lemma A.4, applied with ε1/2\varepsilon^{1/2} in place of ε\varepsilon, then leads to Lemma A.5.

Lemma A.7.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a triangulation with boundary, so that the degree of each face of 𝒯\mathcal{T} except for the external face is equal to 3. Let Perim⁡(𝒯)\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}) be the degree of the external face. Then

#​ℰ​(𝒯)=3​#​𝒱​(𝒯)+3−Perim⁡(𝒯).\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})=3\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T})+3-\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}). (A.22)
Proof.

Let ℱ⁡(𝒯)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T}) be the set of faces of 𝒯\mathcal{T}, including the external face. By the Euler characteristic formula,

#​ℰ​(𝒯)=#​𝒱​(𝒯)+#​ℱ​(𝒯)−2.\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})=\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T})+\#\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})-2. (A.23)

Each edge of 𝒯\mathcal{T} either lies on the boundary of exactly two faces in ℱ⁡(𝒯)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T}) or lies on the boundary of a single face but has multiplicity 2 there. Therefore,

OPEN#​ℰ​(𝒯)=12​∑f∈ℱ⁡(𝒯)deg⁡(f)=32​(#​ℱ​(𝒯)−1CLOSE)+12​Perim⁡(𝒯).\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})}\operatorname{deg}(f)=\frac{3}{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\#\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})-1}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}). (A.24)

Re-arranging (A.24) shows that

#​ℱ​(𝒯)=23​#​ℰ​(𝒯)+1−13​Perim⁡(𝒯).\#\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})=\frac{2}{3}\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})+1-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}). (A.25)

Plugging this into (A.23) gives

#​ℰ​(𝒯)=#​𝒱​(𝒯)+23​#​ℰ​(𝒯)+1−13​Perim⁡(𝒯),\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})=\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T})+\frac{2}{3}\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})+1-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}), (A.26)

which gives (A.22) upon re-arranging. ∎

We now define the triangulations with boundary to which we will apply Lemma A.7. For ε>0\varepsilon>0, n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N}, and y∈n​ε​ℤy\in n\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}, we let 𝒯yn,ε\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon} be the subgraph of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} induced by (y−nε,y]∩(εℤ)(y-n\varepsilon,y]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}). Then x∈𝒱​𝒯yn,εx\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon} if and only if the cell HxεH_{x}^{\varepsilon} of 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} is contained in the cell Hyn​εH_{y}^{n\varepsilon} of 𝒢n​ε\mathcal{G}^{n\varepsilon}. We also define

∂𝒯yn,ε:={x∈𝒱𝒯yn,ε:x∼x′ in 𝒢ε for some x′∉𝒱​𝒯yn,ε}.\partial\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}:\text{$x\sim x^{\prime}$ in $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ for some $x^{\prime}\notin\mathcal{V}\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}$}}}\right\}. (A.27)

Then 𝒯yn,ε\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon} is a planar triangulation with boundary.

Lemma A.8.

There are universal constants c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0 such that the following is true. Let ε>0\varepsilon>0, let n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N}, and define ∂𝒯yn,ε\partial\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon} for y∈n​ε​ℤy\in n\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z} as in (A.27). Then

ℙ[#∂𝒯yn,ε>m]≤c1e−c2m/n1/2,∀m∈ℕ.\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\#\partial\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}>m}}\right]\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}m/n^{1/2}},\quad\forall m\in\mathbbm{N}. (A.28)

We will prove Lemma A.8 using the Brownian motion representation of the mated-CRT map. For this purpose we need the following lemma.

Lemma A.9.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a standard linear Brownian motion. For n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N}, let 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} be the number of intervals [k−1,k][k-1,k] for k∈[1,n]ℤk\in[1,n]_{\mathbbm{Z}} which contain a running minimum of ℬ\mathcal{B} (relative to time 0). Then for m∈ℕm\in\mathbbm{N},

ℙ[𝒦n>m]≤c1e−c2m/n1/2\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathcal{K}_{n}>m}}\right]\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}m/n^{1/2}} (A.29)

for constants c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0.

Proof.

Let τ0=0\tau_{0}=0 and inductively let τm\tau_{m} for m∈ℕm\in\mathbbm{N} be the first time after τm−1+1\tau_{m-1}+1 at which ℬ\mathcal{B} attains a running minimum. We observe that

𝒦n≤2max{m∈ℕ:τm<n}.\mathcal{K}_{n}\leq 2\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{m\in\mathbbm{N}:\tau_{m}<n}}\right\}. (A.30)

By the strong Markov property, the increments τm−τm−1\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1} are i.i.d. By a standard Brownian motion estimate,

ℙ[τm−τm−1>t]≍t−1/2,∀t>1.\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1}>t}}\right]\asymp t^{-1/2},\quad\forall t>1. (A.31)

Therefore, for m,n∈ℕm,n\in\mathbbm{N},

ℙ[τm<n]≤ℙ[supj∈[1,m]ℤ(τj−τj−1)<n]≤(1−c0n−1/2)m≤c1e−c2m/n1/2,\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{m}<n}}\right]\leq\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sup_{j\in[1,m]_{\mathbbm{Z}}}(\tau_{j}-\tau_{j-1})<n}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-c_{0}n^{-1/2}}}\right)^{m}\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}m/n^{1/2}}, (A.32)

for universal constants c0,c1,c2c_{0},c_{1},c_{2}. Combining this with (A.30) gives (A.29) (with c2/2c_{2}/2 in place of c2c_{2}). ∎

Proof of Lemma A.8.

Recall the Brownian motion (L,R)(L,R) used to define 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon} in (1.2). From (1.2), we get that ∂𝒯yn,ε\partial\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon} is the same as the set of x∈(y−nε,y]∩(εℤ)x\in(y-n\varepsilon,y]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}) such that either

inft∈[x−ε,x]Lt=inft∈[y−n​ε,x]Ltorinft∈[x−ε,x]Lt=inft∈[x−ε,y]Lt\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,x]}L_{t}=\inf_{t\in[y-n\varepsilon,x]}L_{t}\quad\text{or}\quad\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,x]}L_{t}=\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,y]}L_{t} (A.33)

or the same is true with RR in place of LL.

By Brownian scaling and the translation invariance of the law of (L,R)(L,R), it suffices to prove (A.28) in the case when ε=1\varepsilon=1 and y=n​εy=n\varepsilon. By (A.33) and the symmetry of the law of (L,R)(L,R) under reversing time and/or swapping LL and RR, it suffices to prove that

ℙ[#{x∈[1,n]ℤ:inft∈[x−1,x]Lt=inft∈[0,x]Lt}>m]≤c1e−c2m/n1/2\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\#\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{x\in[1,n]_{\mathbbm{Z}}:\inf_{t\in[x-1,x]}L_{t}=\inf_{t\in[0,x]}L_{t}}}\right\}>m}}\right]\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}m/n^{1/2}} (A.34)

for universal constants c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0. This is precisely the content of Lemma A.9. ∎
